sections.heading: The agent–environment loop
sections.sourceHtml:
The agent–environment loop

Reinforcement learning has one loop, repeated over and over:

  1. The environment hands the agent an observation describing the current situation.
  2. The agent chooses an action.
  3. The environment applies that action, moves to a new situation, and hands back a reward (a single number saying how good that step was) plus the next observation.
  4. Repeat until the episode ends.

Nothing else in RL is more than an elaboration of this loop. The agent's only job is to learn a policy — a rule for picking actions from observations — that makes the running total of rewards as large as possible.

Generic example

In a video game, the observation might be the screen pixels, the action a joystick direction, and the reward the score delta. The agent never sees "the rules of the game" directly — it only ever sees observation → action → reward, over and over, and has to infer good behaviour from that alone.

This project

The observation is a 16-number description of the race (laps remaining, tyre compound and age, weather, whether a safety car is out); the action is one of six choices (stay out, or pit for one of five compounds); the reward is the negative lap time. Nothing about "tyre degradation" or "the pit-loss penalty" is ever told to the agent directly — it has to discover, purely from rewards, that pitting for softs late in dry weather is a bad idea.

sections.heading: The reward hypothesis
sections.sourceHtml:
The reward hypothesis

RL rests on one assumption, sometimes called the reward hypothesis: any goal you care about can be expressed as maximizing the expected cumulative sum of a scalar reward signal. This is a real design constraint, not a footnote — if you can't collapse "what we want" into a single number per step, you don't have an RL problem yet, you have a reward-design problem to solve first.

This project

This is exactly the tension Phase 1's "Reward design" section wrestles with. The obvious goal is "win the race," but the reward actually used is -lap_time on every single lap. The plan spends real effort proving that summing -lap_time over the whole race is mathematically identical to -total_race_time — with no shortcut left for the agent to exploit, like getting free reward by pitting during a safety car. You'll see this same proof step again in Phase 5's reward-shaping decisions.

sections.heading: Episodes, and episodic vs. continuing tasks
sections.sourceHtml:
Episodes, and episodic vs. continuing tasks

An episode is one complete run of the loop from a starting situation to a natural ending. Some RL tasks never end (continuing tasks — e.g., a thermostat runs forever), but most have a clear boundary, and this project does too: one episode = one full race, from lap 1 to the chequered flag. Phase 1 fixes the episode length in advance, which is a fixed-length episode. This matters later because terminated (the race genuinely finished) and truncated (we cut it off early for some other reason) are different signals in Gymnasium, and Phase 1 explicitly sets truncated = False always — there's no artificial cutoff, the episode only ends when the race does.

sections.heading: Exploration vs. exploitation
sections.sourceHtml:
Exploration vs. exploitation

At any point the agent can either exploit — take the action it currently believes is best — or explore — try something else, to find out if it's actually better. Too much exploitation and the agent gets stuck on a mediocre strategy it found early and never questions again. Too much exploration and it never settles into using what it's learned. Balancing the two is a central, recurring problem across almost every RL algorithm. Phase 1 doesn't need a resolution to it — no algorithm is trained here — but it's worth naming because it's the reason the next section (fresh-sampled stochasticity) matters as much as it does: an environment an agent can memorize gives exploration nothing real to discover.

This project

Phase 1 doesn't implement exploration itself — that's the agent's job, in Phases 3 onward — but it shapes how hard the problem is. The curriculum hook (options={"curriculum": "dry_no_sc"}) exists specifically to make early exploration easier: by restricting episodes to dry weather with no safety cars, the agent faces a smaller, less noisy version of the problem first. This is curriculum learning — start simple, increase difficulty once the easy version is solved.

sections.heading: Why stochasticity is sampled fresh, not replayed
sections.sourceHtml:
Why stochasticity is sampled fresh, not replayed

A subtler point Phase 1 is very deliberate about: safety cars are sampled from a hazard process every episode, not replayed from a fixed set of historical race templates. If only 3–4 fixed scenarios existed, and the agent's observation includes laps_remaining, the agent could simply memorize "an SC always arrives around lap 12 in scenario #2" — a lookup table dressed up as a policy, learning nothing generalizable. This failure mode has a name: reward hacking (or environment overfitting) — the agent finds a way to score well that exploits an accident of the environment's construction rather than solving the real problem.

Guarding against it is why the plan splits weather (replayed from real history, where variety is desirable) from safety cars (freshly sampled every episode, where memorization would be a bug).

sections.heading: The formal tuple
sections.sourceHtml:
The formal tuple

An MDP is defined by five things, usually written as the tuple (S, A, P, R, γ):

  • S — the state space. The set of all possible situations the agent could be in.
  • A — the action space. The set of all choices available to the agent (sometimes state-dependent, via a mask — more below).
  • P — the transition function. P(s' | s, a) — the probability of ending up in state s' given you were in state s and took action a. Encodes "how the world works."
  • R — the reward function. The scalar reward received for a transition, often written R(s, a, s').
  • γ (gamma) — the discount factor, a number in [0, 1] controlling how much the agent should value future reward relative to immediate reward.
Generic example

A robot navigating a grid. States are grid cells, actions are {up, down, left, right}, P says moving "up" succeeds 90% of the time and slips sideways 10% of the time, R is −1 per step (encouraging speed) with a bonus at the goal cell.

This project

S is the set of all possible 16-dimensional observation vectors; A is the 6 pit choices; P is compute_lap_time plus the tyre-age and weather-trace bookkeeping in step() — stochastic, since lap time includes Gaussian noise and weather/safety-car draws are random; R is -lap_time (or the terminal −500 penalty); γ = 1.0, chosen deliberately (below). Every one of these five objects has a literal, named counterpart in dynamics.py or f1_strategy_env.py — that correspondence is exactly what "Phase 1 defines the MDP" means in practice.

sections.heading: The Markov property
sections.sourceHtml:
The Markov property

The "Markov" in MDP refers to the Markov property: the future depends only on the current state, not on the history of how you got there. Formally, P(s'|s, a) must not need to know anything about states before s. This is a design requirement, not something automatically true — if it doesn't hold, the state representation is incomplete.

This project

This is precisely why Phase 1 derives tyre_age and the out-lap warmup penalty the way it does, and explicitly rejects tracking a second, separate laps_since_pit counter: tyre_age alone already determines warmup (tyre_age == 1 means out-lap), so adding a second variable would be redundant — and worse, redundant variables that can drift out of sync are a way for hidden, un-observed history to sneak back into the transition function without you noticing.

sections.heading: Policies
sections.sourceHtml:
Policies

A policy, written π, is the agent's strategy: a mapping from states to actions (deterministic) or to a probability distribution over actions (stochastic). "Solving" an MDP means finding the policy that gets the most total reward. Nothing about the policy lives in Phase 1 — Phase 1 builds the world the policy acts in — but every later phase (baseline heuristics in Phase 3, learned Q-tables in Phase 4, neural networks in Phase 5) is a different way of representing and improving a policy for this exact MDP.

Nothing about the policy lives in Phase 1 — Phase 1 builds the world the policy acts in — but every later phase (baseline heuristics in Phase 3, learned Q-tables in Phase 4, neural networks in Phase 5) is a different way of representing and improving a policy for this exact MDP.

sections.heading: Return and the discount factor
sections.sourceHtml:
Return and the discount factor

The return is the actual quantity an agent tries to maximize: the (possibly discounted) sum of all future rewards from a given point onward:

G_t = R_(t+1) + γ·R_(t+2) + γ²·R_(t+3) + γ³·R_(t+4) + ...

γ controls the trade-off between immediate and future reward. γ = 0 makes the agent totally short-sighted; γ close to 1 makes it weigh distant future rewards almost as much as immediate ones. γ strictly less than 1 is also what keeps the return finite in a continuing (never-ending) task.

This project

Phase 1 uses γ = 1.0 exactly, which looks mathematically dangerous (an unbounded sum) and isn't. Episodes are fixed-length (every race is exactly total_laps laps), so the return sum is always finite no matter what γ is. Given that, γ = 1 is not just safe but correct: with γ = 1, the return is Σ(-lap_time) over the whole race with every lap weighted equally — exactly -total_race_time. Any γ < 1 would instead make later laps count for less than earlier ones, biasing the agent toward good early-race pace at the expense of the finish, with no basis in what a race actually rewards. This is the reasoning behind the plan's comment "γ = 1.0 (fixed-length episodes; avoids late-race pace bias)."

sections.heading: Action masking
sections.sourceHtml:
Action masking

Real MDPs are sometimes written with a fixed action space for every state, with invalid actions made unattractive (e.g. reward -∞) so the agent learns to avoid them on its own. When it's known in advance which actions are invalid — as it is here — it's faster and more reliable to remove them directly. This is action masking: alongside each state, a boolean vector saying which actions are currently legal.

This project

The action mask enforces exactly the kind of hard constraints real racing regulations impose: intermediate tyres are illegal in the dry, slicks are illegal in the wet, you can't "pit" for the compound you're already on, and the two-dry-compound rule forces a pit stop once it's the only way left to satisfy it. Because both the environment and the Phase 3.5 dynamic-programming oracle must agree on exactly which actions are legal, the plan implements masking as a single shared free function (compute_action_mask in dynamics.py) that both consumers call — one place the rule can be gotten wrong, not two places that could silently disagree.

sections.heading: Worked example: one lap, two possible actions
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked example: one lap, two possible actions

Take a concrete state s and push it through P and R by hand, using illustrative but realistic constants of the shape calibration.json actually holds. This is exactly the arithmetic compute_lap_time performs — nothing here is simplified away.

State s: lap 30 of 52, fitted compound MEDIUM, tyre age 14 laps, DRY, no safety car, only MEDIUM used so far.

Constants used (illustrative):

base_pace92.000 s
compound_pace_offset[MEDIUM]0.000 s (reference compound)
compound_pace_offset[HARD]+0.550 s
MEDIUM: base_deg / cliff_age0.030 s/lap / 18 laps
fuel: consumption / sensitivity1.600 kg/lap / 0.033 s/kg
weather_compound_penalty[DRY][MEDIUM]0.000 s (matched tyre)
pit_loss (GREEN)22.000 s

Action A: STAY_OUT

Tyre age 14 is below MEDIUM's cliff_age of 18, so degradation is still in its linear phase: 0.030 × 14 = 0.420 s. With 22 laps remaining, fuel load contributes (22 × 1.600) × 0.033 = 1.162 s. Weather penalty and warmup are both zero (matched compound, tyre long past its out-lap). Called with rng=None — the exact-expectation form the DP oracle relies on — noise is omitted entirely:

lap_time = 92.000 + 0.000 + 0.420 + 1.162 + 0.000 + 0.000 = 93.582 s reward = −93.582

The next state s': lap 31, same compound, tyre_age = 15, one lap closer to the end.

Action B: PIT_HARD

The pit-lap ordering rule from the plan applies here: this lap is still run on the old tyre — MEDIUM at age 14 — so the base lap time is identical, 93.582 s. A pit-lane loss is added on top, undiscounted because there's no safety car active:

lap_time = 93.582 + pit_loss(GREEN) = 93.582 + 22.000 = 115.582 s reward = −115.582

The next state s': lap 31, compound now HARD, tyre_age = 1 (next lap is the out-lap, so its warmup penalty will apply then, not now) — and compounds_used now contains both MEDIUM and HARD, satisfying the two-compound rule for the rest of the race.

Comparing the two rewards, −93.582 vs. −115.582, is precisely the trade-off the agent must learn to weigh: pitting costs about 22 seconds right now, in exchange for fresher tyres and — critically, per the Bellman equation on page 3 — a better expected outcome over every lap that follows. A single-step comparison always favours STAY_OUT; the whole reason this is a sequential decision problem, and not a greedy one, is that the right comparison is between the two full returns, not the two immediate rewards.

sections.heading: State-value function, V
sections.sourceHtml:
State-value function, V

V^π(s) is the expected return if you start in state s and follow policy π from then on:

V^π(s) = E_π[ G_t | S_t = s ]

In plain language: "if I'm in this situation and I play according to my current strategy, how much total (discounted) reward do I expect to get from here to the end?"

This project

V^π(s) for a given race state — say, lap 30 of 52, on a 14-lap-old MEDIUM, dry — is the expected total remaining -lap_time if the current policy is followed from here on. A better policy has a higher (less negative) value in every state, because it means less total time to the finish.

sections.heading: Action-value function, Q
sections.sourceHtml:
Action-value function, Q

Q^π(s, a) is one step more specific: the expected return if you take action a right now, in state s, and then follow π for everything after:

Q^π(s, a) = E_π[ G_t | S_t = s, A_t = a ]

The difference matters in practice: V tells you how good a situation is, but doesn't by itself tell you what to do — for that you need to compare Q(s, a) across all the actions available in s and pick the best one. This is exactly why Phases 4 and 5 (Q-learning and DQN) both learn Q, not V — a table or network of Q-values directly gives you a policy for free: "pick the action with the highest Q-value in this state," subject to the action mask.

This project

Q^π(s, PIT_SOFT) at lap 30 on old mediums, versus Q^π(s, STAY_OUT) in that same state, is precisely the comparison a race engineer makes in their head when deciding whether now is the moment to pit. Learning good Q-values is learning race strategy.

sections.heading: The Bellman equations
sections.sourceHtml:
The Bellman equations

The Bellman equations are the recursive relationship that makes value functions tractable: the value of a state can be written in terms of the immediate reward plus the (discounted) value of wherever you end up next. It isn't an extra assumption bolted onto the return — it falls straight out of the definition of G_t from page 2, by peeling off the first term.

Deriving it, step by step

Start from the definition of the return, and split off the very first reward:

G_t = R_(t+1) + γ·R_(t+2) + γ²·R_(t+3) + ... = R_(t+1) + γ·( R_(t+2) + γ·R_(t+3) + ... ) = R_(t+1) + γ·G_(t+1)

The bracketed term is just G_(t+1) — the return starting one step later — factored out by γ. That's the whole trick: the return at any point is this step's reward plus γ times the return from the next state on. Now take the expectation of both sides, conditioned on being in state s and taking action a, which by definition is Q(s,a):

Q^π(s,a) = E[ R_(t+1) + γ·G_(t+1) | S_t=s, A_t=a ] = E[ R_(t+1) | s,a ] + γ·E[ G_(t+1) | s,a ]

The first term is just the expected immediate reward. The second term — the expected return from wherever you land next — is, by definition, the expected value of V^π(s') (or Q^π(s',a') under the next action) over the distribution of next states P(s'|s,a). Writing that out explicitly, and switching to the optimal policy (which always picks max_a' rather than averaging over π), gives the Bellman optimality equation:

Q*(s, a) = Σ_s' P(s'|s,a) · [ R(s,a,s') + γ · max_a' Q*(s', a') ]

Nothing here is a new axiom — it's the return's own recursive structure, made explicit. This equation is the engine behind almost everything downstream:

  • Q-learning makes a table of Q-values satisfy this equation approximately, by repeatedly nudging Q(s,a) toward R + γ·max Q(s',a') from observed transitions. (How to do that is Phase 4's job, not this page's — the point here is only that the equation itself comes from page 2's return, not from anywhere new.)
  • Dynamic programming (Phase 3.5's oracle) solves this equation exactly, working backward from the last lap of the race — because with a finite, fixed-length episode and a known transition model, the true optimal Q-values can be computed directly, no learning or sampling required.
This project

This is exactly why the plan insists compute_lap_time(rng=None) must return the exact expected lap time, not an approximation — the DP oracle needs a noise-free version of the transition model to plug directly into this equation.

It isn't an extra assumption bolted onto the return — it falls straight out of the definition of G_t from page 2, by peeling off the first term. sections.heading: Why γ = 1 doesn't break the Bellman equation here
sections.sourceHtml:
Why γ = 1 doesn't break the Bellman equation here

The γ·V(s') term is what makes value "recursive" — it lets an agent reason about consequences several steps into the future without simulating the whole future explicitly. Setting γ = 1 (page 2) simply removes the discount: future lap-time reward counts exactly as much as the current lap's. Nothing about the equation breaks, because the episode is guaranteed finite, so the recursion still bottoms out at the last lap rather than running forever.

sections.heading: Why this matters for reward scale
sections.sourceHtml:
Why this matters for reward scale

The plan's reward centring step is a direct, practical consequence of this page.

This project

With γ = 1 and roughly 52 laps at around −95 reward per lap, V^π and Q^π for a typical state are around −5,000 — the value function literally sums up all remaining rewards to the end of the episode, undiscounted. A Q-table initialized at zero, or a freshly initialized neural network centred near zero, then has to learn a value ~5,000 away from its starting point before it represents anything useful — slow, and in practice a common reason a training run "runs but doesn't learn anything."

The centring proof, worked with numbers

Claim: subtracting a fixed constant c from every step's reward shifts every policy's return by exactly the same amount, so it cannot change which policy is optimal. Take two candidate policies over the same fixed-length, T = 52-lap race, with per-lap rewards centred around, say, −93 for the better policy and −97 for the worse one (a 4-second-per-lap difference, accumulated):

Return(better) ≈ 52 × (−93) = −4,836 Return(worse) ≈ 52 × (−97) = −5,044 Difference: Return(better) − Return(worse) = 208 (better wins, by 208)

Now centre every reward by subtracting c = base_pace = 92 from each step before summing — reward_offset="base_pace" in the plan:

Return(better)_centred ≈ 52 × (−93 − (−92)) = 52 × (−1) = −52 Return(worse)_centred ≈ 52 × (−97 − (−92)) = 52 × (−5) = −260 Difference: Return(better)_centred − Return(worse)_centred = 208

The absolute numbers shrank by roughly two orders of magnitude — exactly what makes them learnable — but the difference between the two policies, 208 in both cases, is untouched. That's the whole proof: subtracting the same constant c from every one of T equal-length episodes' rewards shifts every policy's return by exactly c × T, a term that doesn't depend on which policy you're looking at, so it cancels out of every comparison between policies. The ranking — and therefore the optimal policy — is provably unchanged. This is why the plan notes it needs no potential function and isn't reward shaping in the technical sense: it's a fixed additive constant, not something that depends on the state, and info["lap_time"] is defined to always report the true, uncentred value regardless of this setting.

sections.heading: The Gymnasium API
sections.sourceHtml:
The Gymnasium API

The literal interface f1_strategy_env.py must implement — and the one nearly the whole RL ecosystem writes against.

Gymnasium (the maintained successor to OpenAI's original gym library) is the standard interface almost the entire RL ecosystem writes against. If your environment implements Gymnasium's contract correctly, every algorithm library that supports Gymnasium works with it automatically, with no per-algorithm integration code. Phase 1's whole job is to implement this contract for the F1 race MDP.

sections.heading: The Env class and its two core methods
sections.sourceHtml:
The Env class and its two core methods

class MyEnv(gym.Env):
    def reset(self, seed=None, options=None) -> tuple[obs, info]:
        """Start a new episode. Returns the first observation."""

    def step(self, action) -> tuple[obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info]:
        """Advance one step. Apply the action, return what happened."""

reset() is called once at the start of every episode — it re-randomizes whatever needs re-randomizing and returns the starting observation. step() is called once per timestep thereafter and returns exactly five things:

  • obs — the new observation after the action.
  • reward — the scalar reward for this step.
  • terminated — True if the episode ended because the task genuinely finished.
  • truncated — True if the episode ended for an external reason unrelated to the task's own logic (e.g. a step-count limit). Gymnasium deliberately splits this from terminated because algorithms compute returns differently for the two: a truncated episode still has value beyond its last step; a terminated one, by definition, does not.
  • info — a free-form dictionary for anything else worth returning that doesn't belong in the observation.
This project

reset() samples a new weather scenario and a new safety-car trace, and returns lap 1's observation. step() computes the lap time for the action taken, applies pit loss if the agent pitted, updates tyre state, and returns the next lap's observation. terminated becomes True exactly when current_lap > total_laps. truncated is always False — Phase 1 deliberately has no external time limit; a race episode only ends when the race itself ends.

sections.heading: Spaces: describing what observations and actions look like
sections.sourceHtml:
Spaces: describing what observations and actions look like

Gymnasium requires every environment to declare, up front, the shape and bounds of its observations and actions — this is what lets a generic algorithm library build a neural network with the right input/output sizes without knowing anything else about your environment.

  • spaces.Box(low, high, shape, dtype) — a (possibly multi-dimensional) array of continuous values within given bounds. Used for observations.
  • spaces.Discrete(n) — one of n distinct integer choices, 0 through n-1. Used for actions.
This project

The observation space is Box(low=0.0, high=1.0, shape=(16,)) — every one of the 16 features is normalized into [0, 1] on purpose. This uniform scaling matters in practice: neural networks train far more reliably when every input feature is on a comparable scale, rather than one feature ranging in the hundreds while another ranges in single digits. The action space is Discrete(6) — the six choices STAY_OUT through PIT_WET.

Everything above is easiest to trust once you've seen it in a working example — and the example this page uses, GridWorldEnv, is a deliberately generic one: an agent moving around a small grid toward a goal. It has nothing to do with F1, tyres, or lap times. That's the point — the Gymnasium contract is a general-purpose interface, and seeing it hold up for a completely different kind of problem is what makes clear which parts of the contract are universal (every custom environment needs them) versus which parts are specific to racing (covered starting page 5). GridWorld is also the closest thing RL teaching has to a "hello world" for writing a custom gym.Env from scratch.

The setup: a 5×5 grid, rows and columns numbered 0–4. The agent starts at the top-left corner (0, 0) and must reach the goal at the bottom-right corner (4, 4). Four actions — up, down, left, right — move it one cell at a time. Build it up one piece at a time, rather than all at once.

First, the constants and the class shell. Nothing but the action labels and the spaces Gymnasium needs declared:

import numpy as np
import gymnasium as gym
from gymnasium import spaces

UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT = 0, 1, 2, 3
GRID_SIZE = 5
MAX_STEPS = 50          # gives truncation something to do -- see below

class GridWorldEnv(gym.Env):
    metadata = {"render_modes": ["human"]}

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # obs = [row_normalized, col_normalized], both in [0, 1]
        self.observation_space = spaces.Box(low=0.0, high=1.0, shape=(2,), dtype=np.float32)
        self.action_space = spaces.Discrete(4)   # UP | DOWN | LEFT | RIGHT

Two design choices worth pausing on, because both generalize directly to the real project. First, the observation is normalized to [0, 1] rather than left as raw grid coordinates 0..4 — the same reason page 6 gives for the real environment's 16-dim vector: it keeps every input feature on a comparable scale, which matters once a neural network is reading it. Second, the position is encoded as two continuous numbers rather than one Discrete(25) state — a modelling choice, not a forced one; a tabular method (page 3) would be just as happy with the Discrete version, but a Box generalizes better to a neural network and mirrors how the real project encodes its own state as a vector of features rather than one big enumerated index.

Next, reset(). It has exactly one job: put the agent back at the start and hand back the first observation.

    def reset(self, seed=None, options=None):
        super().reset(seed=seed)
        self._row, self._col = 0, 0
        self._steps = 0
        return self._get_obs(), {}

    def _get_obs(self):
        return np.array([self._row / (GRID_SIZE - 1),
                          self._col / (GRID_SIZE - 1)], dtype=np.float32)

Pulling the observation-building into its own _get_obs() helper rather than inlining it in both reset() and step() is a small habit worth adopting early — the real F1StrategyEnv._get_obs() (page 7) exists for exactly this reason: one place that builds the vector, called from everywhere that needs one.

Now step(), movement first. Apply the action, then clamp the result to the grid so the agent can't walk off the edge:

    def step(self, action):
        assert self.action_space.contains(action)

        if action == UP:
            self._row = max(0, self._row - 1)
        elif action == DOWN:
            self._row = min(GRID_SIZE - 1, self._row + 1)
        elif action == LEFT:
            self._col = max(0, self._col - 1)
        elif action == RIGHT:
            self._col = min(GRID_SIZE - 1, self._col + 1)

Then the reward and the two ways an episode can end. Every step costs -1 — the standard way to encourage a shortest-path solution, since the return is maximized by reaching the goal in as few steps as possible. Reaching the goal terminates the episode (the task genuinely finished). Running out of steps without reaching it truncates instead — the distinction page 4's opening section named but didn't yet have a live example for:

        self._steps += 1
        at_goal = (self._row == GRID_SIZE - 1) and (self._col == GRID_SIZE - 1)

        reward = -1.0
        terminated = at_goal
        truncated = (self._steps >= MAX_STEPS) and not at_goal

        return self._get_obs(), reward, terminated, truncated, {}

That's the whole class: __init__, reset(), _get_obs(), and step(), assembled in that order under class GridWorldEnv(gym.Env):. Now run it:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    from stable_baselines3.common.env_checker import check_env
    env = GridWorldEnv()
    check_env(env)   # raises if the Gymnasium contract is violated

    obs, info = env.reset(seed=0)
    total_reward = 0.0
    print(f"start  obs={obs}")
    for t in range(MAX_STEPS):
        action = RIGHT if t % 2 == 0 else DOWN   # zig-zag toward the goal
        obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(action)
        total_reward += reward
        print(f"step {t+1:2d}  action={action}  obs={obs}  reward={reward:.1f}")
        if terminated or truncated:
            print("terminated" if terminated else "truncated")
            break
    print(f"episode return: {total_reward:.1f}")

Running it prints one line per step, the agent's position visibly approaching [1.0, 1.0] (the bottom-right corner in normalized coordinates), and a final terminated once it arrives. Change the zig-zag policy to something that never reaches the corner — say, always UP — and watch truncated fire instead once MAX_STEPS runs out, with a worse (more negative) total return, since the episode ran the full length without ever reaching the goal. That contrast is the cheapest way to actually feel why Gymnasium keeps terminated and truncated as two separate booleans rather than collapsing them into one "episode over" flag.

sections.heading: check_env: validating the contract
sections.sourceHtml:
check_env: validating the contract

Stable-Baselines3 ships a utility, check_env (used in the script above), that runs an environment through a battery of sanity checks — do reset() and step() return the right types and shapes, do observations stay within the declared bounds, does the reward come back as a plain number. Passing check_env is a necessary, not sufficient check: it verifies your environment obeys the interface, not that your physics (grid movement, or in the real project, lap times and tyre degradation) is correct.

This project

check_env is a Definition-of-Done item precisely because interface bugs (returning a float64 where float32 was declared, an observation that briefly exceeds 1.0 from a rounding edge case) are easy to introduce silently and hard to spot by eye, but check_env catches them immediately.

sections.heading: Action masking in Gymnasium
sections.sourceHtml:
Action masking in Gymnasium

Gymnasium's core spec doesn't have a first-class notion of "some actions are invalid right now" — the convention used by sb3-contrib's MaskablePPO is a separate method, action_masks(), exposed alongside step() and reset(), returning a boolean array the same length as the action space. Algorithms that support masking call this every step and exclude False actions. Algorithms that don't will happily attempt invalid actions.

GridWorld above didn't need this — walking into a wall was handled by clamping the position rather than by forbidding the action, which is a perfectly valid design choice for a grid but a poor fit once "invalid" has real consequences (page 6: pitting for the compound you're already on, running an intermediate tyre in the dry). Where clamping silently absorbs a bad action into a no-op, masking prevents the agent from taking it at all — the right choice whenever an action is invalid for a reason the agent should learn to recognize, not just a boundary to bounce off of.

This project

This is exactly why Phase 1 keeps the −500 terminal penalty in step() as a defence-in-depth backstop, in case an agent or a bug bypasses action_masks() entirely.

blocks.text: This is exactly why Phase 1 keeps the −500 terminal penalty in step() as a defence-in-depth backstop, in case an agent or a bug bypasses action_masks() entirely.

sections.heading: Building the Environment, Step by Step
sections.sourceHtml:
Building the Environment, Step by Step

The same piece-by-piece method page 4 used on GridWorld, applied to a new, race-flavoured toy — one complication added at a time, never a whole class dumped at once.

Page 4 built GridWorldEnv — a standard, domain-agnostic environment — piece by piece: constants and spaces first, then reset(), then step() split into its movement half and its reward/termination half. This page uses the same piece-by-piece method on a new, race-flavoured toy, adding one real-world complication at a time: multiple tyre compounds trading pace for life, a wear cliff, fuel burning off, weather punishing the wrong tyre, a pit stop charged to the old tyre rather than the new one, a safety car that arrives at random, and rules about which actions are even legal.

Every function and class name below is invented for this page (toy_pace, toy_wear, ToyRaceEnv, and so on) and deliberately does not match any name in dynamics.py or f1_strategy_env.py. The goal is to arrive at the same shape of solution independently, so that when you later open the real files (page 6 grounds them, page 7 reads them) you recognise the structure because you built something like it yourself.

At every stage, only the new or changed piece is shown — never the whole class again. Assemble each piece into the running script yourself as you go; typing it in rather than copy-pasting a finished block is a large part of where the understanding comes from.

sections.heading: Stage 1 — one compound, the GridWorld way
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 1 — one compound, the GridWorld way

Start from exactly the shape page 4 used: constants and spaces, then reset() with a _get_obs() helper, then step() split into two halves.

Constants and the class shell:

import numpy as np
import gymnasium as gym
from gymnasium import spaces

STAY_OUT, PIT = 0, 1
HORIZON = 10
PIT_LOSS = 2.0

class ToyRaceEnv(gym.Env):
    metadata = {"render_modes": []}

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # obs = [tyre_age_normalized] -- one feature, in [0, 1]
        self.observation_space = spaces.Box(low=0.0, high=1.0, shape=(1,), dtype=np.float32)
        self.action_space = spaces.Discrete(2)   # STAY_OUT | PIT

reset() and its _get_obs() helper — the same pattern as GridWorld, for the same reason: one place builds the observation vector, called from everywhere that needs one.

    def reset(self, seed=None, options=None):
        super().reset(seed=seed)
        self._lap = 1
        self._age = 1
        return self._get_obs(), {}

    def _get_obs(self):
        return np.array([min(self._age / HORIZON, 1.0)], dtype=np.float32)

step(), the timing half first — compute this lap's time from the current tyre age, before anything about the action changes state:

    def step(self, action):
        assert self.action_space.contains(action)
        lap_time = 1.0 + 0.05 * (self._age ** 2)   # quadratic wear
        if action == PIT:
            lap_time += PIT_LOSS

Then the bookkeeping half — apply the action, advance the lap, and return:

        if action == PIT:
            self._age = 0
        self._age += 1
        self._lap += 1

        reward = -lap_time
        terminated = self._lap > HORIZON
        info = {"lap_time": lap_time, "age": self._age}
        return self._get_obs(), reward, terminated, False, info

Assemble those four pieces under class ToyRaceEnv(gym.Env): in order, add a small if __name__ == "__main__": driver like page 4's (reset, loop step() for HORIZON laps, print each lap's reward), and run it. Everything from here modifies this skeleton.

sections.heading: Stage 2 — more than one tyre: pace vs. life
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 2 — more than one tyre: pace vs. life

Real tyres aren't interchangeable — a grippier compound is faster when fresh and wears out sooner; a harder compound is slower but lasts. Without that trade-off, "which tyre" isn't a real decision.

First, just the data and the two pure functions — no class changes yet:

# Each compound: (pace_penalty, wear_rate). A is faster but wears quicker than B.
COMPOUNDS = {
    "A": {"pace": 0.0, "wear_rate": 0.09},
    "B": {"pace": 0.6, "wear_rate": 0.03},
}

def toy_pace(compound: str) -> float:
    """Fixed pace penalty of a compound relative to the fastest one."""
    return COMPOUNDS[compound]["pace"]

def toy_wear(compound: str, age: int) -> float:
    """Quadratic wear, rate depends on which compound is fitted."""
    return COMPOUNDS[compound]["wear_rate"] * (age ** 2)

Now the three places ToyRaceEnv has to change to use them. The spaces grow by two (one-hot for which compound is fitted), and the action space grows by one (PIT_A/PIT_B instead of a single undifferentiated PIT):

STAY_OUT, PIT_A, PIT_B = 0, 1, 2

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # obs = [tyre_age_norm, compound_is_A, compound_is_B]
        self.observation_space = spaces.Box(low=0.0, high=1.0, shape=(3,), dtype=np.float32)
        self.action_space = spaces.Discrete(3)

_get_obs() needs to report which compound is fitted, alongside the age it already tracked:

    def _get_obs(self):
        onehot = [1.0, 0.0] if self._compound == "A" else [0.0, 1.0]
        return np.array([min(self._age / HORIZON, 1.0), *onehot], dtype=np.float32)

And step()'s timing half now calls the two new functions instead of a single hardcoded formula, while reset() picks a starting compound and the bookkeeping half switches on whichever PIT_* action was taken:

        lap_time = 1.0 + toy_pace(self._compound) + toy_wear(self._compound, self._age)
        ...
        if action == PIT_A:
            self._compound, self._age = "A", 0
        elif action == PIT_B:
            self._compound, self._age = "B", 0

(reset() additionally sets self._compound = "A" alongside self._age = 1.) Run it with a policy that switches to B partway through and watch the total return change — that's the same compound-choice trade-off page 2's worked example computed by hand.

sections.heading: Stage 3 — a wear cliff, capped
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 3 — a wear cliff, capped

Real degradation isn't smoothly quadratic forever — tyres are fine for a while, then fall off a cliff, then the damage plateaus. Model that as two pieces: gentle linear wear below an age threshold, a steep — but capped — penalty above it. Only toy_wear and the COMPOUNDS data change; nothing else in the class does:

COMPOUNDS = {
    "A": {"pace": 0.0, "wear_rate": 0.05, "cliff_age": 4, "cliff_severity": 0.15, "cliff_cap": 4.0},
    "B": {"pace": 0.6, "wear_rate": 0.02, "cliff_age": 7, "cliff_severity": 0.08, "cliff_cap": 4.0},
}

def toy_wear(compound: str, age: int) -> float:
    """
    Piecewise wear: linear below the cliff age, a squared-and-capped
    penalty above it. The cap matters: without one, a single very old
    tyre can produce a wear number so large it swamps every other
    signal in the reward, and every other decision stops mattering.
    """
    c = COMPOUNDS[compound]
    linear = c["wear_rate"] * age
    over = max(0, age - c["cliff_age"])

COMPOUNDS = {
    "A": {"pace": 0.0, "wear_rate": 0.05, "cliff_age": 4, "cliff_severity": 0.15, "cliff_cap": 4.0},
    "B": {"pace": 0.6, "wear_rate": 0.02, "cliff_age": 7, "cliff_severity": 0.08, "cliff_cap": 4.0},
}

def toy_wear(compound: str, age: int) -> float:
    """
    Piecewise wear: linear below the cliff age, a squared-and-capped
    penalty above it. The cap matters: without one, a single very old
    tyre can produce a wear number so large it swamps every other
    signal in the reward, and every other decision stops mattering.
    """
    c = COMPOUNDS[compound]
    linear = c["wear_rate"] * age
    over = max(0, age - c["cliff_age"])
    cliff = min(c["cliff_severity"] * (over ** 2), c["cliff_cap"])
    return linear + cliff

sections.heading: Stage 4 — fuel burning off
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 4 — fuel burning off

A car gets faster as it burns fuel over the race — a real, separate effect from tyre wear, and one that doesn't depend on which tyre is fitted at all. One new function:

def toy_fuel_penalty(laps_left: int) -> float:
    """Heavier car = slower lap. Burns off linearly as the race goes on."""
    FUEL_PER_LAP = 0.08     # kg-equivalent burned per lap, in toy units
    SENSITIVITY = 0.02      # seconds of penalty per unit of fuel remaining
    return (laps_left * FUEL_PER_LAP) * SENSITIVITY

And one line added to step()'s timing half:

        lap_time += toy_fuel_penalty(HORIZON - self._lap)

Print toy_fuel_penalty(laps_left) for laps_left = HORIZON down to 0 before wiring it in — it should shrink smoothly to exactly zero at the finish, which is the toy equivalent of the real project's fuel effect vanishing on the last lap.

sections.heading: Stage 5 — weather, and the wrong tyre for it
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 5 — weather, and the wrong tyre for it

Introduce a second axis entirely separate from tyre choice: track conditions. First, just the penalty table and its lookup function:

DRY, WET = 0, 1

# Penalty for running each compound in each condition. Large off-diagonal
# terms are the point: the wrong tyre for the weather should be costly
# enough that the agent has to actually track the weather, not ignore it.
WEATHER_PENALTY = {
    DRY: {"A": 0.0, "B": 0.0},
    WET: {"A": 6.0, "B": 5.5},   # both toy dry compounds are bad in the wet
}

def toy_weather_penalty(weather: int, compound: str) -> float:
    return WEATHER_PENALTY[weather][compound]

Then the observation grows by two more (a weather one-hot), reset() samples a weather value for the episode (held fixed for the whole toy episode to keep this stage simple — the real plan varies it lap-by-lap from a historical trace, which you don't need to reproduce to get the idea: self._weather = self.np_random.integers(0, 2)), and step()'s timing half gets one more added term:

        lap_time += toy_weather_penalty(self._weather, self._compound)

Run one episode with self._weather forced to WET and watch every lap get visibly slower regardless of which compound is fitted — that's the mismatch penalty doing its job.

sections.heading: Stage 6 — the pit-lap ordering rule
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 6 — the pit-lap ordering rule

This is the subtlest stage, and the easiest one to get backward by accident. A pit stop happens at the end of a lap: the driver completes the whole lap on the old tyre, then peels into the pits. So the lap just driven should be timed on the old compound at its old age, and only the next lap should reflect the new tyre — including a fresh out-lap warmup penalty for being cold.

First, the warmup function on its own:

def toy_warmup(age: int) -> float:
    """Cold-tyre penalty: full on the out-lap, half the next lap, gone after."""
    if age <= 1:
        return 1.2
    if age == 2:
        return 0.5
    return 0.0

Then the timing half of step(), now complete — every term so far, all evaluated against the state before any pit stop is applied:

        lap_time = (1.0
                    + toy_pace(self._compound)
                    + toy_wear(self._compound, self._age)
                    + toy_fuel_penalty(HORIZON - self._lap)
                    + toy_weather_penalty(self._weather, self._compound)
                    + toy_warmup(self._age))
        if action != STAY_OUT:
            lap_time += PIT_LOSS

And only now, the bookkeeping half — the pit stop takes effect strictly after lap_time above has already been computed:

        if action == PIT_A:
            self._compound, self._age = "A", 0
        elif action == PIT_B:
            self._compound, self._age = "B", 0
        self._age += 1
        self._lap += 1

Try writing it the wrong way round — switch the compound before computing lap_time — and watch what happens to a pit lap's cost: it drops, because the pit lap would then get the new tyre's fresh pace and dodge the old tyre's wear and dodge the out-lap warmup, all at once, while also paying pit loss. Comparing the two versions side by side is the fastest way to feel why this ordering is a real bug class, not a stylistic preference.

sections.heading: Stage 7 — a safety car that isn't scripted
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 7 — a safety car that isn't scripted

So far every episode with the same starting conditions plays out identically except for the agent's own choices. Add something genuinely random. First, the sampler on its own, completely separate from the environment class:

HAZARD_PER_LAP = 0.06     # chance any given green lap starts a safety car
SC_DURATION_MEAN = 3
SC_PIT_DISCOUNT = 0.4     # pitting under SC costs this fraction of the normal loss

def sample_sc_trace(horizon: int, rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Independently, each green lap has a HAZARD_PER_LAP chance of starting
    a safety car that then runs for a random duration. Sampled fresh every
    call -- two episodes should very rarely have the SC on the same laps.
    """
    trace = np.zeros(horizon, dtype=bool)
    lap = 0
    while lap < horizon:
        if not trace[lap] and rng.random() < HAZARD_PER_LAP:
            duration = max(1, int(rng.normal(SC_DURATION_MEAN, 1)))
            trace[lap:lap + duration] = True
            lap += duration
        else:
            lap += 1
    return trace

Before touching the environment, call this on its own five times with different seeds and print the resulting trace each time — confirm the safety car really does land on different laps almost every call. Only once that's visibly true does it earn a place in reset():

        self._sc_trace = sample_sc_trace(HORIZON, self.np_random)

Then step() gets one new branch at the very top, before any of Stage 6's terms:

        if self._sc_trace[self._lap - 1]:
            lap_time = 8.0   # fixed, slow flag-lap time -- no term above applies
            if action != STAY_OUT:
                lap_time += PIT_LOSS * SC_PIT_DISCOUNT
        else:
            lap_time = (1.0 + toy_pace(...) + ...)   # Stage 6's full formula
            if action != STAY_OUT:
                lap_time += PIT_LOSS

The point of sampling fresh every episode rather than reusing one fixed trace: an agent that could memorise "the SC always comes on lap 6" would learn a lookup table, not a strategy.

sections.heading: Stage 8 — action masking
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 8 — action masking

Not every action is legal in every situation. Build the mask function up rule by rule rather than all at once. First, just the "can't repeat the current compound" rule:

def toy_action_mask(compound, weather, laps_left, compounds_used) -> np.ndarray:
    mask = np.array([True, True, True])   # STAY_OUT, PIT_A, PIT_B
    if compound == "A":
        mask[PIT_A] = False
    else:
        mask[PIT_B] = False
    return mask

Then add the weather rule — suppose B is unsafe in the wet in this toy world:

    if weather == WET:
        mask[PIT_B] = False

Then the "must use both compounds eventually" rule:

    if len(compounds_used) < 2 and laps_left <= 1:
        mask[STAY_OUT] = False

And finally a safety net, so the function never returns "nothing is legal":

    if not mask.any():
        mask[STAY_OUT] = True
    return mask

Wire this up as an action_masks() method exactly like page 4's toy did, but this time it actually forbids things. Try running a random policy (env.action_space.sample()) with and without respecting the mask, and compare how often each version ends the toy race having never used compound B — that's the concrete difference masking makes.

sections.heading: Stage 9 — centring the reward
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 9 — centring the reward

With enough laps and consistently negative per-lap rewards, the total return can get large in magnitude (page 3 covers why that's a learning-speed problem). The fix doesn't need to live inside the environment's core logic — wrap it:

class RewardCentringWrapper(gym.Wrapper):
    """Subtracts a fixed constant from every step's reward. Does not change
    which policy is optimal (page 3's proof) -- only the scale of the numbers."""
    def __init__(self, env, offset: float):
        super().__init__(env)
        self.offset = offset

    def step(self, action):
        obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = self.env.step(action)
        info["true_reward"] = reward          # keep the real number available
        return obs, reward + self.offset, terminated, truncated, info

env = RewardCentringWrapper(ToyRaceEnv(), offset=1.5) shifts every episode's return by the same fixed amount without touching the environment's own code at all — a clean illustration of an important general pattern: a transformation that changes training signal without changing the environment's actual physics belongs in a wrapper, not baked into step().

sections.heading: Stage 10 — what you've built
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 10 — what you've built

Stages 1 through 9, assembled, form a small but complete environment with the same shape as a real pit-strategy MDP: multiple compounds trading pace for life, a capped wear cliff, fuel burn-off, weather mismatch, correctly-ordered pit stops with warmup, a freshly-sampled safety car with a discounted pit, action masking, and an optional reward-centring wrapper. Nothing about the numbers, the exact function names, or the file organisation matches the real project — and it shouldn't. The value of this stage isn't a finished script sitting in front of you; it's that every piece of it passed through your own hands, in an order where each new complication made sense on its own before the next one was added.

That's the preparation page 6 assumes. It won't repeat any of the code above — instead it names which piece of the real dynamics.py and f1_strategy_env.py corresponds to which stage here, so you can go read the real files already knowing what each part is for.

sections.heading: The state space, S
sections.sourceHtml:
The state space, S

The observation is a 16-dimensional vector, entirely in [0, 1]:

IndexFeatureEncoding
0Laps remainingNormalized fraction of the race left
1–5Tyre compoundOne-hot: SOFT, MEDIUM, HARD, INTERMEDIATE, WET
6Tyre ageNormalized (capped at an assumed max age of 50 laps)
7–9Weather regimeOne-hot: DRY, DAMP, WET
10Track temperatureRescaled from a 15–65 °C range
11Safety car activeBinary
12–14Compounds usedBitmask over SOFT/MEDIUM/HARD
15Mandatory pit neededBinary — derived from 12–14 and the two-compound rule

Every feature here is either directly observable in a real race broadcast or trivially derivable from it — a deliberate modelling choice: the agent gets exactly the information a strategist actually has, no more (it never sees the exact calibration constants) and no less.

sections.heading: The transition function, P
sections.sourceHtml:
The transition function, P

dynamics.py is where P lives, and by the time you're reading it, none of its shape should be a surprise — page 5 built exactly this transition function, term by term, in a toy of your own: a pace term per compound, a degradation term with a cliff, a fuel term, a weather-mismatch term, a warmup term, all summed into one lap time, with an explicit escape hatch for a fixed, calibrated time on safety-car and VSC laps where nobody's choices affect the outcome. What's different in the real file is only scale and precision — real calibrated constants instead of illustrative ones, five real compounds instead of a toy's two or three, a proper weather-mismatch table instead of a single penalty — not structure. If any piece of that composition feels unfamiliar, that's the signal to go back to page 5 and build the missing piece as a toy before reading the real file.

The tyre-age, weather-regime, and compounds-used bookkeeping that turns one state into the next lives in F1StrategyEnv.step(), and it embeds the same ordering rule page 5's pit-stop stage built by hand: a pit stop is charged against the lap you're currently finishing, on the tyre you started that lap on — the new tyre (and its warmup penalty) only takes effect from the next lap. Getting this order backward would let a pit stop simultaneously avoid a lap of degradation, dodge the warmup penalty, and gain fresh-tyre pace — three unearned advantages stacked on the exact lap where the model should be charging the agent the most, not the least.

Two further pieces of P are stochastic and sampled independently at every reset(): weather (ScenarioLoader, from real historical race traces) and safety cars (SafetyCarSampler, drawn fresh from a calibrated hazard rate every episode, deliberately not replayed from history — see page 1's note on reward hacking, and page 5's own hazard-sampling stage for why "fresh every episode" has to be true in code, not just in principle).

sections.heading: The reward function, R
sections.sourceHtml:
The reward function, R

R = -lap_time on every single lap, safety cars included, plus a -500 terminal backstop if the race ends without the mandatory two-dry-compound rule satisfied (structurally unreachable in normal play — see the mask section below). An optional reward_offset setting subtracts a constant (base_pace) from every step for numerical reasons (page 3) without changing which policy is optimal; info["lap_time"] always reports the true, uncentred value regardless of this setting.

sections.heading: The discount factor, γ
sections.sourceHtml:
The discount factor, γ

sections.heading: The action mask
sections.sourceHtml:
The action mask

compute_action_mask encodes five rules as a single boolean array, shared verbatim between the environment and the Phase 3.5 DP oracle:

  1. Slick compounds (SOFT/MEDIUM/HARD) are only legal in DRY or DAMP.
  2. INTERMEDIATE is only legal in DAMP or WET.
  3. WET is only legal in WET.
  4. You cannot "pit" for the compound you're already on.
  5. STAY_OUT is forced off if the two-compound rule isn't yet satisfied and only 2 laps remain — unless the race has been declared wet, which voids the rule entirely (the real regulation).

Rule 5 is why the -500 terminal penalty above should never actually fire during ordinary play: the mask makes the violation it punishes structurally impossible for any agent that respects action_masks(). The penalty exists purely as a backstop for consumers that bypass masking, and the Phase 1 test suite treats "the penalty never fires in normal play" as a success condition, not a gap in test coverage.

sections.heading: Worked example: a complete step() call
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked example: a complete step() call

Page 2 hand-computed the lap-time arithmetic for one decision. Here's the same decision — PIT_HARD, lap 30 of 52, on a 14-lap-old MEDIUM, DRY, track temperature 42°C, only MEDIUM used so far — carried all the way through step(): the full 16-dim observation before and after, and the info dict returned alongside it. This is every idea on this page, in one trace.

Observation before the call (laps_remaining = (52−30+1)/52, tyre age 14 → 14/50, track temp (42−15)/50, only MEDIUM used so the two-compound rule isn't met yet):

IndexMeaningValue
0laps_remaining0.4423
1–5compound one-hot (S,M,H,I,W)0, 1, 0, 0, 0
6tyre_age norm0.2800
7–9weather one-hot (DRY,DAMP,WET)1, 0, 0
10track_temp norm0.5400
11safety_car_active0
12–14compounds_used (S,M,H)0, 1, 0
15mandatory_pit_needed1.0

Call: obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(PIT_HARD)

Inside step(), in order: the lap is timed on the tyre that was fitted coming into it — MEDIUM, age 14 — giving 93.582 s exactly as on page 2; pit loss is added since the action isn't STAY_OUT (+22.000 s, GREEN flag, total 115.582 s); then the compound switches to HARD and tyre_age resets, effective from next lap; the lap counter advances to 31; terminated stays False (31 ≤ 52).

Observation after the call — HARD is now active, its age is 1 (this coming lap is HARD's out-lap), both dry compounds have now been used so the mandatory-pit flag clears:

IndexMeaningValue
0laps_remaining0.4231
1–5compound one-hot (S,M,H,I,W)0, 0, 1, 0, 0
6tyre_age norm0.0200
7–9weather one-hot (DRY,DAMP,WET)1, 0, 0
10track_temp norm0.5400
11safety_car_active0
12–14compounds_used (S,M,H)0, 1, 1
15mandatory_pit_needed0.0

Returned alongside it: reward = -115.582, terminated = False, truncated = False, and an info dictionary — the plan's public contract, described here rather than reproduced, since it's a specification other phases depend on, not something to copy-paste:

KeyValue this callNote
lap31the lap just started, not the one just finished
compound"HARD"the newly fitted tyre
tire_age1HARD's out-lap is next
compounds_used["MEDIUM","HARD"]both dry compounds now used
two_compound_rule_metTruethe mandatory-pit condition has cleared
track_status0 (GREEN)authoritative flag state
pit_laps[30]history of pit stops so far
lap_time115.582true, uncentred, regardless of reward_offset
pit_doneTruethis lap included a pit stop
lap_time_compound"MEDIUM"the old tyre this lap was actually run on — not HARD
lap_time_tyre_age14the old tyre's age when that lap was timed
action_masks(recomputed)legal actions for lap 31, not for the lap the action was chosen in

Two entries are worth noticing precisely because they're easy to get backward: lap_time_compound is MEDIUM, not HARD — it records what the just-completed lap was actually run on, which is the old tyre, per the ordering rule above. And action_masks describes what's legal next (lap 31, on HARD), not what was legal when the action was chosen — a consumer reading this for the state the action was taken in is reading the wrong lap's mask.

sections.heading: Why one shared implementation matters more here than usual
sections.sourceHtml:
Why one shared implementation matters more here than usual

Nothing above is unusual RL design in isolation — every piece has a name and a textbook description on pages 1–5. What is specific to this project is the insistence that P and the action mask exist in exactly one place (dynamics.py), called identically by the environment, the baselines, and the DP oracle. A DP oracle that computes optimal Q-values against a subtly different transition function than the one agents actually train against produces numbers that look authoritative and are simply wrong — and because both implementations would look individually correct, this class of bug is close to invisible without the "single implementation, multiple callers" discipline the plan insists on.

sections.heading: dynamics.py — pure functions only, and why
sections.sourceHtml:
dynamics.py — pure functions only, and why

Every function in this file takes its inputs explicitly (compound, tyre_age, params, ...) and returns a value with no side effects and no reference to any class state. This is a deliberate constraint, not an accident of style: three different consumers — the live environment, human-written baseline strategies, and the Phase 3.5 dynamic-programming oracle — all need to call the same physics with different inputs at different times. A pure function is trivially safe to share: call it with the same arguments from anywhere, get the same answer, no hidden state to keep synchronized. A method on a stateful class would tie the physics to one particular environment instance, making it awkward or unsafe for the DP oracle — which needs to evaluate lap times for hypothetical states the live environment was never actually in — to reuse.

Reading order within the file, and what each function is for:

  • compound_pace_offset — the fixed, compound-level pace difference. What makes compound choice a real decision rather than noise.
  • tyre_degradation — piecewise: linear up to cliff_age, then a capped quadratic beyond it. The cap (cliff_cap) is as important as the cliff shape — an earlier, uncapped version let one very old tyre's degradation swamp every other signal in the reward.
  • out_lap_warmup — derived entirely from tyre_age (no second counter), decaying from full penalty at tyre_age == 1 to zero by tyre_age == 3.
  • fuel_effect — linear in laps_remaining; the car gets faster as the race burns fuel.
  • weather_compound_penalty — a lookup table keyed by (weather, compound): the physical cost of running the wrong tyre for the conditions.
  • compute_lap_time — composes all of the above, with an explicit branch for safety car / VSC laps and an rng parameter that, when None, returns the exact expected lap time rather than a sampled one — required by the DP oracle.
  • compute_pit_loss — the time cost of a pit stop, discounted under SC/VSC because the whole field is circulating slowly anyway.
  • compute_action_mask — the five-rule mask from page 6, as one shared function.

sections.heading: f1_strategy_env.py — the stateful Gymnasium wrapper
sections.sourceHtml:
f1_strategy_env.py — the stateful Gymnasium wrapper

The class holds exactly the state a race actually has — current lap, fitted compound, tyre age, which compounds have been used, the sampled weather scenario and safety-car trace for this episode — and every method is a thin layer that reads that state, calls into dynamics.py for any actual physics, and writes the result back.

  • __init__ — loads calibration.json, builds observation_space (Box(16,)) and action_space (Discrete(6)). No episode state is created here — that's reset()'s job.
  • reset() — samples a new weather scenario and safety-car trace independently, sets tyre_age = 1 for the starting tyre (lap 1 is the out-lap — cars start on tyres fitted on the grid), and honours options={"starting_compound": ...} and the curriculum hook.
  • step() — the order-of-operations rule from page 6 lives here: compute this lap's time on the current (old) tyre first, add pit loss if pitting, then switch the fitted compound and reset tyre_age to 0.
  • _get_obs() — assembles the 16-dim vector from current state, and asserts both the shape and the [0, 1] bounds every single call, not just in tests — a cheap habit that catches a normalization bug the moment it's introduced.
  • action_masks() — delegates to dynamics.compute_action_mask; deliberately does not reimplement any rule locally.
  • _get_info() — returns the public contract dictionary. info.get(...) in Python returns None rather than raising when a key is missing, so a renamed key breaks every downstream phase silently, with no exception to point at the bug. Adding new keys is always safe; renaming or removing one is a breaking change.

sections.heading: What "≥10 tests" in test_env.py are actually checking
sections.sourceHtml:
What "≥10 tests" in test_env.py are actually checking

The test list in the plan isn't an arbitrary coverage quota — each test targets one specific way the implementation could plausibly go wrong, most tied directly to a design decision covered on this page or page 6:

  • test_return_equals_negative_race_time — the core identity from page 3 (return = −total race time) actually holds in code, not just on paper.
  • test_pit_lap_runs_on_old_tyre — the pit-lap ordering rule above wasn't silently inverted.
  • test_sc_timing_is_not_memorizable — safety cars are genuinely re-sampled per episode, not accidentally replayed (page 1's reward-hacking concern).
  • test_cliff_is_capped — the degradation cap actually caps, rather than only capping the quadratic term while some other path still lets values blow up.
  • test_action_mask_forces_pit_near_end / test_two_compound_rule_violation_penalty — the mask and the backstop penalty each do their half of the two-compound rule correctly.

Reading the test file alongside the implementation file is, in effect, reading a list of "here is every way an earlier draft of this plan was found to be wrong" — worth treating as required reading, not optional verification.

sections.heading: Glossary
sections.sourceHtml:
Glossary

Every term used across pages 1–7 — nothing beyond them. Keep this open while reading the Phase 1 plan or the code.

Scope note

Terms belonging to algorithm training (Q-learning's tabular update rule, DQN, PPO, replay buffers, and the rest) aren't listed here because they aren't covered by this doc set; that material starts once Phase 1 is done and a later phase's prerequisites take over.

Action
A choice available to the agent at a given step. Here, one of six: stay out, or pit for SOFT/MEDIUM/HARD/INTERMEDIATE/WET.
Action masking
Restricting which actions are legal in a given state, provided as a boolean array alongside the observation, so the agent never has to learn illegal-action avoidance purely from trial and error.
Agent
The decision-maker in the RL loop; the thing being trained. Not implemented in Phase 1 — Phase 1 builds the world the agent will act in.
Bellman equation
The recursive relationship expressing a state's (or state-action pair's) value in terms of immediate reward plus the discounted value of what follows; derived from the return's own definition on page 3.
Curriculum learning
Training on an easier version of a task first, then increasing difficulty once the easier version is solved. This project's dry_no_sc curriculum hook is an instance of this.
Discount factor (γ)
A number in [0, 1] controlling how much future reward counts relative to immediate reward. This project uses γ = 1.0 — see pages 2 & 3.
Environment
The world the agent interacts with; here, F1StrategyEnv, implementing the Gymnasium Env contract.
Episode
One complete run of the agent–environment loop from start to a natural end; here, one full race.
Exploration vs. exploitation
The trade-off between trying new actions to learn more (exploration) and using the best-known action so far (exploitation). Named on page 1; resolving it is an agent's job in a later phase, not Phase 1's.
Gymnasium
The standard Python API for RL environments (reset, step, spaces), successor to OpenAI Gym. See page 4.
Markov property
The requirement that the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on any earlier history. See page 2.
MDP
Markov Decision Process — the formal tuple (S, A, P, R, γ) defining a sequential decision problem. See pages 2 & 5.
Observation
What the agent actually sees each step. Here, the 16-dimensional normalized vector.
Policy (π)
A mapping from states to actions (or to a distribution over actions); the agent's strategy. Not implemented in Phase 1.
Q-learning
Mentioned only as the algorithm whose update rule the Bellman equation (page 3) makes possible: repeatedly nudging a table of estimated Q-values toward R + γ·max Q(s',a') from observed transitions. Not implemented in Phase 1 — how to do the nudging is a later phase's prerequisite, not this doc set's.
Q-value / action-value function (Q)
The expected return from taking a specific action in a specific state, then following a policy thereafter. See page 3.
Return (G)
The (possibly discounted) sum of future rewards from a given point onward; what the agent is actually trying to maximize.
Reward
The scalar feedback signal received after each step. Here, -lap_time.
Reward hacking
An agent finding a way to score well by exploiting an accident of the environment's construction rather than solving the intended problem. This project's fresh-sampled safety cars exist specifically to prevent one instance of this. See page 1.
Reward hypothesis
The assumption underlying all of RL: any goal can be expressed as maximizing the expected cumulative sum of a scalar reward. See page 1.
State
The underlying situation the environment is in. In this project the full state is observable, so state and observation coincide.
Transition function (P)
The (possibly stochastic) rule for how the environment moves from one state to the next given an action. Here, compute_lap_time plus the episode bookkeeping in step().
Value function (V)
The expected return from a given state onward, following a given policy. See page 3.

sections.heading: Why this project is an RL problem at all
sections.sourceHtml:
Why this project is an RL problem at all

An F1 race strategist makes a sequence of decisions — stay out, or pit for a given tyre — under uncertainty (weather, safety cars, rivals) with a single, measurable goal: minimize total race time. That is exactly the shape of problem reinforcement learning is built for: an agent that repeatedly observes a state, picks an action, and receives a reward, with the goal of maximizing total reward over time. Supervised learning has no answer to "what should I do next, given that today's action changes tomorrow's options" — that sequential, consequence-carrying structure is what makes this an RL problem and not a classification problem.

This exists because Phase 1 is "the intellectual heart of the project" — it defines the simulator every future agent trains inside. A mistake here (a wrong reward, a leaky observation, a masking bug) silently corrupts every phase that follows.

Scope, precisely

Phase 1 builds an environment. It does not train an agent — no Q-learning, no neural networks, no policies. So this doc set teaches exactly two things in depth: the math that defines what an environment is (an MDP), and the software contract (Gymnasium) that f1_strategy_env.py must implement. Everything below is in service of one or the other. Algorithm training (Phases 4, 5, 9) is a different set of prerequisites for a different day — nothing about it is covered here, even in preview.
sections.text: Why this project is an RL problem at all An F1 race strategist makes a sequence of decisions — stay out, or pit for a given tyre — under uncertainty (weather, safety cars, rivals) with a single, measurable goal: minimize total race time. That is exactly the shape of problem reinforcement learning is built for: an agent that repeatedly observes a state, picks an action, and receives a reward, with the goal of maximizing total reward over time. Supervised learning has no answer to "what should I do next, given that today's action changes tomorrow's options" — that sequential, consequence-carrying structure is what makes this an RL problem and not a classification problem. This exists because Phase 1 is "the intellectual heart of the project" — it defines the simulator every future agent trains inside. A mistake here (a wrong reward, a leaky observation, a masking bug) silently corrupts every phase that follows. Scope, precisely Phase 1 builds an environment. It does not train an agent — no Q-learning, no neural networks, no policies. sections.heading: How this folder teaches the implementation half
sections.sourceHtml:
How this folder teaches the implementation half

Nowhere in pages 1–7 is the real project's code reproduced. Instead, page 5 has you build a sequence of small, runnable toy environments under your own names, each adding one real-world complication a plain toy ignores — multiple tyre compounds, a capped wear cliff, fuel burn-off, weather mismatch, correctly-ordered pit stops, a randomly-sampled safety car, action masking, reward centring — until the toy's shape converges on what the real environment needs, without ever looking like the real environment's actual code. Only after that does page 6 name which piece of the real dynamics.py and f1_strategy_env.py corresponds to which toy stage — grounding, not transcription.

sections.heading: Two ways to solve an MDP
sections.sourceHtml:
Two ways to solve an MDP

Page 1 of the Phase 1 prerequisites established the RL loop: an agent observes a state, acts, receives a reward, and repeats — learning, over many such interactions, which actions tend to pay off. That framing quietly assumes the agent does not know the transition function or reward function in advance; it has to find out by trying things and observing what happens. Every algorithm downstream of Phase 1 in this project's plan — Q-learning, SARSA, DQN, PPO — is built around that assumption. They are all model-free methods: they never see P(s'|s,a) written down anywhere. They infer good behaviour from samples.

But this project's MDP isn't actually unknown. dynamics.py is the transition function, in closed form, and the reward is simply -lap_time. Nothing about how a lap plays out is hidden from the person who wrote the simulator. When the model is fully known like this, a different family of methods becomes available: planning — compute the optimal policy directly from the model, with no trial and error, no exploration, and no sampling error. Dynamic programming is the classic planning method, and it's what Phase 3.5 builds.

Learning (Phases 4, 5, 9)Planning (Phase 3.5)
Needs the model?No — learns from sampled (s,a,r,s') transitionsYes — needs P and R written down explicitly
Exploration?Yes — epsilon-greedy, has to try things to find out what's goodNone — every consequence is already computable
Answer qualityApproximate, improves with more trainingExact, for the model as written
What can go wrongSlow convergence, reward hacking, unstable trainingOnly: the model itself is wrong, or the state space is too large to enumerate
This project

Because Phase 3.5's oracle uses the exact same dynamics.compute_lap_time function the live environment and every learning agent train against, its answer isn't a competing model of the world — it's the provably best possible play within the world the agents already live in. That's what makes "optimality gap" a meaningful number rather than a comparison between two different simulators.

sections.heading: Why "exact" is possible here at all
sections.sourceHtml:
Why "exact" is possible here at all

Solving an MDP exactly by exhaustively considering every state is, in general, hopeless — most interesting MDPs have astronomically large or continuous state spaces (imagine trying to enumerate every possible pixel-frame of an Atari game). Exact solving is a size argument, not a different kind of intelligence: it works exactly when the number of distinct situations the agent can be in is small enough to fit in memory and iterate over in reasonable time.

This project's single-car race state is unusually small for a reason worth naming explicitly: every feature in it was chosen, back in Phase 1, to be a compact, discretizable summary — lap number, which of five compounds is fitted, tyre age in laps, a three-bit used-compound mask, whether a safety car is active, which of three weather regimes is in effect. None of that is an accident of convenience; it's the direct payoff of Phase 1's insistence on a minimal, disciplined state (page 2 of the Phase 1 prerequisites' "sufficient statistic" argument). A state design bloated with continuous, high-precision features would have made this phase impossible.

This project

Multiplying out lap × compound × tyre_age × used_mask × sc_active × weather gives roughly 55 × 5 × 55 × 8 × 2 × 3 ≈ 363,000 states, times 6 actions. A modern laptop can fill a value table of that size, for every lap of a race, in well under a second using NumPy array operations — page 2 works through exactly why. Most of those 363,000 combinations are actually unreachable (a tyre can't be older than the number of laps run so far, and the used-mask is implied by which compounds could plausibly have been fitted) — a reachability pass typically cuts the real work by another 5–10×.

sections.heading: What planning buys that learning can't
sections.sourceHtml:
What planning buys that learning can't

The headline reason this phase exists is evaluation. "My RL agent beat the rule-based baseline I also wrote" is a comparison against a strawman of your own construction — the baseline's weaknesses are exactly the weaknesses you happened to think of. "My RL agent came within 0.4 seconds of the provably optimal strategy, and here's exactly where the remaining time is lost" is a claim about the ceiling of the problem itself, independent of anyone's cleverness in writing rules.

There's a second, quieter benefit: an exact solver is also the strongest possible test of the simulator. If backward induction — which cannot make a mistake, only report the true optimum of the model as written — discovers a policy that saves an implausible amount of time, that isn't a strategic insight. It's a bug in dynamics.py, found before an RL agent spent three days learning to exploit it and getting blamed for "not really understanding strategy." Page 6 returns to this as the single highest-value test in the whole DP oracle test suite.

One discipline to hold onto now

The oracle computes an answer; it must never teach one. Training an RL agent to imitate the DP policy's actions is a legitimate technique in its own right (imitation learning), but it is a different project from what Phases 4, 5, and 9 are trying to demonstrate — that an agent can discover good strategy from experience, without being shown the answer first. The oracle's role for the rest of this project is strictly evaluator, never teacher.

"My RL agent beat the rule-based baseline I also wrote" is a comparison against a strawman of your own construction — the baseline's weaknesses are exactly the weaknesses you happened to think of. "My RL agent came within 0.4 seconds of the provably optimal strategy, and here's exactly where the remaining time is lost" is a claim about the ceiling of the problem itself, independent of anyone's cleverness in writing rules.

If backward induction — which cannot make a mistake, only report the true optimum of the model as written — discovers a policy that saves an implausible amount of time, that isn't a strategic insight. It's a bug in dynamics.py, found before an RL agent spent three days learning to exploit it and getting blamed for "not really understanding strategy." sections.heading: Backward Induction
sections.sourceHtml:
Backward Induction

The last decision in a race is always the easiest one to get right — because nothing comes after it. Backward induction is just that observation, applied one lap at a time, from the end of the race to the start.

sections.heading: Starting from a Bellman equation you already have
sections.sourceHtml:
Starting from a Bellman equation you already have

Phase 1 page 3 derived the Bellman optimality equation from first principles, by peeling the first reward off the return:

Q*(s, a) = Σ_s' P(s'|s,a) · [ R(s,a,s') + γ · max_a' Q*(s', a') ]

That page noted the equation admits two very different uses: Q-learning nudges a table toward satisfying it approximately, from sampled experience. Dynamic programming — this page — solves it directly, because for this project the right-hand side is fully computable: P and R are dynamics.py, not a mystery to be inferred.

The obstacle to just "solving" this equation directly is that it's circular — Q*(s,a) on the left depends on Q*(s',a') for other states on the right, which in turn depend on further states, and so on. In the general, infinite-horizon case, breaking that circularity requires iterating the whole equation repeatedly until the values stop changing (value iteration — see the aside below). A race doesn't need that trick, because it has something most MDPs in a textbook don't: a hard, known ending.
