sections.heading: The horizon breaks the circularity
sections.sourceHtml:
The horizon breaks the circularity

A race is exactly T laps long. After lap T, there is no lap T+1 — nothing to be uncertain about, and nothing left to optimize. That single fact turns the equation from circular into a straight-line recursion, computable in one backward pass:

V_(T+1)(s) = 0 (terminal condition — nothing follows the last lap) for t = T down to 1: for every state s reachable at lap t: V_t(s) = min_a [ cost(s, a) + E_s'[ V_(t+1)(s') ] ] π*_t(s) = argmin_a [ ... ] (the action achieving that minimum)

(This project's reward is -lap_time, so the oracle works in cost — minimizing total lap time — rather than maximizing reward. The two are the same optimization with a sign flip; page 6 makes the convention explicit for the real code.)

Read it lap by lap: V_t(s), "the best possible total cost from lap t to the finish, starting in state s and playing optimally," is computable the instant V_(t+1) is fully known for every state — because every term on the right-hand side only refers to t+1, never back to t itself. Start at the last lap, where V_(T+1)=0 makes the recursion trivial to evaluate, and each earlier lap becomes solvable in turn, using only work already finished. By the time the pass reaches lap 1, V_1(s_0) is the exact optimal expected cost of the entire race from the start — computed without ever having simulated one.

Why this is dynamic programming, not just algebra

The name "dynamic programming" refers to two properties this recursion exploits. Optimal substructure: the optimal plan from lap t onward is built from the optimal plan from lap t+1 onward — you never have to reconsider a later decision once its value is known. Overlapping subproblems: many different paths through the race arrive at the same (lap, tyre_age, compound, ...) state, and V_t(s) is computed for that state exactly once, then reused by every path that reaches it — the table is the memoization. Skip the table and recompute from scratch for every path, and the same tractable problem becomes exponential.

sections.heading: Worked example: when does pitting actually pay off?
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked example: when does pitting actually pay off?

A tiny 4-lap toy race, one tyre, one decision each lap: STAY or PIT. Deterministic — no safety cars or weather yet, that's page 3's job. Lap time grows with tyre age; pitting resets age to 1 but costs a fixed penalty charged to the lap you pit on:

lap_time(age) = 10 + 3·(age − 1) (age is laps since this tyre was fitted, starting at 1) pit_loss = 6 cost(age, STAY) = lap_time(age), next age = age + 1 cost(age, PIT) = lap_time(age) + pit_loss, next age = 1 race starts lap 1 with age = 1 (fresh tyre from the grid)

Fill the value table backward, one lap at a time. Lap 4 (the last lap): with V_5 = 0, pitting only adds +6 for no benefit — the last lap never justifies a pit stop, because there is no lap 5 left to recoup the cost on. So π*_4 = STAY for every age, and V_4(age) = lap_time(age):

ageV_4(age)π*_4
110.0STAY
213.0STAY
316.0STAY
419.0STAY

Lap 3 — now there's exactly one lap left afterward, so pitting can start to pay for itself. For age = 3: STAY costs 16 + V_4(4) = 16 + 19 = 35; PIT costs 16 + 6 + V_4(1) = 22 + 10 = 32. Pitting wins, by 3 — the extra 6 spent now buys a fresh tyre worth 9 less on lap 4 than the badly worn one would have been:

ageSTAY totalPIT totalV_3(age)π*_3
110 + V_4(2) = 2316 + V_4(1) = 2623.0STAY
213 + V_4(3) = 2919 + V_4(1) = 2929.0STAY (tie)
316 + V_4(4) = 3522 + V_4(1) = 3232.0PIT

Lap 2, using the V_3 column just computed — only ages 1 and 2 are reachable here, since the race always starts at age 1:

ageSTAY totalPIT totalV_2(age)π*_2
110 + V_3(2) = 3916 + V_3(1) = 3939.0STAY (tie)
213 + V_3(3) = 4519 + V_3(1) = 4242.0PIT

Lap 1 — only age = 1 is reachable, since every race starts on a fresh tyre:

STAY: 10 + V_2(2) = 10 + 42 = 52 PIT: 16 + V_2(1) = 16 + 39 = 55 V_1(1) = 52, π*_1(1) = STAY
Reading the optimal policy back out

Walk forward through the π* table, always taking the action recorded for the state you're actually in: lap 1 age 1 → STAY (age becomes 2) → lap 2 age 2 → PIT (age resets to 1) → lap 3 age 1 → STAY (age becomes 2) → lap 4 age 2 → STAY (forced, last lap). Total cost: 10 + 19 + 10 + 13 = 52 — matching V_1(1) exactly, as it must. Compare that to the policy that never pits at all: 10 + 13 + 16 + 19 = 58. One well-timed pit stop, at exactly the right lap, saves 6 — and backward induction found both the fact that pitting helps and the single lap where it helps, purely by propagating values backward from a horizon of zero future laps to a horizon of four.

sections.heading: Why a one-step-ahead ("greedy") policy would have missed this
sections.sourceHtml:
Why a one-step-ahead ("greedy") policy would have missed this

A policy that only compares this lap's immediate cost — ignoring V_(t+1) entirely — picks STAY at every single lap in this example, because STAY is cheaper than PIT on every lap taken in isolation (lap_time(age) < lap_time(age) + 6, always). That greedy policy is exactly the always-stay policy above, costing 58. The extra 6 backward induction is willing to spend at lap 2 only makes sense in light of what it buys three laps later — information a one-step-ahead view structurally cannot see. This is the general shape of the pitfall Phase 1's "common pitfalls" section warns about for a rising learning curve, arriving here in a much sharper form: the correct policy is provably not the myopic one.

Backward induction vs. value iteration — a note for the resource map

The plan's resource map points to Sutton & Barto chapter 4, which covers dynamic programming for the infinite-horizon, discounted case: value iteration repeatedly sweeps and updates V(s) for every state using the current estimate of V, and only converges to the true values in the limit, because with no fixed end there's no V_(T+1)=0 to anchor a single clean backward pass. Backward induction — what this page and the DP oracle actually use — is the finite-horizon special case: because a race has a hard, known length, the exact values are obtained in a single pass, lap by lap, with no iteration to convergence required. Chapter 4's ideas transfer directly; the finite horizon is what makes them exact here rather than merely convergent.

sections.heading: Expectations Over Randomness
sections.sourceHtml:
Expectations Over Randomness

Page 2's toy race had no luck in it — every action led to exactly one next state. A real race doesn't get that guarantee: a safety car might arrive, or it might not. This page is the one new piece of math that closes that gap.

sections.heading: What changes when the next state isn't certain
sections.sourceHtml:
What changes when the next state isn't certain

Page 2's recursion assumed each state-action pair leads to exactly one successor state. Once a safety car can arrive at random, that's no longer true: from a given green-flag state, taking STAY leads to two possible next states — still green, or now under a safety car — and the DP has no way to know in advance which one it'll be. The general backward-induction equation already accounted for this with an expectation, written but not yet unpacked on page 2:

V_t(s) = min_a [ cost(s, a) + E_s'[ V_(t+1)(s') ] ]

Unpacking E_s'[...] is this page's whole job. Because there are only two possible outcomes here — safety car arrives, or it doesn't — the expectation is nothing more exotic than a weighted average of two known numbers:

E_s'[ V_(t+1)(s') ] = P(sc_next = 1) · V_(t+1)(s' with sc_active=1) + P(sc_next = 0) · V_(t+1)(s' with sc_active=0)

This is the defining move of stochastic dynamic programming: wherever the deterministic recursion referenced "the" next value, the stochastic version references a probability-weighted average over every next value that could actually occur. Everything else about the backward pass — working from V_(T+1)=0 toward lap 1, one lap at a time — is completely unchanged.

sections.heading: Where the probabilities come from: a hazard-rate model
sections.sourceHtml:
Where the probabilities come from: a hazard-rate model

The two probabilities above need their own small model, calibrated from real safety-car data in Phase 0.5. Treat each green lap as a coin flip with a small, per-circuit chance of triggering a safety car — a standard way to model "how likely is a rare event on any given opportunity" (the same idea survival analysis calls a hazard rate):

P(sc starts next lap | currently green) = hazard (a small per-lap probability, fit per circuit) P(sc continues next lap | currently active) = 1 − 1 / mean_duration (mean_duration in laps)

The second line is a standard property of this kind of model: if a safety car period is expected to last mean_duration laps on average, treating each lap under it as an independent chance to end gives exactly a 1/mean_duration chance of ending on any given lap, so 1 − 1/mean_duration is the chance it's still running next lap.

This project

Real safety-car frequency varies enormously by circuit — historically, street circuits like Singapore have seen a safety car in nearly every race, while Bahrain sees one in only a small fraction. That's exactly why hazard is fit per circuit in Phase 0.5, rather than assumed to be one universal constant: a single hazard rate applied everywhere would make the oracle's optimal pit windows equally wrong at both extremes.

sections.heading: Worked example: how much does the risk of a safety car change today's decision?
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked example: how much does the risk of a safety car change today's decision?

Take page 2's lap-3, tyre-age-2 cell and ask what changes if there's now a 25% chance a safety car arrives on lap 4. Suppose (from a version of the recursion that also tracks sc_active) the two possible V_4 values are already known: V_4(age=3, green) = 16.0 — page 2's own number — and a new one, V_4(sc_active) = 20.0, reflecting that a safety-car lap is slow and pitting under it, discounted, still isn't worth it with no laps left afterward:

E[V_4 | currently green, hazard = 0.25] = 0.25 · V_4(sc_active) + 0.75 · V_4(age=3, green) = 0.25 · 20.0 + 0.75 · 16.0 = 5.0 + 12.0 = 17.0 V_3(age=2, STAY) = lap_time(age=2) + E[V_4] = 13.0 + 17.0 = 30.0

Compare that to page 2's fully deterministic answer for the same cell: 13 + V_4(3) = 13 + 16 = 29. The one-lap risk of a slow safety-car lap next lap raises today's expected cost by exactly 1.0 — a small, honest markup, computed the same way a race strategist reasons informally: "there's a real chance of a safety car soon, and that changes what staying out is actually worth, even though it hasn't happened yet." Nothing about how to compute a backward pass changed from page 2 — only that every reference to "the next value" became a weighted average over the outcomes that could occur.

sections.heading: The pit-under-safety-car discount, and why it belongs in the transition, not the reward
sections.sourceHtml:
The pit-under-safety-car discount, and why it belongs in the transition, not the reward

The Phase 3.5 plan specifies pitting under a safety car costs roughly 40% of the normal pit loss, because the whole field is circulating slowly and the relative time lost by ducking into the pits is much smaller. That's a fact about cost(s, a) — the immediate term in the recursion, computed by dynamics.compute_pit_loss — not about the expectation over next states covered above. Getting the two mixed up is an easy mistake with a large consequence, which is exactly why the design doc calls it out explicitly: zeroing the reward on safety-car laps (rather than discounting the immediate pit-loss term) would also zero out the pit-loss cost, making an SC pit look free instead of merely cheap, and collapsing the optimal policy into "always wait for a safety car" — a strategy that only looks good because of an accounting error, not because it's actually cheap.

sections.heading: Why compute_lap_time(noise=0) is exact, not approximate
sections.sourceHtml:
Why compute_lap_time(noise=0) is exact, not approximate

Backward induction needs a single number for cost(s,a) at every state — not a distribution. But dynamics.compute_lap_time, run inside the live environment, adds a small random noise term to every lap for realism. The DP oracle is allowed to sidestep that noise entirely, and the justification is a two-line argument, not a shortcut taken on faith:

lap_time = deterministic_part(state, action) + noise, where E[noise] = 0 E[lap_time] = E[deterministic_part] + E[noise] = deterministic_part + 0 = deterministic_part = compute_lap_time(..., noise=0)

Because the noise term is additive and zero-mean by construction, dropping it doesn't approximate the expected lap time — it is the expected lap time, exactly. This is precisely why the Phase 3.5 plan insists the DP oracle call dynamics.compute_lap_time itself with noise disabled, rather than reimplementing the lap-time formula: any independent reimplementation would need to separately prove this same zero-mean property for whatever noise model it assumed, and a drift between two "equivalent" formulas is exactly the kind of bug that looks individually correct in each file and is nearly invisible in review.

This project

This is also why the oracle's rollout evaluation (page 6) has to be checked against its own V[s_0]: V[s_0] is the expected race time under the model — computed exactly, using this zero-noise shortcut, throughout the whole backward pass. The rollout mean, run with noise switched back on in the real environment, is the measured value under the actual simulator. If those two numbers diverge by more than sampling noise would explain, either the expectation math above has a bug, or the environment and the oracle have quietly drifted apart — and the test exists specifically to catch whichever one it is.

sections.heading: Markov Chains
sections.sourceHtml:
Markov Chains

Oracle B needs a weather model the agent could plausibly know in advance — not "here is what actually happened," but "here is how likely each condition is to follow the current one." A Markov chain is exactly that model, fit from nothing more than counting.

sections.heading: The same idea page 2 of the Phase 1 prerequisites already taught you
sections.sourceHtml:
The same idea page 2 of the Phase 1 prerequisites already taught you

An MDP's Markov property says the next state depends only on the current state, not on the full history of how you got there — that's what made laps_remaining, not cumulative_race_time_so_far, the right state feature back in Phase 1. A Markov chain is the same idea, stripped of actions and rewards entirely: just a set of states and the probability of moving from each one to each other one at each step. Weather regime is a natural fit — tomorrow's conditions depend mostly on today's, not on the conditions three days ago — which is exactly the assumption Oracle B's weather model makes explicit and calibrates.

sections.heading: The transition matrix
sections.sourceHtml:
The transition matrix

With n states, a Markov chain is completely described by an n × n transition matrix P, where each entry is a conditional probability:

P[i, j] = P(next state = j | current state = i)

Every row of P must sum to 1 — from state i, the chain has to go somewhere at the next step, possibly back to i itself. A matrix with this property is called row-stochastic. For this project, n = 3: DRY, DAMP, WET.

sections.heading: Fitting a chain from data: count, then normalize
sections.sourceHtml:
Fitting a chain from data: count, then normalize

Given a log of observed weather sequences, the transition matrix that makes those exact sequences most probable (its maximum-likelihood estimate) has a famously simple closed form: count how many times each transition i → j actually occurred, then divide by how many times state i occurred as a starting point at all:

n_ij = number of observed transitions from state i to state j n_i = Σ_j n_ij (total number of times state i was the starting point of a transition) P̂[i, j] = n_ij / n_i

No optimization, no iteration — just counting and dividing. This is the standard estimator for a Markov chain's transition probabilities, and it falls directly out of maximizing the likelihood of the observed sequences under a Markov-chain model (a classical result, e.g. Anderson & Goodman 1957). One practical edge case worth knowing before it surprises you: a state that was never observed as a starting point has n_i = 0, making the division undefined — the standard fix is to fall back to a uniform row (equal probability to every state) rather than leaving that row undefined or crashing on it.

sections.heading: Worked example: fitting a 3×3 matrix from three toy races
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked example: fitting a 3×3 matrix from three toy races

Three short, invented 6-lap weather logs (D = DRY, P = DAMP, W = WET), one letter per lap:

Race 1: D D D P P D Race 2: D D P W W P Race 3: D P P D D D

Read off every consecutive pair within each race (never across race boundaries — race 1's last lap says nothing about race 2's first) and tally them by starting state:

From→ D→ P→ WRow total (n_i)
D5308
P2215
W0112

Divide each row by its total to get the fitted transition matrix P̂:

From \ ToDRYDAMPWET
DRY0.6250.3750.000
DAMP0.4000.4000.200
WET0.0000.5000.500

Every row sums to 1, as required. Notice what the matrix quietly encodes just from three short races: DRY is "sticky" (62.5% chance of staying DRY), WET never jumped straight back to DRY in this small sample (a real fit, with far more than three races of data, would likely assign that transition a small but nonzero probability rather than exactly zero — a reminder that a fitted chain is only as good as the data behind it, a point Oracle B's fit-quality reporting takes seriously; see below).

sections.heading: Sampling a trace from a fitted chain
sections.sourceHtml:
Sampling a trace from a fitted chain

To generate a new, synthetic weather trace lap by lap: start in some initial state, then at each step draw the next state from the current row of P̂, treated as a probability distribution over the three states — a single random draw weighted by that row's three numbers, then move to whichever state was drawn and repeat using its row next. Two traces sampled this way, even starting identically, will almost always diverge after a few laps, precisely because each step re-samples the randomness fresh — the same "no memorisable answer key" property page 1 flagged as the reason safety cars can't just be replayed from history.

Worth knowing, not needed for this project

Multiplying the matrix by itself, P², gives two-step transition probabilities; P^k gives k-step ones. As k grows large, most well-behaved chains converge to a fixed stationary distribution — the long-run fraction of time spent in each state, independent of where the chain started. The oracle never needs this (races are short and the exact lap-by-lap distribution is what backward induction consumes, not a long-run average), but it's the concept you'll see if you read further about Markov chains anywhere else.

sections.heading: Why this is what makes Oracle B "achievable" and Oracle A only a "bound"
sections.sourceHtml:
Why this is what makes Oracle B "achievable" and Oracle A only a "bound"

This is the piece that makes the two-oracle design in the Phase 3.5 plan precise rather than hand-wavy:

  • Oracle A conditions the backward induction on one specific, fixed historical weather trace — lap 12 really was DAMP in that particular real race, and Oracle A is allowed to know that in advance while solving. No RL agent, which only observes weather up to the current lap, could ever know that. Oracle A is provably an upper bound the agent cannot reach — not because the agent isn't good enough, but because it's being asked a harder question than the agent is ever asked.
  • Oracle B instead conditions on the fitted transition matrix above, tracking weather_regime as part of the DP state exactly the way the live environment does, and computing the expectation over next-lap weather using P̂'s row for the current regime — precisely the mechanism page 3 introduced for the safety car, applied to a second, independent random process. Because the agent, too, only ever observes the current regime and has to reason probabilistically about what comes next, Oracle B is solving exactly the MDP the agent actually faces. Its value is a target the agent could, in principle, actually reach.
  • The gap between them — Oracle A − Oracle B — is the value of knowing the future in advance: a genuinely interesting number in its own right, not RL underperformance. Page 6 returns to this with the real project's numbers.
This project

weather_markov.py fits one 3×3 matrix like the one above per circuit, from every historical race template Phase 0.5 extracted for that circuit — the exact counting-and-normalizing procedure above, just with far more than three races and far more than six laps behind it. It also reports fit quality (per-transition counts, held-out likelihood): if a circuit's historical sample is too thin for the fitted chain to be trustworthy, the honest response is to say so and lean on Oracle A's information-gap framing instead of quietly presenting a poorly-fit Oracle B as the tight benchmark.

sections.heading: Stage 1 — deterministic backward induction, verified against brute force
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 1 — deterministic backward induction, verified against brute force

Start with exactly page 2's toy race: one tyre, STAY/PIT, no randomness. A dict keyed by (lap, age) stands in for the value table — small enough here that a NumPy array would be overkill:

HORIZON = 4
PIT_LOSS = 6.0

def lap_time(age: int) -> float:
    return 10.0 + 3.0 * (age - 1)

def toy_backward_induction(horizon: int):
    V = {(horizon + 1, age): 0.0 for age in range(1, horizon + 2)}
    policy = {}
    for t in range(horizon, 0, -1):
        for age in range(1, t + 1):
            stay_cost = lap_time(age) + V[(t + 1, age + 1)]
            pit_cost  = lap_time(age) + PIT_LOSS + V[(t + 1, 1)]
            if stay_cost <= pit_cost:
                V[(t, age)], policy[(t, age)] = stay_cost, "STAY"
            else:
                V[(t, age)], policy[(t, age)] = pit_cost, "PIT"
    return V, policy

Before trusting it, verify it the way test_oracle_value_matches_rollout will later verify the real oracle: independently, by brute force, enumerate every one of the 2^HORIZON possible action sequences and find the cheapest by direct simulation:

from itertools import product

def brute_force_best(horizon: int) -> float:
    best = None
    for actions in product(("STAY", "PIT"), repeat=horizon):
        age, total = 1, 0.0
        for a in actions:
            total += lap_time(age) + (PIT_LOSS if a == "PIT" else 0.0)
            age = 1 if a == "PIT" else age + 1
        best = total if best is None else min(best, total)
    return best

V, policy = toy_backward_induction(HORIZON)
assert abs(V[(1, 1)] - brute_force_best(HORIZON)) < 1e-9
print(V[(1, 1)])   # should print 52.0 -- page 2's hand-computed answer, exactly

HORIZON = 4
PIT_LOSS = 6.0

def lap_time(age: int) -> float:
    return 10.0 + 3.0 * (age - 1)

def toy_backward_induction(horizon: int):
    V = {(horizon + 1, age): 0.0 for age in range(1, horizon + 2)}
    policy = {}
    for t in range(horizon, 0, -1):
        for age in range(1, t + 1):
            stay_cost = lap_time(age) + V[(t + 1, age + 1)]
            pit_cost  = lap_time(age) + PIT_LOSS + V[(t + 1, 1)]
            if stay_cost <= pit_cost:
                V[(t, age)], policy[(t, age)] = stay_cost, "STAY"
            else:
                V[(t, age)], policy[(t, age)] = pit_cost, "PIT"
    return V, policy

from itertools import product

def brute_force_best(horizon: int) -> float:
    best = None
    for actions in product(("STAY", "PIT"), repeat=horizon):
        age, total = 1, 0.0
        for a in actions:
            total += lap_time(age) + (PIT_LOSS if a == "PIT" else 0.0)
            age = 1 if a == "PIT" else age + 1
        best = total if best is None else min(best, total)
    return best

V, policy = toy_backward_induction(HORIZON)
assert abs(V[(1, 1)] - brute_force_best(HORIZON)) < 1e-9
print(V[(1, 1)])   # should print 52.0 -- page 2's hand-computed answer, exactly

sections.heading: Stage 2 — a risk the agent can't control: the safety-car hazard
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 2 — a risk the agent can't control: the safety-car hazard

Add the exact expectation machinery page 3 introduced, over a state that now includes sc_active. Only what's new is shown — the shell around it is the same backward pass:

HAZARD = 0.2          # P(SC starts next lap | currently green)
CONTINUE_PROB = 0.5   # P(SC continues next lap | currently under SC)
SC_LAP_TIME = 20.0
SC_PIT_DISCOUNT = 0.4

def sc_transition_prob(sc_now: int) -> float:
    """P(sc_next = 1 | sc_now)."""
    return CONTINUE_PROB if sc_now else HAZARD

def toy_backward_induction_sc(horizon: int):
    V = {(horizon + 1, age, sc): 0.0
         for age in range(1, horizon + 2) for sc in (0, 1)}
    policy = {}
    for t in range(horizon, 0, -1):
        for age in range(1, t + 1):
            for sc in (0, 1):
                p_next = sc_transition_prob(sc)

                def expect(next_age):
                    return (p_next * V[(t + 1, next_age, 1)]
                            + (1 - p_next) * V[(t + 1, next_age, 0)])

                if sc:
                    this_lap, pit_extra = SC_LAP_TIME, PIT_LOSS * SC_PIT_DISCOUNT
                else:
                    this_lap, pit_extra = lap_time(age), PIT_LOSS

                stay_cost = this_lap + expect(age + 1)
                pit_cost  = this_lap + pit_extra + expect(1)
                if stay_cost <= pit_cost:
                    V[(t, age, sc)], policy[(t, age, sc)] = stay_cost, "STAY"
                else:
                    V[(t, age, sc)], policy[(t, age, sc)] = pit_cost, "PIT"
    return V, policy

Run it and compare V_sc[(1, 1, 0)] (starting green) against stage 1's deterministic V[(1, 1)] = 52.0. The stochastic version should come out higher — the mere possibility of a slow safety-car lap somewhere ahead makes the race provably more expensive in expectation, even though this particular race might never actually see one. That direction of change (never favourable, only ever costly or neutral) is worth confirming as a sanity property, not just an interesting number.

sections.heading: Stage 3 — an action that isn't always legal
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 3 — an action that isn't always legal

Add a simple mandatory-service rule, echoing the real two-compound rule: the race must include at least one pit stop, enforced by forcing PIT on the final lap if none has happened yet. That requires one more piece of state, has_pitted, and a mask function consulted before comparing actions:

def toy_action_mask(t: int, horizon: int, has_pitted: bool) -> list[str]:
    if t == horizon and not has_pitted:
        return ["PIT"]              # STAY is illegal here
    return ["STAY", "PIT"]

Inside the backward pass, replace the fixed ("STAY", "PIT") comparison with a loop over toy_action_mask(t, horizon, has_pitted), and thread has_pitted through the state key and the transition (has_pitted becomes True forever once a PIT action is taken). Run it and confirm two things: first, that the policy at the final lap really is always PIT whenever the race arrives there with has_pitted = False; second, that V[(1, 1, ...)] under this rule is never lower than stage 2's unconstrained value for the same starting state — a mask can only remove options, never add value, so a rise (or no change) is the only legitimate outcome, and a mask that somehow makes the optimal race cheaper is a mask with a bug in it.

sections.heading: Stage 4 — a second, independently-random process
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 4 — a second, independently-random process

Add weather, sampled from a small fitted Markov chain — reuse page 4's own worked 3×3 matrix directly, so this stage is also a chance to confirm you can read a transition matrix back out as code:

DRY, DAMP, WET = 0, 1, 2

WEATHER_P = {
    DRY:  [0.625, 0.375, 0.000],   # from page 4's worked example
    DAMP: [0.400, 0.400, 0.200],
    WET:  [0.000, 0.500, 0.500],
}
WEATHER_PENALTY = {DRY: 0.0, DAMP: 1.5, WET: 4.0}   # added to lap_time

Weather and the safety car are treated as independent here (a simplification worth naming, not hiding), so the expectation over both next states is a double sum — weight each combination by the product of its two individual probabilities:

def expect_both(t, next_age, sc_now, w_now, V):
        p_sc = sc_transition_prob(sc_now)
        total = 0.0
        for sc_next, p1 in ((0, 1 - p_sc), (1, p_sc)):
            for w_next, p2 in enumerate(WEATHER_P[w_now]):
                total += p1 * p2 * V[(t + 1, next_age, sc_next, w_next)]
        return total

Wire this into stage 3's loop in place of the single-variable expect(), add WEATHER_PENALTY[w] into this_lap when sc == 0, and extend every state key and the terminal condition with a w component. Run it starting from w = DRY and from w = WET separately, and confirm the WET start produces a strictly higher V[(1, 1, 0, w)] — two independently-random exogenous processes, each contributing its own share of expected cost, exactly the composition Oracle B performs for real.

sections.heading: Stage 5 — the sanity check, before you ever trust a DP answer again
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 5 — the sanity check, before you ever trust a DP answer again

This is the habit the real test_oracle_no_absurd_exploit exists to enforce, built here in miniature first. A correct DP solver that is fed a broken cost model will confidently report an absurdly good "optimal" policy — because nothing about backward induction can tell the difference between "genuinely cheap" and "cheap because the model has a bug." The defence is an independent, hand-reasoned baseline to compare against:

def simulate_fixed_policy(pit_at_lap: int, horizon: int) -> float:
    """A simple, clearly-reasonable baseline: pit exactly once, at a fixed lap."""
    age, total = 1, 0.0
    for t in range(1, horizon + 1):
        total += lap_time(age)
        if t == pit_at_lap:
            total += PIT_LOSS
            age = 1
        else:
            age += 1
    return total

baseline = min(simulate_fixed_policy(lap, HORIZON) for lap in range(1, HORIZON + 1))
dp_value = V[(1, 1, 0, DRY)]   # stage 4's solver, dry start, no SC

assert dp_value <= baseline + 1e-9          # DP can never be beaten by a simpler plan
assert baseline - dp_value < 0.25 * baseline  # ...but shouldn't beat it by an implausible margin either

The first assertion has to hold by construction — DP searches every policy, so nothing can beat it. The second is the interesting one: if the gap between the DP answer and a sensible fixed-lap baseline were huge (say, DP claiming a race can be won in half the time a reasonable human plan takes), that's not a strategic breakthrough, it's the signal that a cost term has the wrong sign or a state transition is wired backward somewhere upstream. Internalizing "check the DP answer against a baseline before believing it" here, on a solver you built and can fully audit in five minutes, is what makes the same check trustworthy later against a codebase with hundreds of lines you didn't write from scratch.

That's the full toy solver: deterministic backward induction, verified against brute force; a stochastic hazard with the expectation machinery from page 3; an action mask; a second independent random process fit as a Markov chain from page 4; and the sanity-check discipline that catches a broken model before it catches you. Page 6 doesn't repeat any of this code — it names which piece of the real dp_oracle.py and weather_markov.py corresponds to which stage here.

The defence is an independent, hand-reasoned baseline to compare against: def simulate_fixed_policy(pit_at_lap: int, horizon: int) -> float: """A simple, clearly-reasonable baseline: pit exactly once, at a fixed lap.""" age, total = 1, 0.0 for t in range(1, horizon + 1): total += lap_time(age) if t == pit_at_lap: total += PIT_LOSS age = 1 else: age += 1 return total baseline = min(simulate_fixed_policy(lap, HORIZON) for lap in range(1, HORIZON + 1)) dp_value = V[(1, 1, 0, DRY)] # stage 4's solver, dry start, no SC assert dp_value The first assertion has to hold by construction — DP searches every policy, so nothing can beat it. The second is the interesting one: if the gap between the DP answer and a sensible fixed-lap baseline were huge (say, DP claiming a race can be won in half the time a reasonable human plan takes), that's not a strategic breakthrough, it's the signal that a cost term has the wrong sign or a state transition is wired backward somewhere upstream. Internalizing "check the DP answer against a baseline before believing it" here, on a solver you built and can fully audit in five minutes, is what makes the same check trustworthy later against a codebase with hundreds of lines you didn't write from scratch. That's the full toy solver: deterministic backward induction, verified against brute force; a stochastic hazard with the expectation machinery from page 3; an action mask; a second independent random process fit as a Markov chain from page 4; and the sanity-check discipline that catches a broken model before it catches you. Page 6 doesn't repeat any of this code — it names which piece of the real dp_oracle.py and weather_markov.py corresponds to which stage here.

blocks.sourceHtml:
def simulate_fixed_policy(pit_at_lap: int, horizon: int) -> float:
    """A simple, clearly-reasonable baseline: pit exactly once, at a fixed lap."""
    age, total = 1, 0.0
    for t in range(1, horizon + 1):
        total += lap_time(age)
        if t == pit_at_lap:
            total += PIT_LOSS
            age = 1
        else:
            age += 1
    return total

baseline = min(simulate_fixed_policy(lap, HORIZON) for lap in range(1, HORIZON + 1))
dp_value = V[(1, 1, 0, DRY)]   # stage 4's solver, dry start, no SC

assert dp_value <= baseline + 1e-9          # DP can never be beaten by a simpler plan
assert baseline - dp_value < 0.25 * baseline  # ...but shouldn't beat it by an implausible margin either

sections.heading: The DP state
sections.sourceHtml:
The DP state

Where Phase 1's environment observation was a flat 16-dimensional vector, the DP oracle's internal state is a small, explicit tuple — it needs to be hashable and enumerable, not shaped for a neural net:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DPState:
    lap: int              # 1..total_laps
    compound: int          # 0..4  (SOFT/MEDIUM/HARD/INTER/WET)
    tyre_age: int          # 1..total_laps
    used_mask: int          # 0..7 -- bits for SOFT/MEDIUM/HARD
    sc_active: int          # 0 or 1
    weather: int           # 0..2  -- Oracle B only; fixed per lap in Oracle A

Every field maps directly onto something pages 2–5 already built a version of:

sc_activesc, stage 2 onward

compound, used_maskNot built in the toy — the real state's compound-choice dimension, masked by compute_action_mask exactly as stage 3's has_pitted masked STAY

sections.heading: The state-space size, arithmetic in full
sections.sourceHtml:
The state-space size, arithmetic in full

Page 1 quoted the headline number; here's where each factor comes from:

lap ≈ 55 (total_laps, circuit-dependent) compound = 5 (SOFT / MEDIUM / HARD / INTER / WET) tyre_age ≈ 55 (capped at total_laps) used_mask = 8 (2³ -- three dry compounds, each used or not) sc_active = 2 weather = 3 (DRY / DAMP / WET) ------------------------------------------- 55 × 5 × 55 × 8 × 2 × 3 ≈ 363,000 states, × 6 actions

Backward induction over that, in NumPy, runs in well under a second per circuit — the plan's stated definition-of-done target is under 10 seconds. Most of the 363,000 are unreachable — tyre_age can never exceed lap, and a fitted compound implies at least one bit of used_mask — so a reachability pass computed forward from the race's actual start state, before solving, typically prunes 5–10× of that off, the same discipline page 1 previewed and every stage of page 5's toy solver practiced by only ever iterating over ages that were actually possible at each lap.

sections.heading: Sign convention: the DP minimises cost, the agent maximises reward
sections.sourceHtml:
Sign convention: the DP minimises cost, the agent maximises reward

Every recursion on pages 2 and 3 was written as a min over cost, matching dp_oracle.py directly. The live environment and every RL agent instead maximise reward = -lap_time. These are the same optimization — argmin(cost) = argmax(-cost) — related by a single sign flip applied once, at the boundary where the oracle's policy is wrapped for use by the shared evaluation harness (below), never scattered through the DP's internals. Keeping the DP itself entirely in cost terms, as pages 2 and 3 did throughout, is what makes it safe to reuse a well-tested minimization loop without re-deriving a maximization version of the same equations.

sections.heading: Oracle A vs. Oracle B, precisely
sections.sourceHtml:
Oracle A vs. Oracle B, precisely

Page 4 introduced the distinction in general terms; here it is exactly as the plan specifies:

Oracle AOracle B
Weather handlingFixed to one specific historical trace; lap alone determines weather, known in advanceTracked in DPState.weather, transitions drawn from the fitted 3×3 matrix (page 4)
What it answers"Best possible time for a strategist who already knows this exact race's weather""Best possible time for a strategist who observes only the current regime, same as the agent"
Achievable by an RL agent?No — provably not, it's an upper bound on a harder questionYes, in principle — it's the optimal policy of the exact MDP the agent trains in
Gap to it decomposes asinformation gap + algorithmic gappure algorithmic gap — the honest number to report

Oracle A − Oracle B is the value of perfect foresight — how many seconds a strategist would save by genuinely knowing the weather in advance, versus only being able to reason about it probabilistically. It's reported per circuit as an interesting result in its own right, not folded into either agent's evaluation.

This project

F1StrategyEnv gains a weather_mode option ("template" or "markov") specifically so Oracle B's assumption — the agent faces a Markov weather process, not a replayed historical trace — is something the environment can actually be run under, not just something the oracle assumes in isolation. Templates stay the default for the dashboard and the historical-race counterfactual in Phase 7, because "this is the real 2023 Dutch GP's actual weather" is a better demo than a sampled chain; "markov" mode exists purely so Oracle B's target is one the agent can be trained and measured against on equal footing.

sections.heading: Worked example: one backward-induction cell, at the real state's scale
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked example: one backward-induction cell, at the real state's scale

Take a state late in a 55-lap race — lap 50, on a 6-lap-old MEDIUM, DRY, safety car currently green, both dry compounds already used (so no mandatory-pit pressure) — and trace the STAY branch's cost exactly as pages 2 and 3 did, just with the real function names in place of the toy ones:

this_lap = dynamics.compute_lap_time(compound=MEDIUM, tyre_age=6, laps_remaining=6, weather=DRY, sc_active=False, rng=None) = (page 3's zero-noise expectation, exactly — not an approximation) expected_next = Σ_{sc'} Σ_{w'} P(sc' | sc_active=False) · P(w' | DRY) · V[lap=51, MEDIUM, age=7, mask, sc', w'] V[lap=50, MEDIUM, age=6, mask, sc=False, w=DRY] = min( this_lap + expected_next, # STAY this_lap + dynamics.compute_pit_loss(sc_active=False) + expected_next_after_pit # PIT_*, for each legal pit target )

Nothing here is new relative to page 5's stage-4 solver — the double sum over sc' and w' is precisely expect_both from that stage, and the min over legal actions is precisely stage 3's masked comparison. The only difference is scale: five real compounds instead of a toy's two or three, a real fitted 3×3 weather matrix instead of the page 4 illustration, and a genuine calibrated hazard instead of an invented 0.2. If any piece of this cell's structure feels unfamiliar, that's the signal to go back and build the missing piece as a toy on page 5 before reading dp_oracle.py itself.

sections.heading: The rollout harness and the optimality-gap metric
sections.sourceHtml:
The rollout harness and the optimality-gap metric

DPOraclePolicy wraps the solved (V, π*) tables behind the same act(obs, action_mask) interface every other agent uses, so evaluate.py's paired-seed harness (Phase 3's own evaluation methodology) runs it unmodified. Crucially, the oracle is scored by rolling it out in the real environment with noise switched back on — never by reading V[s_0] directly. V[s_0] is the expected cost under the model, computed exactly using page 3's zero-noise shortcut throughout; the rollout mean is the measured cost under the actual simulator, noise included. The two should agree within sampling error — test_oracle_value_matches_rollout checks exactly that, and a large divergence points at either a bug in the expectation math or a drift between the oracle's model and the live environment's.

Every results table from Phase 4 onward gains one column, defined here and used unchanged everywhere downstream:

sections.heading: Why one shared implementation matters more here than in Phase 1
sections.sourceHtml:
Why one shared implementation matters more here than in Phase 1

Page 7 of the Phase 1 prerequisites already made the case that dynamics.py being pure functions is what lets the environment, the baselines, and this oracle all call the same physics. It matters even more acutely here: a DP oracle computing optimal values against a transition function that has quietly drifted from what agents actually train against doesn't fail loudly — it produces numbers that look authoritative, get written into a results table, and are simply wrong. compute_action_mask is extracted as one function during Phase 1 specifically so both F1StrategyEnv.action_masks() and the DP import the identical logic rather than two implementations that could each look individually correct while silently disagreeing — test_dp_action_mask_matches_env exists to catch exactly that class of drift, on every commit.

sections.heading: src/evaluation/dp_oracle.py
sections.sourceHtml:
src/evaluation/dp_oracle.py

Reading order within the file, and what each piece is for:

  • DPState — the frozen dataclass from page 6. Indexed into a flat NumPy array via strides rather than kept as a dict of tuples (page 5's toy dicts were fine at a few hundred states; 363,000 states need the flat-array layout to stay fast). np.full(n_states, -np.inf, dtype=np.float64) is the whole value table, one array.
  • The reachability pass — a forward sweep from the race's actual start state, run once before solving, marking which of the 363,000 candidate states can ever actually occur (tyre_age <= lap, a fitted compound implies a bit in used_mask, and so on). This is page 6's 5–10× pruning number, made concrete: the backward pass below only ever touches states this sweep marked reachable.
  • The backward-induction loop — structurally identical to page 5's stage-4 solver: V[T+1, ·] = 0 (plus the two-compound terminal penalty where the rule is unmet, mirroring stage 3's mandatory-service rule), then for each lap from T down to 1, for each reachable state, for each action the (shared) mask permits, compute cost + E[V(s')] and keep the minimum. γ = 1.0, matching the environment — the same justification page 6's Phase 1 prerequisite page gave for the live environment applies unchanged here.
  • The expected-immediate-cost step — calls dynamics.compute_lap_time(..., rng=None) and dynamics.compute_pit_loss(...) directly, never a reimplementation. Page 3's zero-noise argument is why this call is exact rather than an approximation; page 6's "why one shared implementation matters" section is why it has to be this exact function, not an equivalent-looking one.
  • Action validity — imported from dynamics.compute_action_mask, the same function F1StrategyEnv.action_masks() calls. Never restated locally — page 6 explains why a second, independently-written mask would be close to invisible as a bug.
  • DPOraclePolicy — wraps the solved table behind act(obs, action_mask) -> int, the same interface every other agent implements, so evaluate.py's paired-seed harness (Phase 3) runs it with no special-casing.

sections.heading: src/env/weather_markov.py
sections.sourceHtml:
src/env/weather_markov.py

  • Fitting — page 4's counting-and-normalizing procedure, applied per circuit to every historical weather template Phase 0.5 extracted for that circuit: tally observed regime-to-regime transitions, divide each row by its total. The zero-row fallback page 4 mentioned (uniform row when a state was never observed as a starting point) is handled here, not left to crash on a division by zero.
  • Fit-quality reporting — per-transition counts and a held-out log-likelihood, alongside the fitted matrix. This exists so a thin data sample for a given circuit is visible and reported honestly, rather than silently producing a confident-looking matrix from too little evidence (page 4's closing note).
  • Sampling — page 4's cumulative-draw procedure, used both by Oracle B's expectation step and by F1StrategyEnv itself when weather_mode="markov", so the environment and the oracle draw from the identical fitted chain.

sections.heading: scripts/run_dp_oracle.py
sections.sourceHtml:
scripts/run_dp_oracle.py

The driver: solve every circuit (both oracle modes), cache each solved policy to data/processed/{circuit}/dp_policy.npz, and report the per-circuit solve time against the plan's under-10-seconds target. Re-run whenever dynamics.py or the calibration changes underneath it — a stale cached policy solved against an older version of the physics is exactly the kind of silent drift page 6 warns about, just at the level of a cache file instead of a second implementation.

sections.heading: What the test suite is actually checking
sections.sourceHtml:
What the test suite is actually checking

Each test in tests/test_dp_oracle.py targets one specific way this phase could go wrong — reading it alongside the implementation is, in effect, a list of every failure mode this page has already walked through:

  • test_oracle_value_matches_rollout — page 6's V[s_0]-vs-rollout check, made concrete: agreement within a small multiple of the noise standard error over 500 episodes.
  • test_dp_action_mask_matches_env — for 1,000 sampled reachable states, the DP's mask equals env.action_masks() exactly. This is the automated version of page 5's stage-3 sanity habit.
  • test_oracle_no_absurd_exploit — page 5's stage-5 exercise, for real: the oracle's race time must land within 15% of the best hand-computed 1-stop plan. By some distance the highest-value test in the file — it's the thing that would have caught "the agent learned to pit every lap because a warmup penalty has the wrong sign" before three days get spent blaming a learning algorithm for a bug in the model it was faithfully optimizing against.
  • test_oracle_a_dominates_oracle_b — a correctness check on both oracles at once: perfect foresight can never be worse than the achievable version, by page 6's own definition of the two.
  • test_oracle_respects_two_compound_rule / test_oracle_pit_count_plausible — the mandatory-service constraint (page 5's stage 3, for real) actually binds, and the resulting strategy makes a plausible number of stops (1–3 on a dry circuit, never 0, never more than 4).

sections.heading: Glossary
sections.sourceHtml:
Glossary

Every term used across pages 1–7 — nothing beyond them. Keep this open while reading the Phase 3.5 plan or the code.

Scope note

Terms belonging to learned methods (Q-values, TD error, epsilon-greedy, replay buffers, and the rest) aren't listed here because they aren't covered by this doc set — Phase 3.5 plans, it doesn't learn. See the Phase 4 and 5 prerequisites for that vocabulary.

Action mask
The boolean array of which actions are legal in a given state, computed once by dynamics.compute_action_mask and shared verbatim between the environment and the DP oracle. See pages 5 & 6.
Backward induction
The algorithm this phase implements: starting from a known terminal value (zero, after the last lap) and working one lap at a time toward lap 1, computing each lap's exact optimal value from the lap after it. The finite-horizon special case of dynamic programming. See page 2.
Dynamic programming (DP)
Solving a problem by breaking it into overlapping subproblems, solving each exactly once, and reusing the results — as opposed to recomputing shared work repeatedly. Backward induction is this project's instance of it. See page 2.
Expectation (over a random next state)
A probability-weighted average over every possible outcome, used wherever the recursion references "the next value" but the actual next state is uncertain — the safety car, and (for Oracle B) the weather regime. See page 3.
Hazard rate
The per-lap probability that a safety car starts on any given green lap, fit per circuit from historical data. Paired with a continuation probability (1 − 1/mean_duration) for laps already under a safety car. See page 3.
Markov chain
A model of a sequence of states where the next state depends only on the current one — the Markov property, applied to a process with no actions or rewards. Oracle B's weather model is one. See page 4.
Maximum-likelihood estimate (of a transition matrix)
The standard way to fit a Markov chain from data: count every observed i → j transition, divide by how often i occurred as a starting point. No iteration required. See page 4.
Oracle A (per-template DP)
The DP solved with one specific historical weather trace fixed and known in advance — an upper bound the agent provably cannot reach, since the agent never sees the future. See pages 4 & 6.
Oracle B (Markov-weather DP)
The DP solved with weather tracked as part of the state and transitioning according to a fitted Markov chain — exactly the MDP the agent actually faces, and therefore an achievable target. See pages 4 & 6.
Optimality gap
mean_race_time(agent) − mean_race_time(oracle_B), in seconds, reported with a paired bootstrap confidence interval. The headline evaluation metric from Phase 4 onward. See page 6.
Overlapping subproblems
The property that many different paths through a race arrive at the same state, so its value only needs to be computed once and then reused — the reason a value table (not repeated recomputation) makes backward induction tractable. See page 2.
Planning
Computing an optimal policy directly from a fully known model of the environment's dynamics and reward, with no trial and error. Contrasted with learning (Phases 4, 5, 9), which estimates a policy from sampled experience because the model isn't known. See page 1.
Reachability pruning
Marking, in a forward pass before solving, which of the enumerated states can actually occur (e.g. tyre age can never exceed the current lap number) — cutting the states backward induction has to visit by roughly 5–10×. See page 6.
Row-stochastic (matrix)
A matrix whose rows each sum to 1 — the defining property of a valid transition matrix, since the chain has to go somewhere at every step. See page 4.
Stationary distribution
The long-run fraction of time a Markov chain spends in each state, independent of where it started. Mentioned on page 4 for completeness; not used by this project.
Terminal condition
V_(T+1)(s) = 0 for every state — the anchor that makes backward induction a single, non-circular pass rather than requiring iteration to convergence. See page 2.
Transition matrix
The n × n table of probabilities P[i,j] = P(next = j | current = i) that fully describes a Markov chain. See page 4.
Value of perfect foresight
Oracle A − Oracle B: how much a strategist would gain from genuinely knowing the future weather, versus only being able to reason about it probabilistically. An interesting F1 quantity in its own right, not a measure of RL underperformance. See page 6.
Zero-noise expectation shortcut
Calling dynamics.compute_lap_time(..., rng=None) to get the exact expected lap time rather than a sampled one — valid because the environment's noise term is additive and zero-mean, so dropping it doesn't approximate the expectation, it equals it exactly. See page 3.

sections.heading: Why this phase exists, and why it isn't "more RL"
sections.sourceHtml:
Why this phase exists, and why it isn't "more RL"

Every phase before this one either builds the world (Phase 1) or acts in it reactively (Phase 2's dashboard, Phase 3's hand-written rules). Phase 3.5 does something different: it computes the optimal strategy for the single-car race, exactly, by exhaustively working out the consequence of every decision in every reachable situation. Nothing is learned from trial and error here — there is no exploration, no Q-table being nudged toward a target, no gradient step. Given the transition model and reward function Phase 1 already built, the optimal policy is computed directly, once, and cached.

That distinction — planning (compute the answer from a known model) versus learning (estimate the answer from experience) — is the single idea this whole doc set exists to teach. Phases 4, 5, and 9 all learn. Phase 3.5 plans. It is worth being precise about which is which, because the oracle's entire value as an evaluation tool depends on it being the *exact* answer, not an approximation competing with the agents it's meant to judge.

Scope, precisely

Phase 3.5 builds an evaluator, not an agent. So this doc set teaches exactly two things in depth: backward induction (the algorithm that makes exact solving tractable for a finite-horizon MDP) and Markov chains (the tool the oracle's weather model needs). Nothing about Q-learning, TD updates, exploration, or neural networks is covered here, even in preview — that material belongs to Phase 4 and 5's own prerequisites, and this doc set assumes none of it.

sections.heading: How this folder teaches the implementation half
sections.sourceHtml:
How this folder teaches the implementation half

Page 5 has you build a small backward-induction solver yourself, in your own names, across five stages — a deterministic toy first, then a stochastic exogenous event, then an action mask, then a second correlated random process sampled from a small Markov chain you fit yourself, then a sanity test comparing the DP's answer against a brute-force baseline. None of it touches the real project's code. Only page 6 names which piece of the real dp_oracle.py and weather_markov.py corresponds to which toy stage.

sections.heading: From an Equation to an Update Rule
sections.sourceHtml:
From an Equation to an Update Rule

Phase 3.5 solved the Bellman equation exactly because it was handed the model. Q-learning has to estimate the same equation from one sampled transition at a time — and that shift, from solving to nudging, is the entire idea this page exists to teach.

sections.heading: The equation hasn't changed
sections.sourceHtml:
The equation hasn't changed

Phase 1 page 3 derived the Bellman optimality equation, and Phase 3.5 page 2 solved it directly with backward induction:

Q*(s, a) = Σ_s' P(s'|s,a) · [ R(s,a,s') + γ · max_a' Q*(s', a') ]

Backward induction could solve this because the right-hand side was fully computable — P and R were dynamics.py, not a mystery. Q-learning faces the same equation with one crucial difference: it never has P or R written out anywhere. It only ever gets to observe one sampled transition (s, a, r, s') at a time, produced by an environment it can act in but not inspect. There is no sum over every possible s' weighted by its probability — only the single s' that actually happened.

sections.heading: The temporal-difference idea
sections.sourceHtml:
The temporal-difference idea

Given only one sampled transition, an exact expectation over all possible next states is out of reach. The temporal-difference (TD) idea, introduced generally in Sutton & Barto chapter 6, is to use that one real s' as a stand-in for the expectation, and to nudge the current value estimate toward it a little at a time, rather than trying to solve for the exact value in one shot the way DP did. Chapter 4 — Phase 3.5's chapter — covered the case where nothing needs estimating because the model is fully known; this page is chapter 6's case, where it isn't.

"A little at a time" is the operative phrase. Any single transition is a noisy, one-sample glimpse of what usually happens from (s, a) — the race might have hit an unlucky safety car, or a lucky dry stint. Moving the whole way to match one sample would make the table chase noise. Moving a small step toward it, over and over across many episodes, lets the noise average out while the signal accumulates.

sections.heading: TD error, defined once, used by every algorithm in this set
sections.sourceHtml:
TD error, defined once, used by every algorithm in this set

Every update rule in this doc set — Q-learning on page 2, SARSA on page 4 — is one instance of the same general form:

δ = target − Q(s, a) (TD error: "how wrong was my last guess?") Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α · δ (nudge the estimate toward the target)

δ ("delta") is the TD error: the gap between what the table currently believes Q(s,a) is worth, and a fresher estimate — the target — built from the one real transition that was just observed. The two algorithms in this phase, Q-learning and SARSA, differ in exactly one place: what they use as target. Everything else — the α-scaled nudge toward it — is identical, and pages 2 and 4 will make that difference the entire story.

sections.heading: Bootstrapping: learning from a guess about a guess
sections.sourceHtml:
Bootstrapping: learning from a guess about a guess

Look closely at what target is built from in every TD method: it uses the real observed reward r, plus an estimated value of the next state, Q(s', a') — not the true value, which is never available while learning is still in progress. Updating an estimate using another estimate is called bootstrapping, and it's the feature that separates TD methods from Monte Carlo methods, which wait until an entire episode finishes (so the "target" becomes the actual observed return, with no estimate involved) before updating anything.

Why bootstrapping is worth naming, not just using

Bootstrapping is what lets Q-learning and SARSA update every single step, instead of waiting until a race is over — useful, since a race here runs roughly 52–90 steps and waiting for all of them before learning anything would be slow and wasteful of a lap's worth of signal. The cost is that an update can be built from a value that is itself still wrong; that's fine, because the table converges through repeated correction over many episodes, not through any single update being exactly right.

What's still ahead

Page 2 fills in the one piece left unspecified here — exactly what target is for Q-learning, and why max_a' appears in it. Page 3 covers how actions actually get chosen while learning is happening (nothing so far has said how the agent decides what to try). Page 4 repeats page 2's derivation for SARSA, whose target differs in exactly one term, and shows the two algorithms' learned tables diverging on a worked example.

sections.heading: The full update
sections.sourceHtml:
The full update

Q-learning's update fills in page 1's target with a specific choice:

Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α [ r + γ · max_a' Q(s', a') − Q(s, a) ] \_______________/ \__________/ target δ

Matched against page 1's general form: target = r + γ · max_a' Q(s', a'), and δ = target − Q(s, a), exactly as before. Everything here is one concrete instance of the shape already introduced — nothing new in the mechanics, only in what target is built from.

Masks and episode boundaries

The maximum ranges over legal actions at the final next observation. At true task termination the target is just r. An external collection cap truncates a nonterminal task, so its target retains continuation; never replace that final observation with the following reset observation. Stop collection on either flag. The one-cell TD lab demonstrates target 5 versus terminal target 1 and exposes a stored illegal value 99 entering an unmasked backup.

sections.heading: Why max_a': this is what "off-policy" means
sections.sourceHtml:
Why max_a': this is what "off-policy" means

The target assumes the agent will play optimally from s' onward — it takes the best Q-value available at s', regardless of which action the agent actually ends up taking next while it's still exploring. That's a deliberate mismatch: the policy generating the data (ε-greedy, page 3) is not the same policy the update assumes will be followed afterward (purely greedy). This mismatch — updating toward a different policy than the one producing the experience — is precisely what off-policy means. The agent can take a random exploratory action next and the update still credits (s,a) as if the best follow-up action were coming, because max_a' doesn't care what was actually sampled.

sections.heading: Learning rate and discount, in their learning-specific role
sections.sourceHtml:
Learning rate and discount, in their learning-specific role

α (learning rate) and γ (discount) were both named in Phase 1 and used by Phase 3.5, but they do a different job here. α controls how far a single sampled transition is allowed to move an estimate: too high and the table chases noise from one race to the next without settling; too low and learning proceeds at a crawl, needing many more visits to the same cell before it reflects reality. γ stays at 1.0, unchanged from every earlier phase, for the same fixed-horizon reason Phase 1 page 3 gave: a race is a finite number of laps, and there's no reason to discount a lap 40 reward less than a lap 5 one just because it's further away in time.

sections.heading: Worked example: a 3-state toy, hand-run for four steps
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked example: a 3-state toy, hand-run for four steps

A tiny MDP, small enough to track every table cell by hand. Two non-terminal states, s1 and s2; a terminal state s3; two actions, a0 and a1, in every state:

s1, a0 → r = −1, next = s2 s1, a1 → r = −3, next = s3 (terminal) s2, a0 → r = −1, next = s3 (terminal) s2, a1 → r = −2, next = s3 (terminal)

Backward induction (page 2 of the Phase 3.5 set) would solve this exactly in one pass: Q*(s2,a0) = −1, Q*(s2,a1) = −2, so the best move from s2 is a0; then Q*(s1,a0) = −1 + (−1) = −2, Q*(s1,a1) = −3, so the optimal policy is a0 at s1, then a0 at s2. Q-learning is given none of this — only four sampled transitions, in this order, with α = 0.5, γ = 1, and every table cell starting at 0:

#Sampled transitionTargetδUpdated cellNew value
1(s1, a0, r=−1, s2)−1 + max(0, 0) = −1−1Q(s1,a0)0 + 0.5(−1) = −0.5
2(s2, a0, r=−1, s3, terminal)−1 (terminal)−1Q(s2,a0)0 + 0.5(−1) = −0.5
3(s1, a1, r=−3, s3, terminal)−3 (terminal)−3Q(s1,a1)0 + 0.5(−3) = −1.5
4(s1, a0, r=−1, s2)−1 + max(−0.5, 0) = −1−1 − (−0.5) = −0.5Q(s1,a0)−0.5 + 0.5(−0.5) = −0.75

Two things worth reading carefully out of this trace. First, every cell is moving in the right direction — toward the true values Q*(s1,a0)=−2, Q*(s1,a1)=−3, Q*(s2,a0)=−1 — without landing on them exactly after only one or two visits; convergence is a many-episode process, and four steps only establishes the trend. Second, step 4's target used max(Q(s2,a0), Q(s2,a1)) = max(−0.5, 0) = 0 — picking the still-untouched Q(s2,a1) over the already-updated Q(s2,a0), purely because nothing has pulled it down from its optimistic zero initialization yet. That's not a bug; it's the mechanism page 8 leans on when discussing why a table's initial values matter, and a preview of why an all-zero start is mildly optimistic until enough transitions have been seen to correct it.

sections.heading: Convergence, stated but not proven
sections.sourceHtml:
Convergence, stated but not proven

Q-learning is provably guaranteed to converge to Q* given two conditions: every state-action pair is visited infinitely often, and the learning rate α decays appropriately over time (a fixed α, as used throughout this project's plan, converges to a small neighborhood of Q* rather than exactly to it — acceptable in practice, and the reason "train for a lot of episodes" is the theoretical justification behind the real plan's 10,000-episode training runs, not a proof this page needs to reproduce). What matters practically is the shape of the guarantee: nothing here promises fast convergence, only that enough visits eventually get there.

sections.heading: Why greedy-only fails
sections.sourceHtml:
Why greedy-only fails

An agent that always takes whatever action its current Q-table says is best can get permanently stuck on a mediocre policy — not because the table is wrong in some abstract sense, but because it never tries the action that would have revealed something better. If an early, still-unreliable estimate happens to rank a mediocre pit lap above the genuinely optimal one, a purely greedy agent will keep confirming its own mistaken belief forever: it only ever revisits the action it already prefers, so the estimate for the better action never gets the chance to improve. This is the exploration/exploitation tradeoff named on Phase 1 page 1 — exploit what looks best so far, or explore to find out whether something else is actually better — resolved concretely here for the first time.

sections.heading: ε-greedy, defined
sections.sourceHtml:
ε-greedy, defined

with probability ε: act uniformly at random, among LEGAL actions with probability 1 − ε: act greedily — argmax Q(s, ·), among LEGAL actions

"Among legal actions" matters in both branches, tying back to the action mask introduced in the Phase 1 and Phase 3.5 sets: a random draw has to be restricted to actions that are actually available in the current state, and the greedy argmax has to ignore illegal actions' Q-values entirely (masked out, typically by setting them to −∞ before taking the max) rather than accidentally selecting one just because its untrained Q-value happens to look high.

sections.heading: Linear decay, worked with the real plan's numbers
sections.sourceHtml:
Linear decay, worked with the real plan's numbers

A fixed ε never stops exploring as much as it did on day one, which wastes training time once the agent already knows roughly what's good. The real plan decays ε linearly from ε_start = 1.0 (pure exploration at the very start of training) down to a floor ε_end = 0.05 (never fully greedy — always a small chance of trying something else) over decay_steps = 500,000 environment steps:

ε_t = max( ε_end, ε_start − t · (ε_start − ε_end) / decay_steps ) per-step decrement = (1.0 − 0.05) / 500,000 = 0.95 / 500,000 = 1.9 × 10⁻⁶

A race in this environment runs roughly 90 steps (one decision per lap, across a lap count in the 50s–90s depending on scenario). 500,000 steps at ~90 steps/episode is 500,000 / 90 ≈ 5,556 episodes before ε reaches its floor — a little over half of the real plan's 10,000-episode training run. That's a deliberate design point, not a coincidence: the second half of training happens almost entirely at the 5% exploration floor, giving the table time to refine an already-mostly-formed policy rather than continuing to explore at the same rate throughout.

Common pitfall

Decaying ε too fast locks in whatever policy the table happened to prefer early, before enough states have been visited to trust it — the exact same failure mode as the greedy-only case above, just delayed rather than avoided. If a trained agent's learning curve flattens early at a mediocre level, checking whether epsilon_decay_steps was too small relative to the total training budget is one of the first things worth trying, ahead of anything more exotic (this is also why the real plan's risk table names "increase epsilon_decay_steps to 1M" as a mitigation for premature convergence).

sections.heading: Why masking has to apply inside exploration, not just at evaluation time
sections.sourceHtml:
Why masking has to apply inside exploration, not just at evaluation time

It's tempting to think of the action mask as something that only matters for the greedy branch — after all, isn't a random exploratory action supposed to be random? The problem is that "random over all 6 actions" wastes exploration budget on moves that are illegal in the current state and get rejected or corrupt training, when only a handful of those 6 are actually legal here (say, only one valid pit compound is available because the mandatory-service rule restricts choices, or every pit action is illegal on the parade lap). Masking has to narrow the random draw itself to the legal set, not just filter the final choice afterward.

A concrete comparison makes the cost precise. Suppose 6 actions total, of which exactly 3 are legal in some state, and exactly one of those 3 is the useful pit action the agent needs to discover. Over 10 exploratory visits to that state, the chance of trying that one useful action at least once:

Exploration schemeP(pick the useful action), one drawP(tried at least once in 10 draws)
Unmasked — random over all 6 actions1/6 ≈ 0.1671 − (5/6)¹⁰ ≈ 0.838
Masked — random over the 3 legal actions1/3 ≈ 0.3331 − (2/3)¹⁰ ≈ 0.983

Both numbers look reasonably high over 10 draws, but the gap compounds badly at states that are visited rarely (exactly the coarse-table cells page 5 and 6 worry about) or where more than one of the 6 actions is illegal — a state with only 2 legal actions out of 6 more than doubles the masked scheme's per-draw hit rate over the unmasked one. Masking inside exploration isn't a correctness nicety; it's what makes the exploration budget actually land on the decisions the agent needs to learn.

sections.heading: SARSA's update
sections.sourceHtml:
SARSA's update

Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α [ r + γ · Q(s', a') − Q(s, a) ]

Set next to Q-learning's update from page 2, the only change is in the target:

Target
Q-learningr + γ · max_a' Q(s', a')
SARSAr + γ · Q(s', a') — a' is the action actually taken next

Q-learning's target asks "what's the best I could possibly do from s'?" SARSA's target asks "what will I actually do from s', given that I'm still an ε-greedy agent who sometimes acts randomly?" a' in SARSA isn't a hypothetical best action — it's whatever the agent's own ε-greedy policy actually selects as its next move, which the agent commits to before computing this step's update (the "pre-commit" mechanic page 7 builds and page 9 traces through the real code).

sections.heading: On-policy, defined precisely
sections.sourceHtml:
On-policy, defined precisely

SARSA's name is literally its signature: State, Action, Reward, State, Action — the five-tuple (s, a, r, s', a') its update consumes, with the final a' coming from the same policy generating the data. That's what on-policy means: the target is computed using the same policy (ε-greedy) that's actually producing the agent's behavior, not a hypothetical greedy policy it isn't really following yet. Q-learning is off-policy for the opposite reason — its target always assumes the greedy policy, regardless of what the ε-greedy behavior policy actually does next.

The practical consequence: SARSA's learned values account for the real chance that the agent's own future exploration could stumble into something costly. Q-learning's don't — its target is blind to what its behavior policy actually samples, so it never "pays for" the risk of its own exploration inside the value it's learning.

sections.heading: Worked example: a risky push vs. a safe pit, hand-run side by side
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked example: a risky push vs. a safe pit, hand-run side by side

The standard textbook cliff-walking contrast, in this project's own flavor. A decision point s1 with two choices: pit now (known, safe cost) or push one more lap (cheaper if followed by a clean pit, but one lap closer to the tire cliff):

s1, PIT_NOW → r = −12, terminal (safe: known cost, race over) s1, PUSH → r = −1, next = s2 (cheap this lap, but risk waits at s2) s2, PIT → r = −8, terminal (recover cleanly: the good outcome) s2, PUSH_MORE→ r = −30, terminal (the cliff: tire failure)

Ignoring exploration entirely, the greedy-optimal policy is clear: PUSH then PIT costs −1 + (−8) = −9, beating PIT_NOW's −12 outright. But an ε-greedy agent training at s2 doesn't always pick PIT — sometimes, by exploration, it picks PUSH_MORE and pays −30. Whether that real risk gets priced into Q(s1, PUSH) is exactly what separates the two algorithms. Hand-run both from identical rewards, α = 0.5, γ = 1, tables starting at 0, across three training episodes:

Ep.What happens at s2 (ε-greedy draw)Q-learning: Q(s1,PUSH) afterSARSA: Q(s1,PUSH) after
1Explores into PUSH_MORE (r=−30). Both tables start at 0, so Q-learning's max and SARSA's actual a' agree by coincidence (both point at an untrained 0-cell).−0.5−0.5
2Now Q(s2,PIT)=0 > Q(s2,PUSH_MORE)=−15, so both the greedy max and the ε-greedy draw land on PIT (r=−8) — still no divergence.−0.75−0.75
3An unlucky exploratory draw hits PUSH_MORE again (r=−30). Q-learning's target still uses max(Q(s2,PIT)=−4, Q(s2,PUSH_MORE)=−15) = −4 — it ignores that PUSH_MORE is what actually happened. SARSA's target plugs in Q(s2,PUSH_MORE)=−15 directly, because that's the action it actually took next.−2.875−8.375

By the end of episode 3 the two tables have diverged because Q-learning backs up a greedy continuation while SARSA backs up the sampled behaviour action. This does not guarantee different greedy routes after training. At fixed ε, the behaviour continuation from s2, once PIT is the greedy action, is (1−ε/2)×(−8) + (ε/2)×(−30) = −8−11ε. Thus PUSH has expected continuation return −9−11ε, which still beats PIT_NOW's −12 at ε=0.05. Whether a cautious route becomes preferable depends on the reward gap and exploration rate. Finite training with a constant learning rate can fluctuate around these values.

Try the committed-action lab

The action you actually take next lets you commit a slip, inspect its target, and expose the bug of resampling before execution. Its generic shortcut world has risk behaviour value 4.4 at ε=0.2 and greedy value 6; both must be labelled separately from sampled training scores.

sections.heading: Tying back to the real plan
sections.sourceHtml:
Tying back to the real plan

Train and compare both agents with explicit exploration schedules, transition budgets, and multiple seeds. Report training behaviour returns separately from frozen-table greedy evaluation at ε=0, and clear SARSA's pending action before each evaluation episode. Q-learning's greedy target does not guarantee faster learning; SARSA's behaviour target does not guarantee a safer greedy policy. Their update targets answer different questions, and the observed comparison depends on the environment and settings.

sections.heading: State Discretization: The General Tradeoff
sections.sourceHtml:
State Discretization: The General Tradeoff

A Q-table is a dictionary. Dictionaries need hashable, finite keys. The 16-dimensional observation this project's environment hands out is neither — so something has to convert it into one first.

sections.heading: Why tabular methods need a finite table
sections.sourceHtml:
Why tabular methods need a finite table

Q(s, a) as used on pages 1–4 was written as if s were simply a label — s1, s2, and so on. In code, self.Q is a dictionary (or a defaultdict, page 8's choice) keyed by s directly, which means s has to be something a dictionary can use as a key: hashable, and drawn from a finite (or at least enumerable) set. The environment's real observation is a 16-dimensional float32 vector — normalized lap count, tire age, track temperature, and more, each one a continuous number. Two observations that are almost, but not quite, identical would hash to two different dictionary keys and never share a Q-value, which defeats the entire point of a table: generalizing across situations that are effectively the same.

Binning (equivalently, discretization) solves this by converting each continuous feature into a small number of discrete buckets — "tire age between 20 and 25 laps" instead of "tire age is exactly 22.7 laps" — so that nearby observations collapse onto the same table entry and a lookup table becomes possible at all.

sections.heading: The tradeoff, stated generally
sections.sourceHtml:
The tradeoff, stated generally

Binning is a lossy compression of the state, and the compression ratio is a real design choice with real consequences in both directions:

  • Too few bins — genuinely different situations collapse into the same table entry. This isn't a training problem that more episodes or a better learning rate can fix: the agent literally cannot represent a different action for two situations sharing one bin, no matter how well trained the table is. Page 6 works through exactly this failure for the real plan's first-drafted binning scheme.
  • Too many bins — the table becomes too sparse to learn from in any reasonable number of episodes. Every cell needs to be visited many times before its Q-value estimate means anything (page 2's hand-run showed a single visit only moves an estimate a fraction of the way toward the truth); split the same amount of experience across ten times as many cells, and each cell gets roughly a tenth as many visits, most of which still won't be enough to say anything useful.

There's no bin count that dissolves this tension — only a choice of where along it to sit, informed by which of the two failure modes is more costly for the specific decision the table needs to make. This is precisely the tension the real plan's Definition of Done exists to catch, and precisely why Phase 5 exists at all: function approximation (a neural network standing in for the table) sidesteps the tradeoff entirely by generalizing across similar continuous states without needing to bucket them first — named here as the eventual resolution, not developed further; that's Phase 5's own prerequisites' job.
