sections.heading: Worked arithmetic: how many states does a binning scheme actually produce?
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked arithmetic: how many states does a binning scheme actually produce?

The same kind of back-of-envelope arithmetic Phase 3.5 page 6 used to compute its 363,000-state DP enumeration applies here — with a different meaning. Phase 3.5's number was an exact enumeration: every state the DP oracle would ever need to solve for. This number is an approximation budget: how many distinct table entries a chosen binning scheme could ever produce, most of which won't be visited often (or at all) during a finite training run.

The real plan bins the 16-dim observation into eight discrete dimensions:

laps_remaining → 12 bins tire_compound → 5 bins (already discrete: SOFT, MEDIUM, HARD, INTER, WET) tire_age → 10 bins weather_regime → 3 bins (DRY, DAMP, WET) track_temp → 3 bins safety_car → 2 bins (active / not) compounds_used → 8 bins (2³ combinations of 3 dry compounds tried so far) mandatory_pit → 2 bins (yes / no) total states = 12 × 5 × 10 × 3 × 3 × 2 × 8 × 2 = 172,800
Discrepancy worth flagging before implementation

phase-4-q-learning-sarsa.md states this same product as 518,400, and its Risks table sizes the Q-table at "518,400 × 6 float64 ≈ 25 MB" on that basis. Multiplying the eight bin counts it lists, in any order, gives 172,800 — almost exactly a third of the stated figure (518,400 / 172,800 = 3), which suggests either an extra factor of 3 was meant somewhere in the binning scheme (a dimension with 3 bins was perhaps dropped from the list, or one bin count was mistyped) or the 518,400 figure itself is simply an arithmetic slip carried through the plan. Either way, this is worth resolving — by recounting the actual bins intended, not by picking whichever number looks more familiar — before discretize_obs is written, since page 6's "is memory actually the constraint" argument and any capacity planning depend on the real number. At 172,800 states the table is smaller still (172,800 × 6 × 8 bytes ≈ 7.9 MB), which only reinforces that memory was never the binding constraint on this scheme's coarseness.

Whichever total turns out correct, the shape of the exercise is the same one Phase 3.5 page 6 modeled: multiply the enumerated ranges of every state dimension together, and treat the result as a budget to be spent deliberately — coarse where a decision doesn't hinge on the distinction, fine where it does. Page 6 shows exactly what happens when one dimension of that budget is spent too coarsely.

sections.heading: The Binning Bug: When Coarseness Erases the Decision
sections.sourceHtml:
The Binning Bug: When Coarseness Erases the Decision

A binning scheme that runs without error and produces a plausible-sized table is not the same thing as a binning scheme that can represent the optimal policy. This page exists because the real plan's first draft got this wrong, and the fix has to land in discretize_obs before anything else in Phase 4 can be trusted.

Audit finding, quoted directly from the real plan

phase-4-q-learning-sarsa.md flags its own Step 1: "The binning below is too coarse to represent the decision... The agent is structurally prevented from representing the optimum, and no amount of training fixes that." This page exists to make sure that warning is understood before discretize_obs gets written, not discovered afterward from a confusing learning curve.

What proves a representation failure?

Two observations sharing a bin cause a policy limitation when they require different optimal actions and the other encoded features do not distinguish them. Different oracle costs or nearby pit laps alone do not establish that witness. Use reachable observations and compare their best legal actions. The bin-boundary lab gives an explicit pair: x=0.49 needs LEFT, x=0.51 needs RIGHT, and a single bin forces one action distribution for both.

sections.heading: Why that's fatal, connected directly to Phase 3.5's own numbers
sections.sourceHtml:
Why that's fatal, connected directly to Phase 3.5's own numbers

This isn't an abstract concern — it can be checked directly against numbers this project has already validated. Phase 0.5's non-degeneracy check requires the 1-second-optimal pit window (the range of laps within one second of the exact optimal pit lap, as computed by the Phase 3.5 DP oracle) to be ≤12 laps wide, and the Phase 0 audit actually measured windows of 5–10 laps. A 5-lap-wide tire_age bin is frequently narrower than the entire optimal window is wide — meaning two laps the oracle considers meaningfully different can land in the very same table cell.

Concretely: suppose the DP oracle's exact optimal pit lap for some scenario is lap 27, with the 1-second-optimal window running from roughly lap 25 to lap 32 (an 8-lap window, well within the measured 5–10 lap range). Consider two candidate pit laps inside that window, lap 27 and lap 31, both close to optimal but four laps apart:

tire age at lap 27 ≈ 27 → normalized ≈ 0.54 → int(0.54 × 10) = 5 → bin 5 tire age at lap 31 ≈ 31 → normalized ≈ 0.62 → int(0.62 × 10) = 6 → bin 6

Those two happen to land in adjacent bins here — but shift the same window four laps earlier (optimal lap 23, candidates lap 23 and lap 27) and both fall inside bin 4 (ages 20–25) and bin 5 (ages 25–30) respectively only by luck of where the window sits relative to a bin edge; shift it by two laps instead of four (candidates lap 27 and lap 29, both well inside a typical 5–10 lap window) and both round into the same bin 5 (ages 25–30). The table then has no cell in which "pit now" and "wait 2–4 more laps" are different entries — Q(state_with_bin5, PIT) is a single number that has to simultaneously represent the value of pitting at lap 27 and the value of pitting at lap 29, even though the DP oracle can tell these apart and the real cost of picking wrong is real seconds of race time.

This is not underfitting. More training episodes, a better learning rate, a longer epsilon decay — none of it helps, because the representation itself has a ceiling: two states that are genuinely different, with genuinely different optimal actions, are mapped to the same dictionary key before the agent ever sees them. No update rule can recover information the state representation already discarded.

sections.heading: The fix the real plan adopts
sections.sourceHtml:
The fix the real plan adopts

Use 1–2 lap resolution on tire_age (25–50 bins), non-uniform if convenient — fine-grained near the cliff, where the decision is genuinely sensitive to a lap or two either way, coarser far from it, where nothing close to the boundary is at stake and a wider bin costs nothing in decision quality.

The natural objection is that finer binning means a bigger table, but page 5 already computed the actual cost: even the deliberately coarse original scheme comes to roughly 172,800 states (or 518,400, per the discrepancy flagged there — either way, single-digit-to-double-digit megabytes as a float64 table). Widening tire_age from 10 bins to, say, 40 bins multiplies the total by 4×, landing well under 100 MB either way — and because self.Q is a defaultdict (page 8), memory is only ever allocated for states that are actually visited during training, not for the full enumerated space. The aggressive coarseness was never buying back meaningful memory savings; it was only costing the ability to represent the optimum.

sections.heading: The general lesson
sections.sourceHtml:
The general lesson

Echoing Phase 3.5 page 5's own discipline — a clean pipeline isn't a validated pipeline — a binning scheme that runs without error and produces a plausible-sized table is not the same thing as a binning scheme that can represent the optimal policy. The two properties are independent: a scheme can be perfectly bug-free, produce a sensible-looking state count, train without crashing, and still be structurally incapable of distinguishing the decisions that matter.

The concrete test this motivates

discretize_obs must map the Phase 3.5 DP oracle's optimal pit lap, and its immediate neighboring laps, to distinct bins. If it doesn't, Phase 4 isn't measuring the algorithm's ability to learn a good policy — it's measuring the discretization's inability to represent one, and the optimality gap it eventually reports against Oracle B is meaningless regardless of how well Q-learning or SARSA converges on top of it. This test belongs early in tests/test_agents.py, run before any learning-curve result is trusted, in the same spirit as Phase 3.5's test_oracle_no_absurd_exploit sanity check.

sections.heading: Build It Yourself: A Toy Q-Learning and SARSA, Side by Side
sections.sourceHtml:
Build It Yourself: A Toy Q-Learning and SARSA, Side by Side

Six stages: a tiny world small enough to reason about by hand, a shared learner shell, an off-policy learner, an on-policy learner, a run that reproduces page 4's divergence for real, and a bug you deliberately cause yourself.

Every name below (TinyStrategyWorld, OffPolicyLearner, _pending_action, and so on) is invented for this page and deliberately does not match q_learning_agent.py. The goal, same as every prior toy-build in this project's prerequisite sets, is to arrive at the same shape of solution independently, so the real file reads as familiar structure rather than new material when page 9 opens it.

sections.heading: Stage 1 — a tiny world with a genuine risky-shortcut-vs-safe-route contrast
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 1 — a tiny world with a genuine risky-shortcut-vs-safe-route contrast

The exact toy from page 4, made runnable. State 0 is the opening decision; state 1 is reached only by the risky choice; both terminate:

class TinyStrategyWorld:
    """
    State 0: opening decision.
      action 0 (BOX_NOW)  -> reward -12, done          (safe, known cost)
      action 1 (STRETCH)  -> reward  -1, state -> 1     (cheap now, risk later)
    State 1: reached only after STRETCH.
      action 0 (BOX)         -> reward  -8, done        (clean recovery)
      action 1 (OVERSTRETCH) -> reward -30, done        (the cliff)
    """
    N_ACTIONS = 2

    def reset(self):
        self._state = 0
        return self._state

    def legal_actions(self, state: int) -> list[int]:
        return [0, 1]   # both actions legal in both states, in this toy

    def step(self, action: int):
        if self._state == 0:
            if action == 0:
                return None, -12.0, True
            self._state = 1
            return 1, -1.0, False
        else:
            reward = -8.0 if action == 0 else -30.0
            return None, reward, True

sections.heading: Stage 2 — a shared TD-learner shell
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 2 — a shared TD-learner shell

A dict-based table (defaultdict pattern, matching what page 5's arithmetic already justified for a sparsely-visited state space), ε-greedy action selection respecting a supplied legal-action list, and page 3's linear decay schedule — sized for a toy that trains in thousands, not millions, of steps:

from collections import defaultdict
import numpy as np

class TDLearnerShell:
    def __init__(self, n_actions, alpha=0.5, gamma=1.0,
                 eps_start=1.0, eps_end=0.05, decay_steps=2_000):
        self.n_actions = n_actions
        self.alpha, self.gamma = alpha, gamma
        self.eps_start, self.eps_end, self.decay_steps = eps_start, eps_end, decay_steps
        self.epsilon = eps_start
        self._step = 0
        self.table = defaultdict(lambda: np.zeros(n_actions))

    def pick_action(self, state, legal, rng):
        if rng.random() < self.epsilon:
            return int(rng.choice(legal))
        q = self.table[state].copy()
        mask = np.full(self.n_actions, -np.inf)
        mask[legal] = 0
        return int(np.argmax(q + mask))

    def decay(self):
        self._step += 1
        step_size = (self.eps_start - self.eps_end) / self.decay_steps
        self.epsilon = max(self.eps_end, self.epsilon - step_size)

sections.heading: Stage 3 — OffPolicyLearner: page 2's target
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 3 — OffPolicyLearner: page 2's target

class OffPolicyLearner(TDLearnerShell):
    def learn(self, state, action, reward, next_state, done, legal_next, rng):
        if done:
            target = reward
        else:
            q_next = self.table[next_state].copy()
            mask = np.full(self.n_actions, -np.inf)
            mask[legal_next] = 0
            target = reward + self.gamma * np.max(q_next + mask)
        td_error = target - self.table[state][action]
        self.table[state][action] += self.alpha * td_error
        self.decay()

sections.heading: Stage 4 — OnPolicyLearner: page 4's target, with the pre-commit mechanic
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 4 — OnPolicyLearner: page 4's target, with the pre-commit mechanic

The real SARSAAgent has to know a' before it can compute this step's target — but the natural training loop only asks for the next action after stepping the environment. The fix, built here first in miniature: pick a' during learn(), stash it, and hand it back out on the very next call to pick_action:

class OnPolicyLearner(TDLearnerShell):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._pending_action = None

    def pick_action(self, state, legal, rng):
        if self._pending_action is not None:
            action, self._pending_action = self._pending_action, None
            return action
        return super().pick_action(state, legal, rng)

    def learn(self, state, action, reward, next_state, done, legal_next, rng):
        if done:
            target = reward
        else:
            self._pending_action = super().pick_action(next_state, legal_next, rng)
            target = reward + self.gamma * self.table[next_state][self._pending_action]
        td_error = target - self.table[state][action]
        self.table[state][action] += self.alpha * td_error
        self.decay()

sections.heading: Stage 5 — run both, identical seeds, watch them diverge for real
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 5 — run both, identical seeds, watch them diverge for real

def run_episodes(learner, world, n_episodes, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    for _ in range(n_episodes):
        state = world.reset()
        done = False
        while not done:
            legal = world.legal_actions(state)
            action = learner.pick_action(state, legal, rng)
            next_state, reward, done = world.step(action)
            legal_next = [] if done else world.legal_actions(next_state)
            learner.learn(state, action, reward, next_state, done, legal_next, rng)
            state = next_state

off_policy = OffPolicyLearner(TinyStrategyWorld.N_ACTIONS)
on_policy  = OnPolicyLearner(TinyStrategyWorld.N_ACTIONS)
world = TinyStrategyWorld()

run_episodes(off_policy, world, n_episodes=3000, seed=0)
run_episodes(on_policy,  world, n_episodes=3000, seed=0)

print("Off-policy Q(state 0):", off_policy.table[0])
print("On-policy  Q(state 0):", on_policy.table[0])
print("Off-policy prefers:", "STRETCH" if np.argmax(off_policy.table[0]) else "BOX_NOW")
print("On-policy  prefers:", "STRETCH" if np.argmax(on_policy.table[0]) else "BOX_NOW")

Compare multiple seeded runs with their exploration schedules and transition counts visible. At a fixed ε=0.05, the greedy STRETCH continuation value is −9; the behaviour continuation is −9−11×0.05=−9.55, still better than BOX_NOW's −12. Lower SARSA values therefore need not imply a different greedy route. During epsilon decay there is no single fixed behaviour value, and finite constant-step updates fluctuate. Freeze the table, set ε=0, and reset pending actions for a separate evaluation; keep those returns distinct from training returns. The SARSA lab and local comparison pack make these settings explicit.

sections.heading: Stage 6 — catch the leak
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 6 — catch the leak

Deliberately reproduce the bug page 8 and page 9 name against the real SARSAAgent: forget to clear _pending_action between episodes. Comment out (or never implement) a reset() call between calls to world.reset() in the training loop, and run OnPolicyLearner for a few hundred episodes:

# Buggy loop: state resets, but the learner's pending action does not.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
buggy_learner = OnPolicyLearner(TinyStrategyWorld.N_ACTIONS)
for ep in range(500):
    state = world.reset()
    done = False
    while not done:
        legal = world.legal_actions(state)
        action = buggy_learner.pick_action(state, legal, rng)   # no reset() call anywhere
        next_state, reward, done = world.step(action)
        legal_next = [] if done else world.legal_actions(next_state)
        buggy_learner.learn(state, action, reward, next_state, done, legal_next, rng)
        state = next_state

In this particular toy the leak is easy to miss, because every episode always starts at state 0 and both actions are always legal — a stale _pending_action from the end of one episode gets silently returned as the first action of the next episode, applied to a completely different situation than the one it was actually chosen for. Print buggy_learner._pending_action right after each episode ends and watch it carry a non-None value across the reset boundary whenever the previous episode ended by reaching state 1 and picking an action there. In a toy this small the corrupted behaviour mostly just adds noise to the learned table; in the real environment (page 8, page 9), the same leak can apply a stale pre-committed action to an observation from an entirely different race scenario, since the real environment's states are far more varied than this toy's two.

That's the full toy pair: a world with a genuine risk-vs-safety contrast, a shared TD shell, off-policy and on-policy learners implementing exactly page 2 and page 4's update rules, a run that reproduces the hand-worked divergence at scale, and the specific on-policy bug class a reader who built _pending_action here will recognize immediately in the real code. sections.heading: The reward-scale problem, argued numerically
sections.sourceHtml:
The reward-scale problem, argued numerically

The same style of argument Phase 1 page 3 used to prove reward centring doesn't change the optimal policy applies here, with a training-speed consequence layered on top. With γ = 1 and a per-lap reward of roughly −95 seconds over a ≈52-lap race, the true Q-values the table needs to learn are around −95 × 52 ≈ −5,000. The table initializes every cell at 0.

distance a cell must travel: 0 → ≈ −5,000 per-update step size at α = 0.1: roughly 10% of the remaining gap, each visit a cell needs dozens of visits just to get within a small fraction of −5,000, and the value has to propagate backward, lap by lap, before early-race cells see any signal at all — exactly the mechanism page 2's hand-run showed for a table this size, stretched out over a race-length horizon

This is the single most likely cause of "the agent trains without error but the learning curve never moves" — not a bug in the update rule, but a scale mismatch between how far a cell needs to travel and how far a realistic number of visits at α = 0.1 can move it in the time available. The fix is Phase 1's own reward_offset="base_pace" wrapper, which learns on −(lap_time − base_pace) instead of raw lap time — a per-step reward around −5 rather than −95, and Q-values around −250 rather than −5,000. This is safe for exactly the reason Phase 1 page 3 proved: subtracting a constant from every step's reward over a fixed horizon shifts every policy's total return by the same fixed amount, and shifting every option's value equally can never change which one is the argmax.

Why "+10 optimistic init" isn't the fix

The real plan's Risks table suggests an optimistic +10 initialization bonus for pit actions to encourage early exploration of pitting. Against a −5,000-scale problem, +10 is a rounding error — it nudges the very first visit to a pit-action cell by an amount roughly 0.2% the size of the gap that cell needs to close. It is not a substitute for fixing the reward scale; it's a reasonable secondary nudge to apply after reward_offset="base_pace" has already brought the true values down to a range where a small initialization bonus can plausibly matter.

sections.heading: Curriculum learning, concretely
sections.sourceHtml:
Curriculum learning, concretely

docs/idea.md's sequencing tip — train on the easy case before the full scenario library — becomes a two-switch options flag passed to env.reset() for the first curriculum_episodes episodes of training: filter scenario sampling to DRY weather traces only, and force an all-green safety-car trace (both switches are needed because, under the revised environment design, safety cars are sampled stochastically rather than replayed from a fixed trace — filtering weather alone wouldn't also suppress SC events). In terms specific to this state space: restricting to dry, no-SC episodes early in training holds weather_regime and safety_car_active effectively constant, so early training concentrates its limited number of episodes on fewer distinct table cells — more visits per cell, faster movement away from the all-zero start discussed above — before the full scenario library reintroduces the dimensions that were held fixed.

sections.heading: Two bugs recorded against the real plan
sections.sourceHtml:
Two bugs recorded against the real plan

Both are design lessons a reader who did page 7's exercises will already recognize the shape of, not just warnings to memorize:

Evaluated agent still exploring

select_action branches on self.epsilon at every call, and nothing in evaluate.py ever turns exploration off before running a trained agent's evaluation races. At the trained floor ε = 0.05 and a ≈52-step race, the expected number of random actions per evaluated race is 0.05 × 52 ≈ 2.6 — not a rare edge case but a near-certainty on every reported race, some of those random draws landing on a full 18-second pit stop the agent's actual policy would never have chosen. The fix is an explicit eval_mode / deterministic flag that forces pure-greedy action selection, set by evaluate_agent before any comparison run, with a test asserting two evaluation runs on the same seed produce byte-identical trajectories.

The SARSA pre-commit leak, for real

The exact bug reproduced on page 7 stage 6: SARSAAgent._next_action has no reset() and nothing in the training or evaluation loop clears it between episodes, so a pre-committed action chosen for the previous episode's final state can be returned as the very first action of a completely different race — a stale decision applied to an observation it was never chosen for. The fix mirrors what page 7 stage 6 demonstrates is missing: add reset() to SARSAAgent and call it at the start of every episode, both during training and evaluation.

sections.heading: The optimality-gap metric, with real numbers to reference
sections.sourceHtml:
The optimality-gap metric, with real numbers to reference

Carried over unchanged from Phase 3.5: optimality_gap = mean_race_time(agent) − mean_race_time(Oracle B), in seconds, with a paired bootstrap confidence interval. The real Definition of Done's "≥60/100 seeds beating the threshold baseline" is the necessary-but-not-sufficient bar — a trained agent that clears it has shown it learned something better than a fixed heuristic, but the actual headline result this phase reports is how much of the gap between that baseline and the Phase 3.5 DP oracle's exact optimum the agent closed. A Q-learning agent that beats the baseline on 61/100 seeds while leaving most of the baseline-to-oracle gap unclosed has technically passed the DoD bullet and still failed the phase's real pedagogical point.

sections.heading: Reading order, and why it's this order
sections.sourceHtml:
Reading order, and why it's this order

Read discretize_obs first, before either agent class — it's the representation everything else depends on, and page 8 already walked through it dimension by dimension. Then read QLearningAgent: select_action, update, save/load, in that order, since update only makes sense once you've seen how an action gets chosen in the first place. Only after that, read SARSAAgent as a subclass — it overrides exactly two methods, and reading it last means every line that isn't overridden is already familiar.

sections.heading: What to look for in QLearningAgent
sections.sourceHtml:
What to look for in QLearningAgent

  • select_action — confirm it matches page 3's ε-greedy shape exactly: a random draw restricted to np.where(masks)[0] (the legal actions), or an argmax over self.Q[state] with illegal actions set to −inf first. The state key passed in is always the output of discretize_obs, never the raw observation.
  • update — this is page 2's update rule, line for line: target = reward if terminated, else reward + gamma * np.max(next_q) with the next state's illegal actions masked to −inf first, exactly the max_a' from page 2. Confirm the masking happens before the max, not after — an unmasked max could pick an illegal action's stale Q-value as the target, which would be wrong for the same reason unmasked exploration wastes budget on page 3.
  • save / load — the Q-table is a defaultdict at training time (so unvisited states cost nothing, page 5's arithmetic), but pickling a defaultdict with a lambda default factory doesn't round-trip cleanly through every serialization path — check that load reconstructs the defaultdict wrapper explicitly around the loaded plain dict, rather than assuming pickle preserved it.

sections.heading: What to look for in SARSAAgent.select_action's pre-commit mechanic
sections.sourceHtml:
What to look for in SARSAAgent.select_action's pre-commit mechanic

This is page 7 stage 4's _pending_action mechanism, under its real name, _next_action. The reason it exists at all: SARSA's update needs to know a' — the action the agent will actually take next — before it can compute this step's TD target, but Gymnasium's env.step() loop naturally hands back next_obs before the loop asks for the next action. select_action resolves this by checking for a pre-committed _next_action first (consuming and clearing it if present) and only falling back to a fresh ε-greedy draw otherwise; update is where that pre-commit actually gets set, by calling select_action on next_obs one call early. If page 7 stage 6's leak exercise was done first, this pattern — and the exact way it can go stale across an episode boundary if never reset — should already look familiar rather than surprising.

sections.heading: The training loop's curriculum switch and evaluation cadence
sections.sourceHtml:
The training loop's curriculum switch and evaluation cadence

In train_tabular.py, look for the options["curriculum_dry_only"] = True branch, set for episode < curriculum_episodes and passed straight through to env.reset(seed=episode, options=options) — this is page 8's two-switch curriculum, and the environment side of honoring that flag lives in Phase 1's code, not here. Then look at the periodic evaluation block, printed every eval_interval episodes: this is what makes a learning curve trustworthy rather than a single lucky checkpoint. A single evaluation run at the very end of training could land on an unusually easy or unusually hard batch of seeds and give a misleading impression of how training actually progressed; periodic in-training evaluation, checked against the smoothed episode_rewards[-100:] average printed alongside it, is what lets a reviewer distinguish steady genuine improvement from a noisy fluke near the end.

sections.heading: What each new test actually catches
sections.sourceHtml:
What each new test actually catches

In the same spirit as Phase 3.5 page 7's test-by-test walkthrough — read what each test is actually defending against, not just that it exists:

TestWhat it actually catches
test_q_learning_update_changes_q_valuesThe single most basic thing that could silently break: an update call that's a no-op, e.g. because the learning rate never gets applied or the wrong cell gets written. Doesn't check the update is correct, only that it does something.
test_epsilon_decaysThat the decay schedule from page 3 actually decreases epsilon over repeated steps, and respects the floor — not a check on the exact decay curve, just that decay is genuinely happening rather than being silently skipped (e.g. because _step never gets incremented).
test_trained_q_agent_beats_randomAn end-to-end sanity floor, deliberately weak: after only 1,000 training episodes (far short of the real 10,000-episode run), the agent should at least beat an agent that acts uniformly at random. This is a smoke test that the whole pipeline — environment, discretization, update rule, exploration — is wired together correctly, not a claim that the agent has learned good strategy. A model that narrowly fails this test almost certainly has a wiring bug somewhere upstream, not a hyperparameter problem; one that passes it says nothing yet about how it compares to the threshold baseline, let alone the Oracle B optimality gap that's the phase's actual headline metric.

Also worth checking against page 6's audit finding: confirm a test exists (or add one) asserting discretize_obs maps the Phase 3.5 DP oracle's optimal pit lap, and its immediate neighboring laps, to distinct table keys — without it, none of the three tests above can catch the case where the whole training pipeline runs cleanly, reports a plausible-looking learning curve, and is still structurally incapable of representing the optimal policy.

sections.heading: Glossary
sections.sourceHtml:
Glossary

Every term used across pages 1–9 — nothing beyond them. Keep this open while reading the Phase 4 plan or the code.

Scope note

Terms belonging to function approximation (neural networks, replay buffers, target networks, and the rest) aren't listed here because they aren't covered by this doc set — Phase 4 is entirely tabular. See the Phase 5 prerequisites for that vocabulary.

Bootstrapping
Updating a value estimate using another value estimate (rather than a known true value or a fully-played-out return), the way every TD target in this set uses Q(s', a') — itself still being learned — instead of the true value of s'. See page 1.
Curriculum learning
Training on an easier restricted version of the task first (here: dry weather, no safety cars) before introducing the full scenario library, so early episodes concentrate limited experience on fewer distinct table cells. Cross-reference: Phase 1's own entry. See page 8.
Epsilon decay
Linearly shrinking ε from a high starting value toward a small floor over a fixed number of steps, so exploration is heaviest early in training and rarest (but never zero) later. See page 3.
ε-greedy
An action-selection rule: with probability ε act uniformly at random among legal actions, otherwise act greedily on the current Q-table. The standard way to balance exploration against exploitation in tabular TD control. See page 3.
Learning rate (α)
The step size controlling how far a single sampled transition can move a Q-value estimate. Too high: unstable, chases noise. Too low: converges too slowly to be useful in a realistic training budget. See pages 1 & 2.
Off-policy
A learning method whose update target is computed for a different policy (Q-learning's: the greedy policy) than the one actually generating the training data (the ε-greedy behaviour policy). See page 2.
On-policy
A learning method whose update target is computed using the same policy that's actually generating the behaviour — SARSA's target uses the ε-greedy policy's own next action, exploration and all. See page 4.
Optimality gap
mean_race_time(agent) − mean_race_time(Oracle B), in seconds, reported with a paired bootstrap confidence interval — the headline evaluation metric for this phase and every phase after it. Cross-reference: Phase 3.5's own entry. See page 8.
Optimistic initialization
Starting Q-values above what's realistic (e.g. a +10 bonus on pit actions) to bias early exploration toward under-tried actions. Only meaningful relative to the true value scale — see the reward-centring entry below for why a +10 bonus can be negligible or decisive depending on that scale. See page 8.
Reward centring
Learning on reward − constant instead of raw reward (here, reward_offset="base_pace") to bring the true value scale down to a range a fixed learning rate can traverse in a realistic number of visits, without changing which policy is optimal. Cross-reference: Phase 1 page 3's proof that subtracting a constant over a fixed horizon can't change the argmax. See page 8.
State discretization / binning
Converting a continuous observation into a finite, hashable key by bucketing each dimension into a small number of discrete ranges — required because a tabular Q-function is a dictionary, and dictionaries need finite keys. See page 5.
Curse of dimensionality
The exponential growth of a discretized state space as more dimensions or finer bins are added — named here as the general reason tabular methods stop scaling, deferred to the Phase 5 prerequisites, which cover function approximation as the actual resolution. See page 5.
TD error (δ)
The gap between a fresh target estimate and the table's current value for the state-action pair just visited: δ = target − Q(s,a). Every update in this set is Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α·δ. See page 1.
TD target
The fresher estimate an update nudges the table toward — r + γ·max_a' Q(s',a') for Q-learning, r + γ·Q(s',a') for SARSA (or just r if the episode terminated). See pages 1, 2 & 4.
Temporal difference (TD) learning
Estimating a value function from single sampled transitions, bootstrapping off the current estimate of what comes next, rather than solving for the exact expectation (dynamic programming) or waiting for a full episode to finish (Monte Carlo). See page 1.

sections.heading: Why this phase is different from the one before it
sections.sourceHtml:
Why this phase is different from the one before it

Phase 3.5 computed the exact optimal strategy for the single-car race because it was handed the model: dynamics.py gave it P and R in closed form, and backward induction solved the Bellman equation directly, once, with no trial and error. That is planning.

Q-learning and SARSA get no such gift. They never see P or R written out anywhere — they only ever see one sampled transition (s, a, r, s') at a time, generated by actually playing a race and watching what happens. Discovering a good policy purely from that experience, the way an actual rookie strategist would have to, is learning. The DP oracle from Phase 3.5 doesn't disappear once this phase starts — it becomes this phase's ruler, via the optimality-gap metric that measures how close a learned policy gets to the exact answer Phase 3.5 already computed.

Scope, precisely

This set teaches tabular temporal-difference control — Q-learning and SARSA — and the state-discretization problem that representing a Q-value as a lookup table forces on this project. It does not cover neural networks, experience replay, target networks, or anything else specific to function approximation, even as a preview. That material belongs to Phase 5's own prerequisites, which this set assumes nothing from.

sections.heading: How this folder teaches the implementation half
sections.sourceHtml:
How this folder teaches the implementation half

Page 7 has you build a small toy Q-learning agent and a toy SARSA agent side by side, in your own names, that deliberately do not match q_learning_agent.py. You'll run them on an identical toy environment from identical seeds and watch their learned tables genuinely diverge — the same divergence page 4 works out by hand for a handful of update steps. Only page 8 names which piece of the real state design and reward shaping corresponds to what you built, and only page 9 walks the real files themselves.

sections.heading: The tabular update, restated as what it actually is
sections.sourceHtml:
The tabular update, restated as what it actually is

Phase 4 page 02's update rule: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α·δ, where δ = target − Q(s,a). Read mechanically, that line does exactly one thing — it overwrites one cell of a lookup table with a slightly nudged value. Nothing in the derivation of δ, or in the reasoning behind why nudging toward a sampled target eventually converges, depended on the table being the storage mechanism. The table was simply the most direct way to associate a number with each (s,a) pair, not a requirement of the underlying idea.

sections.heading: The curse of dimensionality, with this project's own numbers
sections.sourceHtml:
The curse of dimensionality, with this project's own numbers

Phase 4 page 05 already did the arithmetic: eight binned observation dimensions produce a table with 518,400 states, each needing its own independently-learned number per action. Two states that differ by exactly one lap of tyre age, everything else equal, get assigned to completely unrelated table cells — the table has no way to know they're similar situations, so a hundred visits to one cell teach it nothing whatsoever about the neighbouring cell one lap over. Phase 6's plan (adding per-rival gap features) only multiplies this further: every new continuous-ish dimension that needs binning multiplies the total state count by however many bins it's given, while learning a good estimate for any one cell still takes roughly the same number of visits regardless of how many other cells now exist.

This is the general shape of the curse of dimensionality: the size of a discretized state space grows exponentially in the number of dimensions binned, while the training budget (episodes × steps per episode) stays fixed. A table that was already straining to get enough visits per cell in Phase 4's 8-dimensional space becomes hopeless once a 9th or 10th dimension is added — not because the algorithm got worse, but because the representation's cost scales in a way the training budget can't keep up with.

A table that was already straining to get enough visits per cell in Phase 4's 8-dimensional space becomes hopeless once a 9th or 10th dimension is added — not because the algorithm got worse, but because the representation's cost scales in a way the training budget can't keep up with.

sections.heading: Function approximation, defined generally
sections.sourceHtml:
Function approximation, defined generally

Replace the table lookup Q(s,a) with a parameterized function Q(s,a;θ), where θ is a (large) vector of adjustable numbers — the network's weights. Instead of an update overwriting one cell, an update nudges all of θ a little in a direction that reduces error on the transition just seen. Because the same weights are shared across every state the function is ever asked about, a nudge from training on lap 27 also moves the function's output for lap 26 and lap 28, even though neither was directly involved in that update. This sharing — one update changing predictions at states it never directly visited — is what generalization means here, concretely, and it's the property no table can ever have: a table's cells are, by construction, completely independent of one another.

The catch, named up front

Sharing information across states cuts both ways. An update that helps the function's prediction at a nearby state can just as easily hurt its prediction at a state it previously handled well, if the two states are treated as more similar than they should be, or if the update is allowed to move θ too far in one step. Choosing θ so the function actually improves overall, rather than forgetting what it just learned elsewhere every time it's nudged, is what the rest of this set is about: gradient descent (page 02) is the mechanism that nudges θ at all; the target network (page 03) and experience replay (page 04) exist specifically because training a network online, without them, destabilizes that nudging badly enough to prevent learning altogether.

sections.heading: What carries over unchanged
sections.sourceHtml:
What carries over unchanged

Everything about what is being learned stays exactly as Phase 4 left it. The Bellman-derived target — r + γ·max_a' Q(s',a') for the off-policy case Phase 4 page 02 derived — is still the thing every update tries to close the gap toward. The TD-error idea, δ = target − Q(s,a), is still the signal driving every update. Even the ε-greedy exploration schedule from Phase 4 page 03, decay arithmetic and all, is reused without modification (page 10 confirms the real agent's epsilon_start/epsilon_end/epsilon_decay_steps values). The only thing this phase changes is how the number gets stored and updated — a function with shared parameters instead of independent table cells, updated by a gradient step instead of an overwrite. Page 02 makes that gradient step concrete.

sections.heading: A layer as a function
sections.sourceHtml:
A layer as a function

A linear layer computes y = Wx + b: a matrix multiply of the input vector x by a weight matrix W, plus a bias vector b. On its own this is just an affine function — stacking several of them would collapse back into one big affine function, which can't represent anything more expressive than a straight line through the input space. A nonlinearity after each linear layer is what prevents that collapse; this project uses ReLU, max(0, y), applied elementwise.

Traced to the real network's exact shape (Linear(16→128) → ReLU → Linear(128→128) → ReLU, the shared trunk of DuelingDQN): the 16 is Phase 1's normalized observation vector's dimension — nothing new is being invented here, this is the same 16 numbers page 08's discretization used, just fed to a different kind of consumer. The 128 hidden width is a design choice, not derived from anything; it just needs to be large enough for the network to represent the function it's trying to learn without being so large that it trains slower than necessary on a state space this small.

sections.heading: Worked forward pass on a tiny network
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked forward pass on a tiny network

A network far smaller than the real one, small enough to run by hand: 2 inputs, 1 hidden layer of 2 units with ReLU, 1 output, no bias terms (to keep the arithmetic short):

W1 = [[ 1.0, -1.0], x = [2.0, 1.0] [0.5, 0.5]] h_pre = W1 · x = [1.0(2.0) + (-1.0)(1.0), 0.5(2.0) + 0.5(1.0)] = [2.0 - 1.0, 1.0 + 0.5] = [1.0, 1.5] h = ReLU(h_pre) = [max(0, 1.0), max(0, 1.5)] = [1.0, 1.5] W2 = [2.0, -1.0] (output layer, 2 -> 1) y = W2 · h = 2.0(1.0) + (-1.0)(1.5) = 2.0 - 1.5 = 0.5

Every step above is exactly what self.trunk(x) followed by one output head does in the real network, just at a size that fits on paper: a matrix multiply, a ReLU that zeroes out any negative pre-activation (here, nothing needed zeroing — both pre-activations happened to be positive), and a second matrix multiply into the output.

sections.heading: Loss: how wrong is the prediction, as one number
sections.sourceHtml:
Loss: how wrong is the prediction, as one number

Given a prediction ŷ and a target y*, a loss function collapses "how wrong" into a single scalar to minimize. Mean-squared error: L = (ŷ − y*)². The real agent uses smooth L1 / Huber loss instead — quadratic for small errors, linear beyond |error| = 1 — for reasons page 08 covers once there's a concrete number to explain. For now, either one plays the same role: a differentiable scalar that's small when the prediction is close and large when it isn't.

DQN's specific case (developed fully on page 03 and after): ŷ = Q(s,a;θ), the network's current prediction; y* = target, the Bellman-derived TD target. The loss is exactly "how far is the current Q-value estimate from where the Bellman equation says it should be" — the same quantity Phase 4's δ measured, now expressed as a loss to be minimized by gradient descent rather than a nudge applied by hand to one table cell.

sections.heading: Backpropagation, at the level this project needs
sections.sourceHtml:
Backpropagation, at the level this project needs

Backpropagation computes ∂L/∂θ for every weight in θ — how much, and in which direction, nudging that one weight would change the loss — by applying the chain rule layer by layer, working backward from the output. This page states that fact and works one small piece of it by hand; it does not derive the full chain-rule proof for an arbitrary network, which the real project never needs to do since PyTorch's autograd computes it automatically.

One weight's gradient, worked on the tiny network above: take W2's first entry (the weight connecting hidden unit 1 to the output), currently 2.0. If the loss is L = (y − y*)² with y* = 0 (target) and y = 0.5 (this network's output, computed above):

∂L/∂y = 2(y - y*) = 2(0.5 - 0) = 1.0 ∂y/∂W2[0] = h[0] = 1.0 (y = W2[0]·h[0] + W2[1]·h[1], so ∂y/∂W2[0] = h[0]) ∂L/∂W2[0] = ∂L/∂y · ∂y/∂W2[0] = 1.0 · 1.0 = 1.0

Read directly: increasing W2[0] by a small amount would increase the loss (the gradient is positive), so a gradient-descent step should decrease W2[0] a little. That single number, 1.0, is exactly the kind of quantity backpropagation computes for every one of θ's entries — this page only carries the chain rule back one layer; the real network's trunk has several more, each contributing one more application of the same rule.

sections.heading: Gradient descent: the same nudge, computed automatically
sections.sourceHtml:
Gradient descent: the same nudge, computed automatically

The update rule: θ ← θ − lr · ∂L/∂θ, applied to every entry of θ at once. This is worth reading side by side with Phase 4's tabular update, because it is the same idea, not a different one:

Tabular (Phase 4)Function approximation (this page)
Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α·δθ ← θ − lr·∂L/∂θ
One number, one table cellEvery entry of a (possibly large) weight vector
δ: how wrong the current cell's estimate is∂L/∂θ: how wrong the current prediction is, and how each weight contributed to that
α: how far one sampled transition can move one celllr: how far one sampled transition (via its gradient) can move every weight

This is the page's payoff line, and it's worth carrying forward explicitly: DQN is not a different learning idea from Phase 4's Q-learning. It is the exact same "nudge toward a Bellman-derived target" update rule, with the table cell replaced by a gradient step on a shared function. Every technique from page 03 onward exists to make that gradient step trainable in practice, not to change what it's trying to accomplish.

sections.heading: Adam, named but not derived
sections.sourceHtml:
Adam, named but not derived

Plain gradient descent uses the same step size (lr) for every weight, every step. Adam is an optimizer that adapts the effective step size per-parameter based on that parameter's recent gradient history, often used with noisy mini-batch gradients, without a guarantee of faster convergence or higher returns. Nothing here derives Adam's update rule — it's enough to recognize torch.optim.Adam(self.online_net.parameters(), lr=lr) in the code walkthrough (page 11) as "gradient descent, with a per-parameter adaptive step size," and to know that lr still means the same thing it meant in the table above — the base step size Adam adapts around.

sections.heading: Tensor bridge: implement one update
sections.sourceHtml:
Tensor bridge: implement one update

A Python list becomes a tensor with an explicit shape and dtype. The M4 warm-up uses float64 CPU tensors: input (B,D), weights (A,D), bias (A), prediction (B,A). Its scalar loss is a mean over every prediction entry. backward() accumulates gradients, so clear them before each independent optimizer step. Read shapes as you would function contracts.

x = torch.tensor([[0.25]], dtype=torch.float64)  # (1,1)
optimizer.zero_grad()
prediction = model(x)                           # (1,2)
loss = ((prediction - labels)**2).mean()        # scalar
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

Try the gradient and held-out fitting lab. Fixed labels make this supervised regression; bootstrapped targets and experience collection arrive in the next lab. The local fit uses SGD to expose the update; the stability learner then adds a hidden ReLU layer.

sections.heading: The Target Network
sections.sourceHtml:
The Target Network

The naive way to turn Q-learning into DQN trains a network to chase a target computed by that same network — which keeps moving every time the network gets updated. The fix is a second, slower copy.

sections.sourceHtml:
The naive idea

Page 01 established what doesn't change: the target is still r + γ·max_a' Q(s',a'). The most direct way to use a network for this replaces the tabular lookup with the network's own prediction: target = r + γ·max_a' Q(s',a';θ), and trains the same network θ toward it using page 02's gradient-descent step.

sections.heading: Why that's unstable
sections.sourceHtml:
Why that's unstable

θ is doing two jobs at once: it's the network being trained (Q(s,a;θ), the prediction the loss is computed on), and it's also the network used to compute the very target that prediction is being trained toward (Q(s',a';θ), inside the target). Every gradient step changes θ — and because both the prediction and the target are functions of the same θ, changing it to fix today's error also shifts tomorrow's target. It's chasing a target that runs away every time you get closer to it.

A tiny illustration makes this concrete. Suppose at some state-action pair the network currently predicts Q(s,a;θ) = 3.0, and the target (computed from the same weights) is target = r + γ·max_a' Q(s',a';θ) = 5.0. A gradient step moves θ to close that gap — but θ also appears inside Q(s',a';θ), so the same step that raised Q(s,a;θ) toward 5.0 can simultaneously raise Q(s',a';θ), which raises the target itself, say to 5.4. The gap the next update sees hasn't shrunk to reflect the progress just made — worse, in this example it grew. Nothing here is a bug in gradient descent; it's a direct consequence of one set of weights serving two roles that are supposed to converge toward each other.

sections.heading: The fix: a second, frozen-ish copy
sections.sourceHtml:
The fix: a second, frozen-ish copy

Keep two networks with separate weights: the online network (θ), updated by gradient descent every training step, and the target network (θ⁻), used only to compute the target: target = r + γ·max_a' Q(s',a';θ⁻). Gradient steps only ever touch θ; θ⁻ never receives a gradient directly. The target stops moving out from under the update that's chasing it, because the weights computing it are no longer the same weights that update just changed.

sections.heading: Keeping θ⁻ from going stale forever
sections.sourceHtml:
Keeping θ⁻ from going stale forever

If θ⁻ never changed at all, the online network would eventually be training toward a target computed by an arbitrarily out-of-date network — useful for stability, useless for actually converging to anything close to correct. Two ways to update θ⁻, both named because the real agent implements one of them:

  • Hard update: every N steps, copy θ → θ⁻ directly. Simple, but causes a visible discontinuity in the target every N steps — right after a copy, nonterminal targets may change to reflect how much θ had drifted since the last copy.
  • Polyak / soft update: every step, nudge θ⁻ a little toward θ: θ⁻ ← τ·θ + (1−τ)·θ⁻, with a small τ (the real agent's default: 0.005). No jumps — θ⁻ tracks θ continuously, just much more slowly.

sections.heading: Worked arithmetic: how slow is "slowly"?
sections.sourceHtml:
Worked arithmetic: how slow is "slowly"?

Suppose θ jumps to a new value and then holds perfectly still (an idealization, just to isolate how fast θ⁻ catches up). After n soft-update steps with rate τ, the remaining gap between θ⁻ and θ has shrunk by a factor of (1−τ)ⁿ — each step closes a fixed fraction τ of whatever gap is left, so the untouched fraction keeps compounding. Solving for the number of steps needed to close half the gap:

(1 - τ)^n = 0.5 n = ln(0.5) / ln(1 - τ) τ = 0.005: n = ln(0.5) / ln(0.995) = -0.6931 / -0.005013 ≈ 138.2 → roughly 139 steps for θ⁻ to close half the gap to a θ that jumped and then held still.

That's the concrete meaning behind "slowly tracks": with train_freq=4 (the real agent updates every 4 environment steps), 139 training steps is roughly 556 environment steps, more than ten 52-step episodes. This conversion counts optimizer updates separately from environment transitions; it assumes one soft update per optimizer step and an online network that holds still. Target lag can help stability, but does not guarantee convergence.

target = online aliases the same model. Make an independent copy and compute target outputs under torch.no_grad(); merely delaying an alias does not preserve old parameters. The lab uses hard copies every eight optimizer updates, while the plan may specify soft updates. Both schedules must state their counting units.

Investigate snapshots and replay in the stability lab.

sections.heading: Why in-order training data is a problem, even with a stable target
sections.sourceHtml:
Why in-order training data is a problem, even with a stable target

Consecutive transitions within an episode can be highly correlated. Updating repeatedly from a narrow slice can overemphasize those states and forget earlier ones. Random replay reduces dependence on collection order and reuses experience; it does not make the environment stationary or guarantee independent data. Gradient descent itself does not require i.i.d. inputs in all settings.

Concretely: if the last 20 gradient steps were all computed from laps 30–50 of the same race, the network has effectively been told "the world looks like late-race, high tyre age" 20 times in a row. Its weights drift to fit that narrow slice well, at the expense of whatever they'd learned about early-race states — not because early-race states got harder, but because nothing about them has been seen in a while. This is the same class of problem as page 03's, from the other side: page 03 was about the target drifting under the network being trained; this is about the network drifting because of what it's being shown, moment to moment.

sections.heading: The fix: store, then sample
sections.sourceHtml:
The fix: store, then sample

Instead of training on the transition that just happened, store every transition (s, a, r, s', terminated, truncated) in a buffer as it's experienced, and train on a randomly sampled mini-batch drawn from the whole buffer. This buys two distinct things, worth naming separately because page 07 revisits both:

  • Breaking temporal correlation — a random sample from a buffer holding thousands of transitions from many different points in many different races looks far closer to i.i.d. than the raw stream of one race's laps in order.
  • Sample efficiency — each transition, once stored, can be sampled and trained on many times over its life in the buffer, instead of being used for exactly one gradient step and discarded, getting more learning signal out of the same amount of environment interaction.

sections.heading: A minimal replay buffer
sections.sourceHtml:
A minimal replay buffer

As a baseline idea, before page 07 complicates it: fixed capacity; once full, the oldest transition is overwritten by the newest (a ring buffer, FIFO); sampling draws a batch uniformly at random from whatever is currently stored. Nothing about "which transitions are more useful to revisit" enters yet — every stored transition is equally likely to be picked, regardless of how surprising or routine it was.

Not all transitions are equally worth replaying

Uniform sampling treats a routine "stay out, nothing changes" transition exactly the same as a rare, strategically decisive pit-stop transition — even though the buffer will hold vastly more of the former than the latter simply because "stay out" is the correct action on most laps. Named here, developed fully on page 07 once the dueling architecture (page 05) and Double DQN (page 06) have given the target network something more refined to compute, and once there's a concrete number — how rare pit transitions actually are in this project's races — to make the problem specific rather than abstract.

Uniform replay samples retained entries with replacement; each has probability 1/N. A minibatch can include duplicates. A positive sampling probability is not a promise that a rare item appears in a particular batch. Stop collection at termination or truncation, but retain the distinction for target bootstrapping.

Try FIFO retention and seeded replay sampling.

sections.heading: The Dueling Architecture: Separating "How Good Is This Spot" from "Which Move Helps"
sections.sourceHtml:
The Dueling Architecture: Separating "How Good Is This Spot" from "Which Move Helps"

On this problem, one action is correct on roughly 85% of laps. A network that must learn six independent numbers per state is solving a harder problem than it needs to.

sections.heading: The motivating observation
sections.sourceHtml:
The motivating observation

In this project's races, "stay out" is the correct action on roughly 85% of laps — the real plan's own estimate. A single shared output head, predicting Q(s,a) for all six actions from the same trunk with no further structure, still has to learn a genuinely separate number for every one of those six actions at every state, even though five of them are usually near-identical, low-value alternatives to the one action that actually matters at that moment.

sections.heading: Value/advantage decomposition
sections.sourceHtml:
Value/advantage decomposition

Split the question "how good is action a at state s" into two smaller questions:

  • V(s) — how good is it to be in this state at all, regardless of which action gets taken next.
  • A(s,a) — how much better or worse is this specific action than the state's average action.

Combined: Q(s,a) = V(s) + A(s,a). Why this helps concretely for this problem: V(s) can absorb "it's lap 15, tyres are fine, this is generally a fine spot to be in" once, shared across all six actions, while A(s,a) only has to capture the much smaller signal "...and pitting right now specifically would be a mistake." The large, mostly action-independent part of the answer and the small, action-specific correction are learned by two different parts of the network, instead of one head having to learn their sum from scratch, independently, for each of six actions.

sections.heading: The identifiability problem
sections.sourceHtml:
The identifiability problem

Q(s,a) = V(s) + A(s,a) has no unique solution for V and A given only Q. Adding any constant c to V(s) and subtracting the same c from every A(s,a) at that state leaves every Q(s,a) unchanged:

Suppose the true Q-values at some state are Q = [-2, -5, -3] (3 actions) Decomposition A: V = 0, A = [-2, -5, -3] → V + A = [-2, -5, -3] ✓ Decomposition B: V = -10, A = [8, 5, 7] → V + A = [-2, -5, -3] ✓ Both decompositions produce identical Q. Nothing in the sum alone can tell them apart.

A network trained only on the resulting Q could put an arbitrary, unconstrained shifting constant into either stream — V could drift toward +1,000,000 and A toward −1,000,002 and the loss would never notice, since the loss only ever sees the sum.

sections.heading: The fix: pin the advantage stream's mean to zero
sections.sourceHtml:
The fix: pin the advantage stream's mean to zero

Replace the plain sum with Q(s,a) = V(s) + (A(s,a) − mean_a A(s,·)). Subtracting the mean of A(s,·) forces mean_a A(s,·) = 0 to hold by construction, which removes the shifting degeneracy: exactly one decomposition now satisfies both "sums to the right Q" and "the advantage stream's mean is zero" — decomposition B above fails that second requirement (mean([8, 5, 7]) ≈ 6.67 ≠ 0), decomposition A passes it (mean([-2, -5, -3]) ≈ -3.33... — actually check with the corrected version below):

Decomposition A, mean-subtracted: A' = A - mean(A) = [-2, -5, -3] - (-10/3) = [-2+3.33, -5+3.33, -3+3.33] = [1.33, -1.67, 0.33] V' = V + mean(A) = 0 + (-10/3) = -3.33 Check: V' + A' = [-3.33+1.33, -3.33-1.67, -3.33+0.33] = [-2, -5, -3] ✓, and mean(A') = 0 ✓ Decomposition B, mean-subtracted: A' = A - mean(A) = [8, 5, 7] - 6.67 = [1.33, -1.67, 0.33] V' = V + mean(A) = -10 + 6.67 = -3.33 Check: same V' and A' as decomposition A — the mean-subtraction collapses every degenerate decomposition onto the same unique one.

Both starting decompositions land on the same (V', A') once the mean is subtracted — the formula makes the split unique, no matter what arbitrary constant a not-yet-converged network happened to put into V versus A.

sections.heading: Architecture: two heads on a shared trunk
sections.sourceHtml:
Architecture: two heads on a shared trunk

Matched to the real DuelingDQN: the shared trunk from page 02 (Linear(16→128) → ReLU → Linear(128→128) → ReLU) feeds two separate small heads — a value stream (Linear(128→64) → ReLU → Linear(64→1), producing the single scalar V(s)) and an advantage stream (Linear(128→64) → ReLU → Linear(64→6), producing one scalar per action, A(s,·)). The two streams' outputs are combined by this page's formula to produce the six Q(s,a) values the rest of the agent uses exactly as before. This is the first place the primer's forward-pass mechanics (page 02) get used on something DQN-specific rather than a toy example — everything about how each linear layer and ReLU computes its output is unchanged; only the fact that there are now two output heads sharing one trunk is new.

sections.heading: Double DQN
sections.sourceHtml:
Double DQN

Vanilla DQN uses r+γ max Qtarget(s′,a). Double DQN separates action selection from evaluation: online selects the largest legal estimate, target supplies its value. Target computation is detached and true termination has no continuation.

selected = online_next.masked_fill(~legal, -torch.inf).argmax(1)
continuation = target_next.gather(1, selected[:, None]).squeeze(1)
target = reward + gamma * continuation

Apply this only to nonterminal rows; terminal rows may have no legal successor. For online [5,4,100], target [1,7,99] and mask [true,true,false], reward 1 and γ=.5 give Double target 1.5, versus vanilla 4.5. Noisy maximization can produce upward bias; the method mitigates a source of bias without a universal performance guarantee.

Primary Double DQN paper

sections.heading: Prioritized experience replay
sections.sourceHtml:
Prioritized experience replay

Retain raw priority p=|TD error|+ε. The sampling mass is p^α, so probabilities normalize those masses. α=0 recovers uniform replay. Insert a new item with the maximum retained raw priority, or 1 for an empty buffer. Applying α before storage and again at sampling is a different, erroneous exponent.

Importance weights are (N P(i))^(−β). The lab normalizes by the maximum over all retained entries; this convention differs from minibatch-only normalization. β=0 removes correction. Use mean(weight × per-item squared error), with weights detached. For [1,4,9], α=.5, β=1: probabilities [1/6,1/3,1/2], weights [1,.5,1/3].

Sampling is with replacement. Uniform replay does not make rare retained entries impossible to sample; PER changes allocation and introduces a correction problem.

Primary PER paper

sections.heading: The reward-scale trap
sections.sourceHtml:
The reward-scale trap

Reward magnitudes affect target magnitudes, losses and gradients. If predictions and targets both scale by c, squared loss scales by c². A fixed optimizer step or clipping threshold therefore need not behave equivalently after scaling.

Large or flat loss alone does not identify a reward-scale bug. Inspect finite tensors, selected-action shapes, terminal flags, detached targets, reward ranges and gradient norms first. Compare returns on the original reward scale. Report any normalization and undo it for comparisons that require original units.

Exercise: compute MSE for errors [1,−2], then [10,−20]. The losses are 2.5 and 250. Explain why that calculation does not predict an agent’s return.

sections.heading: Build it yourself
sections.sourceHtml:
Build it yourself

Use four small stages rather than one large agent. First implement tensor prediction, mean loss and an SGD update against fixed labels. Next implement FIFO replay and a detached, independently stored target. Then add online selection with target evaluation and a centered dueling head. Finally implement raw priorities and fixed importance weights.

Run each downloaded pack’s checks before integrating it. The stability pack also provides a small chain-training CLI and three equal-budget ablations. Run multiple seeds; do not require one variant to win. The supervised fit is a warm-up, not DQN.

Help remains opt-in in each lab; predictions and explanations are yours.

sections.heading: This project, formalized
sections.sourceHtml:
This project, formalized

Transfer the mechanisms through contracts. State features form an input batch (B,D); the value network returns (B,A); a chosen action gathers one prediction per transition. Replay stores state, action, reward, next state, true termination and truncation separately. Only true termination removes a continuing-task bootstrap.

Legal masks must match the action space and enter exploration and successor selection. Specify whether target synchronization counts environment steps or optimizer updates. The teaching chain uses hard copies every eight optimizer updates; a project may instead specify soft updates. These are different schedules.

Before following your Phase 5 implementation plan, map its feature/action sizes, reward units, replay capacity, target schedule and raw priority convention to these contracts. The small lab hyperparameters are teaching choices, not recommended production settings.

sections.heading: Code walkthrough
sections.sourceHtml:
Code walkthrough

This walkthrough refers to the supplied standalone exercise files, which you can inspect and run now. It does not assume a production DQN agent has already been implemented.

  1. README.md defines functions, shapes and run commands.
  2. exercise_common.py defines validation helpers and the small witness CLI.
  3. starter.py is your implementation surface; broken.py contains deliberate defects.
  4. checks.py imports your chosen candidate and verifies independent numerical examples and invariants without importing the solution.
  5. In the network pack, compare.py fits fixed labels and reports held-out error. In stability, it collects chain transitions, samples replay, computes detached targets, updates selected predictions, then synchronizes on the optimizer schedule.

Optional solution.py is reference help. Inspect it only when you request it. Trace one transition through the learner before scaling up.

sections.heading: Glossary
sections.sourceHtml:
Glossary

Forward pass
Compute outputs from inputs and parameters.
Scalar loss
One objective differentiated by autograd.
Replay
Resample retained transitions; FIFO controls retention, not sampling order.
Target snapshot
Independent parameter storage with a specified refresh schedule.
Detachment
Prevent a computation from contributing gradients.
Double DQN
Online selects the successor action; target evaluates it.
Dueling
Value plus row-centered advantages represent action values.
Raw priority
Positive error-derived quantity before exponentiation.
Importance weight
Correction for changed sampling probabilities, fixed during differentiation.
Ablation
Remove a mechanism under stated budgets and conditions; not a correctness proof.

sections.heading: Why this phase is different from the one before it
sections.sourceHtml:
Why this phase is different from the one before it

Phase 4 page 05 already named the wall tabular methods hit: a Q-table needs a finite number of discrete states, and no binning scheme is fine enough to represent the optimal policy without exploding past what a fixed training budget can visit. Phase 4 page 06 then showed that wall isn't hypothetical — the real plan's first tire_age binning scheme was coarse enough to erase the exact decision the DP oracle could tell apart.

Phase 5 doesn't fix the binning. It removes the table. Q(s,a) stops being a lookup and becomes a function Q(s,a;θ) that a neural network computes — so two states that would never have shared a table cell can still be recognized as "similar" and share what's been learned about them. Everything else carries over unchanged: the Bellman target, the TD-error idea, even the ε-greedy exploration schedule from Phase 4 page 03. Only how the number gets stored and updated changes, and this set exists to make that change concrete rather than magical.

Scope, precisely

This set teaches value-based deep RL exactly as the real plan uses it: a small MLP replacing the Q-table, the two instabilities that come with training a network online (a moving target, correlated data) and their standard fixes (a target network, an experience replay buffer), and the three specific techniques the real agent layers on top — the dueling architecture, Double DQN, and prioritized experience replay (PER) — plus the reward-scale trap the project's own audit already flags as the most likely reason this phase looks broken when it isn't. It does not cover multi-car states, rival modeling, self-play, or anything from Phase 6 onward, even as a preview, and it does not turn into a general deep-learning course — the neural-network primer on page 02 covers exactly the mechanics DQN needs and stops there.

sections.heading: What breaks, and what doesn't
sections.sourceHtml:
What breaks, and what doesn't

Phase 1's state has 16 features, every one of them about the agent's own car — its tyre compound, tyre age, laps remaining, the weather, whether a safety car is out. Adding four more cars to the same race changes none of that. compute_lap_time is unchanged: the agent's own tyres degrade exactly the way Phase 0's calibration says they do, regardless of who else is on track. What's new is a second question layered on top of the first: it's no longer enough to drive your own race well, because now there's a notion of relative outcome — position, gap to the cars around you — that depends on choices the agent never makes.

sections.heading: Three new state features
sections.sourceHtml:
Three new state features

The real plan adds exactly three: gap_to_car_ahead, gap_to_car_behind (both in seconds, normalized by a 60-second cap), and position_normalized (position / n_cars). The observation grows from Phase 1's 16 dimensions to N_OBS_MULTI = N_OBS_SINGLE + N_NEW_FEATURES = 19.

Why these three, and not — say — the full ordered list of every rival's tyre age and compound: the same Markov-sufficiency argument Phase 1 page 06 made about the single-car state applies again. The agent's next decision only needs to know what's immediately relevant to it: is there a car close enough ahead to be worth attacking or close enough behind to be a threat, and roughly how well is the race going overall. The rest of the field's internal state (what tyres rival #3 is on, four cars back) doesn't change what the agent should do this lap, so it doesn't belong in the state any more than cumulative_race_time_so_far belonged in Phase 1's.

Consequence for the Phase 5 network

The observation width changing from 16 to 19 isn't just a documentation detail — it means DuelingDQN's first Linear layer, sized for a 16-wide input, has to be rebuilt for 19. A checkpoint trained on the single-car environment cannot be reloaded as-is for Phase 6; a fresh network has to be constructed with the new input width and trained from scratch. This is worth knowing before training day, not discovering as a shape-mismatch error.

sections.heading: Rivals as fixed scripts, not learners
sections.sourceHtml:
Rivals as fixed scripts, not learners

The other four (or however many) cars in the race are not RL agents. They follow deterministic, pre-defined pit-stop plans — a strategy is just a starting compound and a list of (lap, new_compound) pairs, chosen before the race and never adapted mid-race based on what the agent does. This is a deliberate simplification with a name and a payoff: it sidesteps the multi-agent non-stationarity problem entirely (page 07 explains exactly what that problem is and why avoiding it here is the right call), which is precisely why fixed rivals are the sensible first step before Phase 8's self-play, where rivals do learn and adapt.

From the agent's point of view, a fixed-script rival's behavior is just one more piece of the environment it needs to react to — no different in kind from the weather trace or the safety-car process it already has to handle. All of it is given, not something the agent's actions can change the rules of.

sections.heading: The reward Phase 1 through 5 had
sections.sourceHtml:
The reward Phase 1 through 5 had

-lap_time, every step. Summed over an episode, this equals -total_race_time exactly — the dense, per-step reward literally is the true objective, not a proxy standing in for it. There was never any question of whether the reward measured the right thing; the only open questions were about learning it well.

sections.heading: What the equivalent reward for "race well" would be
sections.sourceHtml:
What the equivalent reward for "race well" would be

If the goal shifts from "go as fast as possible" to "finish as high as possible relative to rivals," the equally honest reward is final position. It exists, and it's exactly what the agent should care about — but it's sparse: known only once, on the terminal step of the episode, after hundreds of per-lap decisions have already been made. Every lap in between contributes to that eventual position, but none of them get told, in the moment, whether the choice just made helped or hurt.

sections.heading: The credit-assignment problem
sections.sourceHtml:
The credit-assignment problem

When a reward arrives many steps after the decisions that caused it, the learning signal has to somehow apportion credit backward across every intervening step — did lap 14's early pit help or hurt the eventual P3 finish, as opposed to lap 31's tyre choice, or lap 40's overtake attempt? TD learning (Phase 4) already does a version of this through bootstrapping, propagating value backward one step at a time. But a reward that's exactly zero for fifty consecutive steps and then one number at the very end gives that machinery very little to work with per update, compared to Phase 1 through 5's fully dense -lap_time, which supplied a learning signal on every single lap.

sections.heading: Dense proxies, and their own failure mode
sections.sourceHtml:
Dense proxies, and their own failure mode

The obvious fix is a denser proxy reward — something computable every lap that's correlated with the true sparse goal. The real plan offers two, and they sit at different points on a real tradeoff:

  • lap_time_plus_position — the familiar dense -lap_time every lap, plus a one-time terminal bonus scaled by final position (position_bonus_scale = 20.0 seconds-equivalent per position). This is still mostly the honest per-lap signal, with a shaped nudge toward caring about position layered on top only at the end.
  • gap_change — a reward every lap for closing the gap to the leader (or car ahead). Dense every step, unlike the terminal-only bonus above — but it's a proxy for the real goal, not the goal itself.

The real plan names gap_change's own risk explicitly, and it's worth taking seriously rather than dismissing as a hypothetical: an agent rewarded for closing gaps every lap has a direct incentive to push its tyres harder right now for a short-term gap-closing gain, even if that means degrading them faster and paying for it with a slower final stint — a decision that could cost a podium finish later in exchange for a reward bump now. This is the general shape of reward hacking (sometimes called Goodhart's-law-style optimization): once a proxy stands in for the real objective, the fastest way to raise the proxy's number isn't always the same as the best way to achieve the thing the proxy was supposed to measure.

Not a hypothetical

docs/idea.md's own "common pitfalls" section names this as the #1 RL debugging trap, project-wide: a rising learning curve isn't proof of anything by itself, because the agent may be exploiting a flaw in the reward function rather than learning good strategy. gap_change is Phase 6's most concrete, plannable instance of exactly that risk — which is precisely why it's worth training deliberately rather than avoiding it out of caution.

sections.heading: Why the real plan trains three designs instead of choosing one
sections.sourceHtml:
Why the real plan trains three designs instead of choosing one

Given this tradeoff, the real plan doesn't try to reason its way to the single best reward design up front. It trains all three — lap_time_plus_position, gap_change, and a third design, potential_shaping (page 03) — and compares what each one actually produces: does gap_change visibly push tyres harder (checkable via average tyre age at pit stops)? Does one converge faster than the others? Which produces the best actual race outcome? This is presented in the real plan as good practice — try the tradeoff empirically and report what happened — not as a gap where the plan should have just picked one.

sections.heading: Ad-hoc shaping can change the answer
sections.sourceHtml:
Ad-hoc shaping can change the answer

Nothing stops a designer from adding any extra term to a reward to make learning faster — a bonus for exploring a certain area, a penalty for a certain action. But nothing about an arbitrary extra term guarantees it leaves the optimal policy alone. A quick illustration: imagine adding a flat bonus for making any pit stop at all, meant only to encourage the agent to try pitting early in training. If that bonus is large enough, it can make pitting look attractive regardless of tyre age — the shaped optimum genuinely becomes "pit constantly," a different, worse policy than the true optimum. Ad-hoc shaping doesn't just risk slowing learning down; done carelessly, it risks teaching the wrong thing outright.

sections.heading: The theorem
sections.sourceHtml:
The theorem

Ng, Harada & Russell (1999) show that shaping terms of one specific form are safe. Given any function of state alone, Φ(s) — a "potential function" — define the shaping reward as the discounted difference in potential between consecutive states:

F(s, a, s') = γ·Φ(s') − Φ(s)

Add this to the base reward at every step. Use the same discount as the task. For a finite episode of T transitions, the shaped return differs by −Φ(s₀) + γ^T Φ(s_T). Zero terminal potential removes the endpoint term, giving the same shift for all routes from a fixed start. For a continuing discounted task, bounded potential and a vanishing discounted tail provide the corresponding condition. These assumptions preserve the objective; faster learning is not guaranteed.
