sections.heading: Why, without the full proof
sections.sourceHtml:
Why, without the full proof

Take any policy π and check what the shaped action-value function Q'^π(s,a) works out to, using the ordinary Bellman equation with the shaped reward substituted in:

Q'^π(s,a) = E[ r + F(s,a,s') + γ·V'^π(s') ] Try the guess V'^π(s) = V^π(s) − Φ(s) (shift every value by the potential at that state) and check it's self-consistent: Q'^π(s,a) = E[ r + γ·Φ(s') − Φ(s) + γ·(V^π(s') − Φ(s')) ] = E[ r + γ·V^π(s') ] − Φ(s) (the γ·Φ(s') terms cancel) = Q^π(s,a) − Φ(s)

Under those boundary conditions, the guess checks out: Q'^π(s,a) = Q^π(s,a) − Φ(s), for every policy π, including the optimal one. This holds state by state, not just at the start of an episode. Since Φ(s) doesn't depend on the action a, subtracting it from every Q(s,a) at a given state shifts all of that state's action-values by the same amount — which can never change which action has the highest value there:

argmax_a Q'*(s,a) = argmax_a [ Q*(s,a) − Φ(s) ] = argmax_a Q*(s,a)

The optimal action at every single state is unchanged. This is the same "subtracting something constant across the choice being compared can't change the argmax" move Phase 5 page 08 used for reward centring — reused here in a per-state rather than per-episode form.

sections.heading: One hand-worked example
sections.sourceHtml:
One hand-worked example

A toy 3-state chain: start at A, choose either a two-step route through B or a one-step direct route to the terminal state C. γ = 1. Potential: Φ(A) = 5, Φ(B) = 2, Φ(C) = 0 (zero terminal potential removes the endpoint term in this stopped-episode example).

Unshaped rewards: A→B: −3 B→C: −1 A→C (direct): −10 Unshaped returns: via B: −3 + −1 = −4 direct: −10 → Optimal choice: via B (−4 beats −10 by 6) Shaping terms, F(s,s') = Φ(s') − Φ(s), since γ=1: F(A,B) = 2 − 5 = −3 F(B,C) = 0 − 2 = −2 F(A,C) = 0 − 5 = −5 Shaped rewards: A→B: −3 + −3 = −6 B→C: −1 + −2 = −3 A→C: −10 + −5 = −15 Shaped returns: via B: −6 + −3 = −9 direct: −15 → Optimal choice: via B (−9 beats −15 by 6 — same gap, same winner)

Both routes' returns shift by exactly −Φ(A) = −5 — the same constant, because Φ(C) = 0 cancels the far end of the telescoping sum and only the shared starting potential is left over. The ranking between the two options — the only thing that determines which policy is optimal — is untouched. This is the numeric face of the algebra above: shift every value at a state by the same amount, and nothing about which action looks best there can change.

The real plan's choice of Φ

The real plan's potential_shaping reward design uses Φ(s) = -position_normalized = -(position / n_cars) — "being in a better position is a better potential," so a car that moves from P4 to P2 gets a positive shaping bump exactly when it improves its standing, but invariance requires the matching task discount and correct endpoint treatment above. A nonzero terminal position potential can change the finite-episode objective. Whether the plan's actual code computes this correctly is a separate question, taken up on page 06.

Investigate all complete routes, mismatched discounts and nonzero endpoint potentials. A continuing-task truncation needs its final observation bootstrap; it is not automatically a zero-potential task terminal.

sections.heading: Dirty air, the real effect
sections.sourceHtml:
Dirty air, the real effect

A trailing F1 car loses downforce running in a leading car's aerodynamic wake — a real, well-documented effect, worse the closer the following distance. The real plan models it as a straight line: a penalty of DIRTY_AIR_MAX_PENALTY = 0.5 seconds at zero gap, falling linearly to 0.0 seconds at DIRTY_AIR_MAX_GAP = 1.5 seconds and beyond:

sections.heading: Probabilistic overtaking
sections.sourceHtml:
Probabilistic overtaking

An overtake can only be attempted within OVERTAKE_ATTEMPT_GAP = 1.0 second, and only when the attacking car is faster this lap (pace_delta < 0, where pace_delta = my_lap_time − their_lap_time). Given an attempt happens, success probability is a sigmoid in the pace advantage:

base_prob(pace_delta) = 1 / (1 + exp(5 · (pace_delta + 0.5)))

Worked by hand at the one point the real plan's own docstring names explicitly — 0.5 seconds faster:

pace_delta = −0.5 (0.5s faster) exponent = 5 · (−0.5 + 0.5) = 5 · 0 = 0 base_prob = 1 / (1 + e^0) = 1 / 2 = 0.50 → 50%, exactly as claimed
Worth checking the other two claimed points too

The real plan's docstring also claims "80% at 1.0s faster, 95% at 1.5s faster." Running the same formula at those two points tells a different story:

pace_delta = −1.0 (1.0s faster) exponent = 5 · (−1.0 + 0.5) = 5 · (−0.5) = −2.5 base_prob = 1 / (1 + e^−2.5) = 1 / (1 + 0.082) ≈ 0.924 → 92.4%, not 80% pace_delta = −1.5 (1.5s faster) exponent = 5 · (−1.5 + 0.5) = 5 · (−1.0) = −5.0 base_prob = 1 / (1 + e^−5.0) = 1 / (1 + 0.0067) ≈ 0.993 → 99.3%, not 95%

The formula and the two later numbers in its own comment don't agree — a small, low-stakes example of exactly the habit page 10 asks for on a larger scale: hand-check a formula against what its own documentation claims, rather than trusting the comment. It changes nothing about whether the model is reasonable (a steeper-than-advertised sigmoid is still a sigmoid), only what the reader should expect to see if they log actual pass rates during training.

On top of base_prob, a small bonus rewards persistence: follow_bonus = min(0.1 × laps_following, 0.2) — up to 0.2 extra probability after two or more consecutive laps within range, capped, and the total capped again at 0.95 so an overtake is never a certainty no matter how large the pace advantage.

A modeling choice, not a law of physics

This sigmoid, with these particular constants, is one reasonable functional form among many — a step function or a differently-shaped curve could stand in just as well. What matters for the rest of this project is understanding what the model is trying to capture (a bigger pace advantage should mean a meaningfully higher pass probability; extended following should help a little), well enough to defend or adjust the constants later, not memorizing this exact formula as the only correct one.

sections.heading: The undercut, as real F1 strategy
sections.sourceHtml:
The undercut, as real F1 strategy

A driver pits before a rival running comparable pace. Fresh tyres let them post much faster out-laps than the rival — still on old, worn tyres — can respond to in time. By the time the rival reacts and pits too, the undercutting driver has converted a pit stop into real track position. This only works because of one specific fact about real racing: the rival cannot simply drive around the pitted car once it rejoins the track. Track position, once lost in traffic, is genuinely hard to get back — that difficulty is the entire reason the undercut is a strategy worth timing carefully, rather than just an incidental side effect of pitting.

sections.heading: What the plan's pseudocode actually computes
sections.sourceHtml:
What the plan's pseudocode actually computes

Every position in the plan's _update_positions() is recomputed each lap by sorting every car's cumulative total_time, ascending. Walk through what that implies directly: if nothing in the model prevents a faster car from instantly passing a slower one — if position is purely a readout of who has accumulated less time — then there is no separate value to timing a pit stop relative to a rival's. "Pit early while you're faster" and "just be faster" become the same statement, because being ahead or behind on track never costs or saves any time on its own. The model has no notion of being stuck.

Why this makes attempt_overtake pointless even before any bug

An overtake model only has something to do if there's a state — being stuck behind a car you can't get past — that succeeding releases you from. Without a constraint that holds a faster car to a slower one's pace, no car in this simulation is ever stuck behind anything. There is nothing for an overtake to overcome, independent of whether attempt_overtake's own bookkeeping is correct (page 06 covers a bug in that bookkeeping too, but fixing that bug alone would not fix this).

sections.heading: The fix: one line that turns position into a resource
sections.sourceHtml:
The fix: one line that turns position into a resource

Add a blocking constraint to the multi-car lap-time model — a car close behind another, that hasn't successfully overtaken it, is held to at best the pace of the car ahead plus the dirty-air cost from page 04:

if gap_to_car_ahead < OVERTAKE_ATTEMPT_GAP and not overtake_succeeded: lap_time = max(own_lap_time, car_ahead_lap_time + dirty_air_penalty(gap))

That single line is the entire difference between a race where position is just a scoreboard reading of accumulated time, and a race where being behind has a real, ongoing cost that only an overtake can end. With it in place, attempt_overtake finally has a job: it's the mechanism that releases a car from the pace cap this line imposes. Positions still ultimately follow from cumulative time — nothing about how position is computed changes — but now the lap times feeding into that computation depend on who's stuck behind whom, which is exactly the missing ingredient the undercut needs to exist at all.

sections.heading: Traced forward: why this blocks Phase 8, not just Phase 6
sections.sourceHtml:
Traced forward: why this blocks Phase 8, not just Phase 6

Phase 8's headline Definition of Done is a bimodal undercut/overcut pit-timing histogram emerging from training — pit-lap choices clustering around "just before a rival" and "just after," arising on their own rather than being explicitly programmed. That emergence is unreachable without this fix, for the same reason stated above: an agent cannot learn to exploit a track-position advantage that its simulator doesn't actually grant for being ahead. Phase 8's own Risks table, written before this gap was found, misdiagnoses the eventual symptom (undercut/overcut not appearing) as a possible bug in the out-lap warmup penalty. The warmup penalty is implemented correctly — the missing piece was always here, one phase earlier, in whether position carries any cost or benefit of its own.

The general shape of this kind of gap

This isn't an off-by-one or a typo — it's a case where a system was built with all the visible pieces of a mechanism (overtaking probabilities, dirty air, position tracking) but missing the one structural constraint that makes those pieces interact meaningfully. Worth recognizing the shape: individually-reasonable components can add up to nothing, if the piece connecting them to consequence is never added. A test proving a faster car stuck behind a slower one gains no time until it overtakes is the concrete way to confirm this constraint actually exists, rather than assuming its presence from the existence of the surrounding pieces.

sections.heading: E1 — Rival lap times are double-counted
sections.sourceHtml:
E1 — Rival lap times are double-counted

RivalState.advance_lap already ends with self.total_time += lap_time. The plan's F1MultiCarEnv.step() then loops over every rival and adds the same lap time a second time. Every rival accumulates roughly double its true race time and finishes near-last, every single race.

The general lesson: two different pieces of code, written at different points in the plan, both believing they own the update to the same piece of state. This is an ordinary class of mistake — but here its effect (rivals always finish last) looks exactly like a learning curve succeeding. An agent evaluated against permanently-crippled rivals will "beat" all of them from the very first untrained episode, and a rising reward curve on top of that tells the developer nothing true about whether strategy is being learned. sections.heading: E2 — The overtake result gets silently overwritten
sections.sourceHtml:
E2 — The overtake result gets silently overwritten

When attempt_overtake succeeds, the plan decrements self._agent_position by one. Two lines later, _update_positions() recomputes every position from scratch from cumulative time — discarding that decrement, since the underlying total_time values never changed.

The general lesson: a stateful, partial update to a quantity, immediately followed by a from-scratch recomputation of that same quantity in the same step, where the recomputation silently wins. This pattern — update, then unconditionally recompute — is worth recognizing on sight as a place bugs like to hide, because both halves individually look correct in isolation; the bug only exists in their sequencing.

sections.heading: E3 — Dirty air is charged to the reward but not the dynamics
sections.sourceHtml:
E3 — Dirty air is charged to the reward but not the dynamics

Even once page 05's blocking fix is in place, the plan's _compute_reward separately subtracts dirty_air from the reward — but dirty_air is never added to agent_lap_time, so it never reaches _agent_total_time, never affects position, and never affects gaps.

The load-bearing lesson of this page

The agent is penalized in its reward for a pace loss that its own recorded lap time says never happened. Whenever a reward disagrees with what the dynamics actually did, the fastest way for a learning agent to raise its reward is to exploit the gap between what it's scored on and what actually moves it through the environment — that gap is a reward-hacking surface, not a cosmetic inconsistency. docs/idea.md's "common pitfalls" section names exactly this shape of failure as the single most common RL debugging trap on this entire project: a rising learning curve isn't proof of anything by itself, because the agent may be exploiting a flaw in the reward function rather than learning good strategy. Page 05's fix (adding dirty air to the lap time itself, so -lap_time picks it up automatically) is what closes this specific instance of the gap.

sections.heading: E5 — A principled label on an unprincipled implementation
sections.sourceHtml:
E5 — A principled label on an unprincipled implementation

Directly following from page 03. The plan's reward_type="potential_shaping" branch computes:

return base_reward - dirty_air + (1/n_total if pos_norm < 1.0 else 0)

That is a flat bonus for not being in last place — a constant, awarded regardless of whether position improved, worsened, or stayed the same this lap. It stores no Φ(s) from the previous step and computes no difference. Page 03's theorem — that potential-based shaping provably cannot change the optimal policy — says nothing whatsoever about this reward, because this reward is not potential-based shaping in the sense the theorem covers. It's ad-hoc shaping (page 03's own opening example, a flat bonus unrelated to any state-only potential difference) shipping under the theorem's name.

The fix: store self._prev_potential in reset() and at the end of each step(), and compute the actual difference F = γ·Φ(s') − Φ(s) with Φ(s) = -position_normalized, exactly as page 03 worked through.

The general lesson: naming a piece of code after a theorem doesn't make the theorem's guarantee apply to it. The guarantee attaches to the specific mathematical form, not the variable or branch name — worth checking that an implementation actually matches the form a cited result depends on, rather than trusting a comment or a config string that claims it does.

sections.heading: E6 — Four smaller items, same discipline of asking "why"
sections.sourceHtml:
E6 — Four smaller items, same discipline of asking "why"

ItemWhat's wrongWhy it matters
E6apace_delta = agent_lap_time − car_ahead.total_time / self._current_lapCompares this lap's agent time to a rival's career-average time-per-lap, not that rival's time this lap (available in rival_lap_times). Silently distorts every overtake-probability calculation from page 04, worst early or late in a race when the average is furthest from current pace.
E6bsuper().step() increments _current_lap; rivals then advance using the pre-increment value while gap computations run on the post-increment valueAn off-by-one class of bug where two halves of the same step silently disagree about what lap it currently is — worth an explicit test that agent and rivals are always on the same lap index.
E6c_compute_gap_to_ahead returns a 99.0 sentinel when leading, normalized to min(99/60, 1) = 1.0Identical to the normalized value for "60 seconds behind the car ahead." The network has no way to distinguish "I am winning" from "I am a lap down" — a state-representation bug, a different category from a dynamics bug like E1–E3, worth telling apart. An explicit is_leader feature is the fix.

sections.heading: The assumption everything through Phase 5 relies on
sections.sourceHtml:
The assumption everything through Phase 5 relies on

Standard RL theory — the convergence arguments behind tabular Q-learning (Phase 4) and DQN (Phase 5) alike — assumes a fixed environment: the same state, given the same action, produces transitions drawn from the same fixed distribution no matter when it's visited. Every proof and every practical guarantee this project has leaned on so far takes that for granted.

sections.heading: How multiple learning agents break it
sections.sourceHtml:
How multiple learning agents break it

The assumption holds by default in every phase through Phase 5, where there's exactly one thing in the environment that changes its behavior over time: the agent itself, as it learns. It breaks the moment more than one agent in the same environment is learning simultaneously. From the RL agent's point of view, "the environment" now includes every other agent's policy — and if those policies are themselves changing as they learn, the transition dynamics the agent is trying to learn are being pulled out from under it while it learns them.

Concretely, for a version of this project where a rival was also a learning DQN: a pit-under-safety-car move that worked well against last week's version of that rival's policy might not work at all against this week's, purely because the rival adapted — not because anything about the track, the tyres, or the weather changed. The thing the agent is trying to model as "the environment's response" is itself a moving target, which is exactly the kind of situation Phase 4 and Phase 5's convergence arguments were never built to handle.

sections.heading: Why Phase 6's fixed-script rivals sidestep this cleanly
sections.sourceHtml:
Why Phase 6's fixed-script rivals sidestep this cleanly

RivalState follows a predetermined pit_laps / pit_compounds plan, decided before the race starts, with no learning update anywhere in it. From the agent's perspective, the rivals behave exactly like the weather trace or the safety-car arrival process it already has to react to: given, external, and — crucially — not changing in response to what the agent does. That's precisely what "stationary" means here. All of Phase 4 and Phase 5's theory keeps applying completely unmodified; the only things that got bigger going into Phase 6 are the state (page 01) and the reward (pages 02–03), not the class of environment the agent is learning in.

Why this is the sensible order, not a cop-out

Building the interaction machinery — gaps, blocking (page 05), overtaking, position-based reward (pages 02–03) — against opponents that hold still means every one of those pieces can be debugged and trusted on its own, without also having to ask "is this behaving oddly because of a bug, or because my rival just changed strategy mid-training?" Phase 8 adds the second, much harder problem — learning opponents — only once the first problem (does the interaction model itself work at all) is already solved and tested. Fixed rivals aren't a simplification taken because non-stationarity is hard to think about; they're a simplification taken so that everything else in Phase 6 has a fair chance to be verified correctly before a second source of difficulty is layered on top.

sections.heading: Stage 0 — a toy race, deliberately built without any blocking rule
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 0 — a toy race, deliberately built without any blocking rule

Two cars, a fixed number of ticks, each with a per-tick pace the reader scripts directly (no compound/tyre model needed — that's not what this page is teaching):

class ToyCar:
    def __init__(self, name, pace_schedule):
        self.name = name
        self.pace_schedule = pace_schedule   # list of per-tick pace, one entry per tick
        self.total_time = 0.0

    def tick_pace(self, t):
        return self.pace_schedule[t]


class TinyPaddockRace:
    """No blocking rule yet — every car's time this tick is just its own pace."""
    def __init__(self, cars):
        self.cars = cars

    def run(self, n_ticks):
        history = []
        for t in range(n_ticks):
            for car in self.cars:
                car.total_time += car.tick_pace(t)
            history.append({c.name: c.total_time for c in self.cars})
        return history

    def standings(self):
        return sorted(self.cars, key=lambda c: c.total_time)

sections.heading: Stage 1 — reproduce page 5's diagnosis: timing stops mattering without blocking
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 1 — reproduce page 5's diagnosis: timing stops mattering without blocking

Script one car (FAST) to be consistently quicker per tick than another (SLOW) that starts ahead by virtue of a head start on lap 0, and model a "pit" as one tick of a large fixed penalty added to whichever car's schedule includes it. Run it twice — pit FAST early, then pit it late — and check whether when it pits changes anything about the final gap between the two cars:

def make_schedule(base_pace, n_ticks, pit_tick=None, pit_penalty=20.0):
    sched = [base_pace] * n_ticks
    if pit_tick is not None:
        sched[pit_tick] += pit_penalty
    return sched

n_ticks = 30
slow = ToyCar("SLOW", make_schedule(base_pace=5.0, n_ticks=n_ticks))
fast_pits_early = ToyCar("FAST", make_schedule(base_pace=4.5, n_ticks=n_ticks, pit_tick=5))
fast_pits_late  = ToyCar("FAST", make_schedule(base_pace=4.5, n_ticks=n_ticks, pit_tick=25))

for fast in (fast_pits_early, fast_pits_late):
    race = TinyPaddockRace([slow, fast])
    race.run(n_ticks)
    gap = fast.total_time - slow.total_time
    print(fast.total_time, slow.total_time, gap)
# Both runs land on the same gap: pit timing only ever shifts the pit tick's
# one-time penalty, never anything about how the two cars' paces interact.
# "Pitting first when you're faster" and "just being faster" are the same
# number here — exactly page 5's conclusion, now verified by running it.

sections.heading: Stage 2 — add the blocking constraint and rerun the identical scripts
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 2 — add the blocking constraint and rerun the identical scripts

Page 05's fix, transplanted into the toy: when two cars are within a following threshold and no pass has happened this tick, the trailing car is held to (at best) the pace of the car ahead:

FOLLOW_GAP = 1.0

class BlockingPaddockRace(TinyPaddockRace):
    def run(self, n_ticks):
        history = []
        for t in range(n_ticks):
            paces = {c.name: c.tick_pace(t) for c in self.cars}
            ordered = sorted(self.cars, key=lambda c: c.total_time)
            for i, car in enumerate(ordered):
                if i == 0:
                    continue   # leader is never blocked
                ahead = ordered[i - 1]
                gap = car.total_time - ahead.total_time
                if gap < FOLLOW_GAP:
                    paces[car.name] = max(paces[car.name], paces[ahead.name])
            for car in self.cars:
                car.total_time += paces[car.name]
            history.append({c.name: c.total_time for c in self.cars})
        return history

Rerun the exact same fast_pits_early / fast_pits_late pair against BlockingPaddockRace instead of TinyPaddockRace. Now the two runs land on different final gaps — pitting early, while still ahead of (or level with) SLOW, lets FAST build a lead before SLOW can close within the follow gap and start capping its pace; pitting late risks getting caught behind SLOW first. The undercut is now representable in a system small enough to have built and checked by hand.

sections.heading: Stage 3 — a toy overtake model as the only way out of blocking
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 3 — a toy overtake model as the only way out of blocking

def try_pass(pace_advantage, rng, base_rate=0.4):
    """Simplified stand-in for page 4's sigmoid — a flat rate scaled by advantage."""
    if pace_advantage <= 0:
        return False
    prob = min(0.95, base_rate + 0.3 * pace_advantage)
    return rng.random() < prob

Wire try_pass into BlockingPaddockRace so a trailing car within FOLLOW_GAP gets one pass attempt per tick, and — if it succeeds — is exempted from the pace cap that tick. Run many seeds of a faster car starting directly behind a slower one, and log how many ticks it takes to get clear, comparing a faster-trapped car against a same-pace-trapped car:

import numpy as np

def laps_stuck(pace_gap, n_trials=500, max_ticks=40):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    stuck_counts = []
    for _ in range(n_trials):
        stuck = 0
        for t in range(max_ticks):
            if not try_pass(pace_gap, rng):
                stuck += 1
            else:
                break
        stuck_counts.append(stuck)
    return np.mean(stuck_counts)

print("faster car, avg ticks stuck:", laps_stuck(pace_gap=0.8))
print("same-pace car, avg ticks stuck:", laps_stuck(pace_gap=0.0))
# The faster car clears in visibly fewer ticks on average; a car with no
# pace advantage essentially never gets an attempt at all (pace_advantage <= 0
# skips try_pass entirely) — grounding page 4's model in code actually run.

sections.heading: Stage 4 — reward-shaping comparison on a scenario built to make ad-hoc shaping fail
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 4 — reward-shaping comparison on a scenario built to make ad-hoc shaping fail

A tiny two-choice MDP, deliberately built so the dense proxy and the true goal disagree — reusing Phase 4's tabular update rule from its own build-it-yourself page:

# States: START -> (RISKY or SAFE) -> END
# RISKY: big proxy reward now (closes a toy "gap"), but a worse true final spot
# SAFE:  smaller proxy reward now, but the better true final spot
TRUE_REWARD  = {"RISKY": -10.0, "SAFE": -4.0}    # true goal: SAFE is better
PROXY_REWARD = {"RISKY":  +6.0, "SAFE":  +1.0}    # dense proxy: RISKY looks better

POTENTIAL = {"START": 2.0, "RISKY_DONE": 0.0, "SAFE_DONE": 0.0}  # zero potentials at both task terminals

def run_variant(reward_table, shaping=None, n_episodes=3000):
    q = {"RISKY": 0.0, "SAFE": 0.0}
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    alpha, eps = 0.3, 0.2
    for _ in range(n_episodes):
        action = rng.choice(["RISKY", "SAFE"]) if rng.random() < eps else max(q, key=q.get)
        reward = reward_table[action]
        if shaping is not None:
            reward += shaping(action)
        q[action] += alpha * (reward - q[action])
    return q

q_true       = run_variant(TRUE_REWARD)
q_proxy      = run_variant(PROXY_REWARD)                                   # ad-hoc: flat, action-keyed bonus
q_shaped     = run_variant(TRUE_REWARD, shaping=lambda a:
                    POTENTIAL[f"{a}_DONE"] - POTENTIAL["START"])            # real Φ-difference, page 3's formula

for name, q in [("true reward", q_true), ("ad-hoc proxy", q_proxy), ("potential-shaped", q_shaped)]:
    print(name, q, "-> optimal:", max(q, key=q.get))
# true reward:       optimal SAFE   (matches the real goal)
# ad-hoc proxy:       optimal RISKY  (the proxy's own bonus flips the answer)
# potential-shaped:   optimal SAFE   (page 3's theorem, checked empirically:
#                                     the shaped optimum agrees with the true one)

This is page 02's tyre-pushing risk and page 03's theorem, both made concrete in code the reader ran: the ad-hoc proxy genuinely changes which action looks best, while the potential-based version — built from the exact Φ(s') − Φ(s) formula, just with an invented toy Φ — agrees with the unshaped true optimum every time.

sections.heading: Stage 5 — catch the leak: plant E5's bug on purpose
sections.sourceHtml:
Stage 5 — catch the leak: plant E5's bug on purpose

Reproduce the real plan's mistake directly: a reward branch that claims to be potential-based shaping but is actually a flat, state-independent-of-history bonus for "not in the worse outcome":

def mislabeled_shaping(action):
    """Looks like shaping. Is not: no Φ(s) is ever differenced, just a flat bonus."""
    return 0.5 if action == "SAFE" else 0.0

q_mislabeled = run_variant(TRUE_REWARD, shaping=mislabeled_shaping)
print("mislabeled 'shaping':", q_mislabeled, "-> optimal:", max(q_mislabeled, key=q_mislabeled.get))

Run this next to q_shaped from stage 4 on a version of the toy MDP where the true gap between RISKY and SAFE is made small enough for a flat 0.5 bonus to flip it (shrink TRUE_REWARD's gap and rerun both). The real Φ-difference shaping's optimal action tracks the true optimum under matching discounts and zero terminal potentials, by page 3's boundary-qualified theorem; the mislabeled version's optimal action can flip, because nothing about it was ever guaranteed not to. That's the theorem stopping being a fact taken on faith and becoming something just verified directly, on code the reader broke and then compared against code that couldn't be broken the same way.

The one-step potential example shifts both returns by −2. For nontrivial intermediate shaping and a terminal-boundary counterexample, use the route-shaping lab. Also try joint-action credit assignment and connected versus disconnected opponent mechanics.

sections.heading: The real 19-dimensional observation
sections.sourceHtml:
The real 19-dimensional observation

N_OBS_MULTI = N_OBS_SINGLE + N_NEW_FEATURES = 16 + 3 = 19, matching page 01 feature-by-feature: Phase 1's 16-dimensional single-car observation, plus gap_to_car_ahead (normalized by a 60s cap), gap_to_car_behind (same normalization), and position_normalized (position / n_cars).

Consequence for the DQN checkpoint

DuelingDQN's first Linear layer is sized for a 16-wide input (Phase 5 page 05). A Phase 6 agent needs a freshly constructed network with a 19-wide input layer — DuelingDoubleDQNAgent(obs_dim=19) — not a reload of any single-car checkpoint. This is a Definition-of-Done item in the real plan, not an implementation detail left implicit.

sections.heading: The three reward_type configs
sections.sourceHtml:
The three reward_type configs

reward_typeFormula (as written in the plan)Category (pages 02–03)
lap_time_plus_position(base_reward − dirty_air), plus position_bonus_scale × (n_total − position) only on the terminal stepDense true signal + a one-time terminal nudge — the mildest of the three
gap_change−(curr_gap − prev_gap), gap to the leader, every step; 0 during a safety carA dense proxy, with the tyre-pushing risk named on page 02
potential_shapingAs written: base_reward − dirty_air + (1/n_total if pos_norm < 1.0 else 0)Not actually potential-based shaping — this is page 06's finding E5. It's a flat bonus, not a Φ(s′) − Φ(s) difference, despite the name.

That last row is worth sitting with: the plan's own code for the reward design meant to be the "principled" one, per page 03's theorem, is the one design in the table that hasn't earned that theorem's guarantee yet. Fixing it means storing self._prev_potential and computing the real difference with Φ(s) = -position_normalized, exactly as pages 03 and 06 worked through.

sections.heading: Five fixed rival strategies
sections.sourceHtml:
Five fixed rival strategies

build_rival_strategies cycles through five pre-defined plans — each just a starting compound and a list of (pit_lap, new_compound) pairs, decided before the race and never adapted: a classic one-stop (MEDIUM → HARD), an aggressive two-stop (SOFT → MEDIUM → HARD), a conservative plan (HARD → MEDIUM), an early one-stop (SOFT → HARD), and a staggered two-stop (MEDIUM → SOFT → HARD). None of them read any information about the agent's own choices — the concrete instantiation of page 07's "stationary opponent": from the agent's point of view these five scripts are exactly as fixed and unreactive as the weather trace or the safety-car process.

sections.heading: Definition-of-Done items that exist because of pages 05–06
sections.sourceHtml:
Definition-of-Done items that exist because of pages 05–06

Several of the real plan's Definition-of-Done checkboxes are there specifically because of the design gap and bugs this set spent three pages on, not because they're generic "does the feature work" checks:

  • Blocking-model test (page 05) — a demonstrably faster car stuck behind a slower one gains no time until an overtake succeeds. Without this test passing, none of the rest of Phase 6's racing content means what it's supposed to.
  • Overtaking-changes-positions test (page 05) — positions differ between a run with overtaking enabled and one with it disabled. This is the direct check that E2 (page 06) is actually fixed, not just that attempt_overtake runs without crashing.
  • Exact-once rival accumulation (page 06, E1) — a regression test that each rival's total_time only ever increases by one lap's worth of time per tick.
  • Dirty air reaches lap time (page 06, E3) — checking the penalty shows up in _agent_total_time, not only in the reward.
  • Shaped-vs-unshaped optimum agreement (page 03 and page 06, E5) — a test confirming the fixed potential_shaping and the unshaped reward agree on the optimal policy for a small fixed scenario, the same kind of check stage 4 of page 08 just ran by hand.

sections.heading: Reading the Implementation Plan's Code
sections.sourceHtml:
Reading the Implementation Plan's Code

Unlike every code-walkthrough page in the earlier prerequisite sets, this one points at a plan's pseudocode, not a file that has actually been built and run.

Why this page is different

Phase 6 hasn't been implemented — there is no src/env/f1_multi_env.py, rival.py, or overtaking.py in the repository yet. What follows reads the pseudocode inside .antigravity/plans/phase-6-multi-car-rivals.md itself. Part of the point of this page is that a plan's own code sample is not automatically correct just because it's written in a plan — pages 05 and 06 found a missing model and five bugs in it before a single line was ever run. Reading a plan this way, before implementation starts, is the whole reason those findings exist rather than being discovered three weeks into a confusing training run.

sections.heading: Reading order
sections.sourceHtml:
Reading order

rival.py's RivalState.advance_lap first — this is where E1's double-add lives (page 06), and where the plan's own cross-phase audit flags a second issue worth knowing before reading a line further: this file, as sketched in the Phase 6 plan, still calls compute_lap_time with Phase 1's original five-argument signature. Phase 1's revised contract dropped laps_since_pit and replaced safety_car_active: bool with track_status: int — rival.py needs updating for that before it will even run against the real dynamics module. Rivals also need to call compute_pit_loss(track_status, params) rather than reading params["pit_loss"] directly, or they pay full price for pit stops the agent gets at Phase 0.5's calibrated safety-car discount (this is E6d's flip side, from page 06 — rivals need the same discount mechanism, not just a reason to want to pit under SC).

Then overtaking.py, matched directly against page 04's two formulas — nothing new to look for here beyond confirming the constants (OVERTAKE_ATTEMPT_GAP = 1.0, DIRTY_AIR_MAX_GAP = 1.5, DIRTY_AIR_MAX_PENALTY = 0.5) match what page 04 worked through by hand.

Then f1_multi_env.py's step(), in the order page 06 introduced its findings: E2 (the overwritten overtake result), E3 (dirty air reaching the reward but not the lap time), E5 (the mislabeled potential_shaping branch), and E6a–d (the career-average pace_delta, the lap-index ordering, the leader gap sentinel, rivals ignoring safety cars).

A specific pointer: where page 05's fix belongs

f1_multi_env.py's multi-car lap-time computation, as sketched in the plan, has no blocking line at all — position is computed purely from cumulative time, with nothing in the dynamics that caps a trailing car's pace. Page 05's constraint (lap_time = max(own_lap_time, car_ahead_lap_time + dirty_air_penalty(gap))) needs to be added directly to the multi-car lap-time model, not left as a comment or a follow-up — every other piece of the file's overtaking and position logic depends on this constraint existing first, per page 05's argument that attempt_overtake has nothing to overcome without it.

sections.heading: What the plan's own listed tests would — and wouldn't — catch
sections.sourceHtml:
What the plan's own listed tests would — and wouldn't — catch

Test (as listed in the plan)What it actually catchesWhat it misses
test_multi_env_positions_sum_correctlyEvery position from 1 to N is assigned exactly onceNeither E1 nor E2 — both bugs still leave some valid sorted ordering of positions, just the wrong one relative to what actually happened on track. A test that only checks the ordering is well-formed can pass while the ordering itself is meaningless.
test_dirty_air_penalty_at_zero_gap, test_dirty_air_penalty_zero_beyond_thresholdPage 04's formula, correct as written, at its two boundary valuesE3 entirely — these test the formula for dirty air, not whether its output ever reaches agent_lap_time. Both pass even with E3 present, because E3 is about a correctly-computed number never being applied, not about the number being wrong.
test_rival_uses_configured_pit_lapsA rival's tyre age resets to 1 on its scripted pit lapE1's accumulation bug — this test never inspects total_time, only tire_age.

sections.heading: The gap between "the plan's tests pass" and "the phase's goal is reachable"
sections.sourceHtml:
The gap between "the plan's tests pass" and "the phase's goal is reachable"

None of the five tests already written into the plan would catch E4 — the missing blocking model, page 05's central finding — at all. Every one of them can pass in a world with no blocking constraint whatsoever, because none of them ever asks the question page 05's proposed new test asks: does being stuck behind a faster car actually cost anything? That's exactly why the real Definition of Done had to gain new, explicit entries for the blocking model and the overtake-changes-positions check (page 09), rather than trusting the original five tests to cover a finding that came from reading the pseudocode's design, not from running any of its code.

sections.heading: Glossary
sections.sourceHtml:
Glossary

Every term used across pages 1–10 — nothing beyond them. Keep this open while reading the Phase 6 plan or its eventual code.

Scope note

Terms belonging to self-play, PettingZoo, or genuinely non-stationary multi-agent learning aren't listed here because Phase 6 doesn't implement them — page 07 previews why Phase 8 needs them, not what they are. See the eventual Phase 8 prerequisites for that vocabulary.

Multi-car state extension
The three features added to Phase 1's 16-dimensional observation for Phase 6: gap_to_car_ahead, gap_to_car_behind, position_normalized. See page 1.
Race position
A car's rank among all cars in the race, computed by sorting cumulative total_time ascending. Page 5 explains why this computation alone isn't enough to make position matter strategically.
Credit-assignment problem
The difficulty of apportioning a reward that arrives many steps after the decisions that caused it back across those decisions — acute here because "final position" is known only at the very end of an episode. See page 2.
Sparse reward
A reward that's zero (or absent) on most steps and non-zero only rarely, such as final position, known only on the terminal step. Contrasted with Phase 1–5's fully dense -lap_time. See page 2.
Reward shaping
Adding an extra term to a base reward to make learning easier or faster. Can be principled (potential-based, page 3) or ad-hoc (page 2's gap_change, page 3's pit-bonus example), with very different guarantees about whether the optimal policy is preserved.
Reward hacking / proxy optimization
An agent finding the fastest way to raise a proxy reward's number, which isn't always the same as the best way to achieve the real objective the proxy stands in for — the tyre-pushing risk named for gap_change on page 2, and the general lesson behind E3 on page 6.
Potential-based shaping
A shaping term of the specific form F(s,a,s') = γ·Φ(s') − Φ(s), for any function of state alone Φ. Ng, Harada & Russell (1999) prove this form, and only this form, preserves the optimal policy exactly. See page 3.
Potential function Φ(s)
The state-only function a potential-based shaping term is built from — the real plan's choice is Φ(s) = -position_normalized. See pages 3 and 9.
Ng-Harada-Russell theorem
Cross-reference to "potential-based shaping" above — the paper's central result, worked through via a one-step Bellman-consistency check on page 3 rather than the full proof.
Dirty air
The real aerodynamic effect where a trailing car loses downforce, and pace, running close behind another. Modeled as a linear penalty from 0.5s at zero gap to 0s at a 1.5s gap. See page 4.
Following gap / DRS-style attempt gap
The distance threshold (1.0s in the real plan) within which an overtake attempt becomes possible at all. See page 4.
Probabilistic overtaking model
The sigmoid function converting a car's pace advantage over the car ahead into a probability that an attempted pass succeeds, plus a small bonus for consecutive laps spent following. See page 4.
Track position as a resource
The idea that being ahead has value in itself, beyond the time already banked to get there — only true once a blocking constraint exists; without one, position is purely a readout of accumulated time. See page 5.
Blocking constraint
The rule that a trailing car within the following gap, absent a successful overtake, is held to at best the pace of the car ahead (plus dirty air). The one addition that makes track position a real resource. See page 5.
Undercut
Pitting before a rival on comparable pace so that fresh tyres convert into track position the rival can't immediately take back, because — with a blocking constraint in place — the rival can't simply drive around a stopped or slower car. See page 5.
Overcut
The mirror strategy: staying out longer than a rival to bank track position on old tyres before eventually pitting, betting that the time lost to degradation is worth less than the position gained by staying out. Named alongside "undercut" throughout this set; the mechanism is symmetric.
Non-stationarity
The breakdown of the fixed-environment assumption underlying standard RL convergence results, once more than one agent in the environment is learning and changing its behavior over time. See page 7; full treatment deferred to the eventual Phase 8 prerequisites.
Stationary opponent / fixed-script rival
An opponent whose behavior is decided in advance and never adapts to what the learning agent does — Phase 6's RivalState, which sidesteps non-stationarity entirely by construction. See pages 1, 7 & 9.
Double-counting bug (E1, as a general pattern)
Two separate pieces of code both updating the same piece of state, each unaware the other already did. See page 6.
Dead-code overwrite (E2, as a general pattern)
A stateful, partial update to a quantity immediately followed by a from-scratch recomputation of that same quantity, where the recomputation silently wins. See page 6.
Reward/dynamics disagreement (E3, as a general pattern)
A reward that penalizes or rewards something the actual state transitions don't reflect — a reward-hacking surface, not a cosmetic inconsistency. See page 6.

Potential-based shaping A shaping term of the specific form F(s,a,s') = γ·Φ(s') − Φ(s), for any function of state alone Φ. Ng, Harada & Russell (1999) prove this form, and only this form, preserves the optimal policy exactly. See page 3. Potential function Φ(s) The state-only function a potential-based shaping term is built from — the real plan's choice is Φ(s) = -position_normalized. See pages 3 and 9. Ng-Harada-Russell theorem Cross-reference to "potential-based shaping" above — the paper's central result, worked through via a one-step Bellman-consistency check on page 3 rather than the full proof. Dirty air The real aerodynamic effect where a trailing car loses downforce, and pace, running close behind another. Modeled as a linear penalty from 0.5s at zero gap to 0s at a 1.5s gap. See page 4. Following gap / DRS-style attempt gap The distance threshold (1.0s in the real plan) within which an overtake attempt becomes possible at all. See page 4. Probabilistic overtaking model The sigmoid function converting a car's pace advantage over the car ahead into a probability that an attempted pass succeeds, plus a small bonus for consecutive laps spent following. See page 4. Track position as a resource The idea that being ahead has value in itself, beyond the time already banked to get there — only true once a blocking constraint exists; without one, position is purely a readout of accumulated time. See page 5. Blocking constraint The rule that a trailing car within the following gap, absent a successful overtake, is held to at best the pace of the car ahead (plus dirty air). The one addition that makes track position a real resource. See page 5. Undercut Pitting before a rival on comparable pace so that fresh tyres convert into track position the rival can't immediately take back, because — with a blocking constraint in place — the rival can't simply drive around a stopped or slower car. See page 5. Overcut The mirror strategy: staying out longer than a rival to bank track position on old tyres before eventually pitting, betting that the time lost to degradation is worth less than the position gained by staying out. Named alongside "undercut" throughout this set; the mechanism is symmetric. Non-stationarity The breakdown of the fixed-environment assumption underlying standard RL convergence results, once more than one agent in the environment is learning and changing its behavior over time. See page 7; full treatment deferred to the eventual Phase 8 prerequisites. Stationary opponent / fixed-script rival An opponent whose behavior is decided in advance and never adapts to what the learning agent does — Phase 6's RivalState, which sidesteps non-stationarity entirely by construction. See pages 1, 7 & 9. Double-counting bug (E1, as a general pattern) Two separate pieces of code both updating the same piece of state, each unaware the other already did. See page 6. Dead-code overwrite (E2, as a general pattern) A stateful, partial update to a quantity immediately followed by a from-scratch recomputation of that same quantity, where the recomputation silently wins. See page 6. Reward/dynamics disagreement (E3, as a general pattern) A reward that penalizes or rewards something the actual state transitions don't reflect — a reward-hacking surface, not a cosmetic inconsistency. See page 6.

The three features added to Phase 1's 16-dimensional observation for Phase 6: gap_to_car_ahead, gap_to_car_behind, position_normalized. See page 1.

sections.heading: Why this phase is different from everything before it
sections.sourceHtml:
Why this phase is different from everything before it

Every phase through Phase 5 had exactly one car on track. The state, the reward, and the very notion of "doing well" were all about that one car's own race — a faster lap was always simply better, no matter what anyone else on track was doing. Phase 6 is the first time another agent's behavior enters the picture at all, even though that other agent is a fixed script, not something learning alongside the RL agent. That single change — one more car existing, with its own pace and its own pit stops, sharing the same track — turns out to touch the state, the reward, and the dynamics all at once, and each of those three gets its own trouble spot in this set.

Scope, precisely

This set teaches exactly what phase-6-multi-car-rivals.md needs: the multi-car state extension (gaps to the cars ahead and behind, race position), the reward-shaping problem that a "finish as high as possible" goal creates instead of "go as fast as possible," potential-based shaping as the principled version of that shaping, a probabilistic overtaking and dirty-air model, and — because the phase's own audit found something serious enough to teach directly rather than leave buried in a plan — the finding that the plan's pseudocode, as written, has no way for the undercut to ever emerge, plus the six smaller bugs that ship alongside that design gap. It does not cover self-play, PettingZoo, or anything else from Phase 8/9, beyond one deliberate exception: a short dedicated page on non-stationarity, scoped tightly to why fixed-script rivals sidestep it, since the real plan names that as the reason this phase is the sensible step before Phase 8.

Read this before anything else

This set is unusual among the five built so far. The code it eventually points to — f1_multi_env.py, rival.py, overtaking.py — does not exist in src/ yet, because Phase 6 hasn't been implemented. Pages 9 and 10 read the plan's own pseudocode, not a real, running file, and part of what they teach is the project's own audit findings against that pseudocode: a design gap serious enough that, unfixed, this phase's most interesting goal (undercut/overcut strategy) literally cannot happen, plus six smaller bugs. Reading a plan critically, before a single line of it is implemented, is itself the skill this set is trying to build alongside the RL content.

sections.heading: Topic contents
sections.sourceHtml:
Topic contents

#PageCoversWhy Phase 6 needs it
01From One Car to NWhat actually changes in the MDP when rivals are added — three new state features, rivals as fixed scriptsFrames every other page as a consequence of this one change
02What "Doing Well" Even Means NowThe credit-assignment problem, sparse vs. dense reward, the real plan's two proxy reward designs and their risksMotivates why the real plan trains and compares three separate reward designs instead of picking one
03Potential-Based ShapingNg, Harada & Russell (1999) — why F = γΦ(s′) − Φ(s) provably can't change the optimal policy, via return decomposition plus a worked exampleThe principled reward-shaping design the real plan claims to use for its third variant
04Overtaking and Dirty AirThe real linear dirty-air penalty and sigmoid overtake-probability formulas, worked against the plan's own calibration numbersThe exact math behind overtaking.py
05Why "Position = Sorted by Time" Kills the UndercutThe audit's central design-gap finding, and the one-line blocking fix that makes track position a real resourceWithout this, Phase 6's most interesting goal — and all of Phase 8 — is unreachable, no matter how long training runs
06Six Ways the Plan's Own Pseudocode Breaks Its Own PhysicsThe double-counted rival time, the dead overtake code, the reward that disagrees with the dynamics, the mislabeled shaping, and four smaller items — each taught as a reusable lessonThese bugs would each individually make a training run look like it worked when it didn't
07Non-Stationarity: Why Fixed Rivals Are the Right First StepWhy a learning opponent breaks the fixed-environment assumption Phase 4/5's theory relies on, and why scripted rivals sidestep it entirelyExplains why this phase's rivals are deliberately not learning agents, and previews why Phase 8 is harder
08Build It YourselfA staged toy multi-car race — reproduce the no-blocking failure, fix it, add overtaking, then compare reward designs on a scenario built to make ad-hoc shaping failUnderstanding by building the exact failure and fix yourself, not just reading about them
09This Project, FormalizedThe real 19-dimensional observation, the three reward_type configs, the five fixed rival strategies, and the Definition-of-Done items that exist specifically because of pages 5–6Bridges the general theory above to the specific files about to be written
10Reading the Implementation Plan's CodeA critical reading guide to the plan's pseudocode, including exactly where each audit finding lives and what its existing tests do and don't catchLine-level understanding before a single line of src/env/f1_multi_env.py gets written
11GlossaryEvery term used above, one paragraph eachQuick lookup while reading the plan or the code

sections.heading: A quick recap of the shield
sections.sourceHtml:
A quick recap of the shield

Standard RL theory — everything Phase 4 and 5 rely on — assumes the environment is stationary: the same state, visited at two different times, produces the same distribution over next states and rewards. Phase 6's rivals follow a predetermined pit_laps plan with no learning update of their own, so from the agent's point of view they're part of a fixed environment, exactly like the weather trace or the safety-car process. All of Q-learning and DQN's convergence arguments keep applying unmodified — only the state and reward got bigger.

All of Q-learning and DQN's convergence arguments keep applying unmodified — only the state and reward got bigger.

sections.heading: What breaks once the opponent is also learning
sections.sourceHtml:
What breaks once the opponent is also learning

Phase 8 lets two (or more) copies of the same kind of learner train against each other. Now the "environment," from any one agent's point of view, includes the other agent's policy — and if that policy is changing over time, so is everything the first agent is trying to learn. A pit-under-safety-car move that worked well against last week's opponent policy might not work at all against this week's, purely because the opponent adapted, not because anything about the track, tyres, or weather changed. The transition dynamics the agent's Q-learning update is trying to converge on are themselves moving under it.

A second, sharper reason experience replay needs care here

Phase 5 justified experience replay by breaking the temporal correlation between consecutive transitions. Self-play adds a second reason to be careful with it: a transition collected against an old opponent checkpoint describes a game that, strictly, no longer exists once that opponent has been replaced by a newer one in the pool. Replaying it later trains the learner against a summary of a game state that isn't the one it will actually face next. This doesn't mean replay has to be abandoned — page 03's checkpoint pool is part of how the real plan manages this — but it's worth naming as a second source of staleness beyond Phase 5's original one.

sections.heading: Three ways to structure multi-agent training
sections.sourceHtml:
Three ways to structure multi-agent training

Given that more than one agent is learning at once, there's a genuine design choice in how their learning is organized. Three points on that spectrum, briefly:

  • Independent learners. Each agent has its own separate value function (its own DQN, its own replay buffer, its own weights) and learns purely from its own experience, with no communication between agents and no shared network. From any one agent's perspective, every other agent is just part of a — now nonstationary — environment. This is the simplest setup and the one the real plan uses.
  • Parameter sharing. All agents use one shared network, trained on the combined experience of everyone. This tends to learn faster, because experience is pooled, but it implicitly assumes the agents are meaningfully symmetric (interchangeable roles) — true here, since every car runs the same strategy problem, but the real plan doesn't exploit this.
  • Centralized-training, decentralized-execution (CTDE). A shared value function (often a "centralized critic") sees the full joint state of every agent during training, while each agent still acts on its own local observation at execution time. This is more powerful — it can directly represent how one agent's action affects another's return — and more complex to implement (the more sophisticated MARL methods, such as MADDPG, are built this way).

Why independent learners is the deliberate choice here, not a corner cut: Phase 5's DuelingDoubleDQNAgent already exists as a complete, working single-agent learner. The real plan reuses it completely unmodified, one instance per car, and treats coordination-shaped behavior — the undercut, the overcut — as something that should emerge from the environment's own payoff structure (once page 06's blocking model exists) rather than something engineered into a shared critic. It's the simplest setup that can, in principle, still produce the interesting result.

Self-play isn't really chasing "the optimal policy" — it's chasing a solution to a two-player game, which is a different, relative notion of "solved."

sections.heading: Why "optimal policy" stops being the right target
sections.sourceHtml:
Why "optimal policy" stops being the right target

Every phase through Phase 6 asked for the policy that maximizes expected return against a fixed environment — a well-defined, single best answer. Self-play changes what's being maximized against: each agent picks a strategy — really, a full pit-timing policy, not a single action — and the return either agent gets depends on both agents' strategies at once. That's a two-player game, not a single-agent MDP, and "optimal" no longer has a fixed target to be optimal relative to.

sections.heading: Nash equilibrium
sections.sourceHtml:
Nash equilibrium

The natural notion of "solved" for a game like this: a pair of strategies where neither player can improve their own return by unilaterally switching strategy, holding the other player's strategy fixed.

(π_A*, π_B*) is a Nash equilibrium if Return_A(π_A*, π_B*) ≥ Return_A(π_A, π_B*) for every alternative π_A Return_B(π_A*, π_B*) ≥ Return_B(π_A*, π_B) for every alternative π_B

Neither side has a unilateral incentive to deviate. This is a genuinely different concept from Phase 4's optimal policy: there, "optimal" meant best against a fixed world; here, each player's "best" depends on what the other player is doing, so the two definitions have to hold simultaneously, each in terms of the other.

sections.heading: Best responses and empirical opponent mixtures
sections.sourceHtml:
Best responses and empirical opponent mixtures

Fictitious play responds to the empirical distribution of earlier opponent strategies. Statements about equilibrium convergence depend on the game and update assumptions and concern empirical mixtures; they do not promise convergence of the latest greedy policy or of a neural learner trained against a finite recency-biased pool.

sections.heading: The full rock-paper-scissors witness
sections.sourceHtml:
The full rock-paper-scissors witness

Rows are learner actions; columns are opponent actions. The opponent receives the negative payoff.

ROCK PAPER SCISSORS ROCK 0 −1 +1 PAPER +1 0 −1 SCISSORS −1 +1 0

Against pure ROCK, PAPER is the best response; against PAPER, SCISSORS; against SCISSORS, ROCK. If both players simultaneously best-respond to the last pure opponent, their latest actions can cycle ROCK→PAPER→SCISSORS→ROCK. Uniform play scores zero against every pure action, and neither player can improve against a uniform opponent. This is a mixed equilibrium of the full game.

The two-action ROCK/PAPER restriction has a different answer: PAPER dominates ROCK and PAPER/PAPER is an equilibrium. Against a 50/50 ROCK/PAPER opponent, PAPER scores +0.5 and ROCK −0.5; that mixture is not an equilibrium. Removing an action can remove the cycle.

Explore mixed strategies and exact opponent coverage. Beating one opponent is not proof of equilibrium.

Population-based training, in one paragraph

AlphaStar (DeepMind), referenced by name in the real plan's own docstring, is the large-scale descendant of this same idea: instead of tracking one running average opponent, maintain a whole population of diverse policies and train against a mixture of them, which both approximates fictitious play's averaging and adds robustness against being over-fit to any single opponent style. This is the direct motivation for why the real plan keeps up to 50 checkpoints in a pool, rather than training against only "the current best" — the next page works through exactly how that pool approximates the running-average idea above with discrete, sampled snapshots instead of literal averaging.

sections.heading: Why "average the strategies" needs a stand-in for a DQN
sections.sourceHtml:
Why "average the strategies" needs a stand-in for a DQN

Fictitious play tracks an empirical average of opponent strategies; a bounded, recency-biased pool is a different practical procedure with no inherited general convergence guarantee. That's a clean operation for a matrix game, where a strategy is just a probability over a handful of actions. It doesn't translate directly to a DQN: there's no meaningful way to "average" the weights of ten different neural networks and expect the result to behave like the average of their policies. The practical fix: instead of averaging weights, keep a pool of past policy snapshots (checkpoints) and sample among them — an empirical distribution over past strategies that approximates fictitious play's running average without ever averaging a single weight.

sections.heading: The real plan's sampling rule
sections.sourceHtml:
The real plan's sampling rule

Not a uniform sample over the whole pool, either. The real plan's CheckpointPool.sample() uses a recency-biased rule: with probability recency_bias = 0.7, sample uniformly from the most recent 20% of the pool; otherwise (probability 0.3), sample uniformly from the older 80%.

pool size n = 50 recent slice = most recent 20% of 50 = 10 checkpoints (n − int(0.8·n) = 50 − 40) older slice = remaining 80% of 50 = 40 checkpoints P(sample any one specific recent checkpoint) = 0.7 / 10 = 0.07 (7% each) P(sample any one specific older checkpoint) = 0.3 / 40 = 0.0075 (0.75% each) Per-checkpoint weighting, recent : older = 0.07 / 0.0075 ≈ 9.3 : 1

Roughly a 9:1 per-checkpoint weighting of recent versus old — not a flat average across all 50. This is a deliberate departure from page 02's pure running-average argument, and worth naming as a trade-off rather than a derived-from-first-principles number:

  • Too much weight on ancient checkpoints wastes training signal on opponents the learner has long since outgrown — every episode spent beating a policy from 15,000 episodes ago teaches little about the current frontier.
  • Too little weight on old checkpoints risks "chasing the tail" — re-learning only to beat the newest policy while forgetting how to beat older styles, exactly the cycling failure page 02's worked example showed for best-responding to the single latest strategy alone.

Recency bias trades current-opponent focus against retained history. Bounded eviction can still remove earlier styles; evaluate held-out coverage rather than assuming forgetting is impossible.

The self-play evaluation trap

A self-play agent's training reward curve going up only proves it's getting better at beating its own recent history — it says nothing about whether it would beat a genuinely different strategy it's never encountered, such as a Phase 3 rule-based agent (assumed background) or a human's intuition. This is exactly why the real plan's Definition of Done checks the trained learner against something outside the self-play loop entirely ("learner's mean finishing position < random agent's"), rather than trusting the self-play reward curve on its own. A rising curve inside a closed loop is evidence of progress relative to that loop, not evidence of skill in any absolute sense.

sections.heading: AEC — Agent Environment Cycle
sections.sourceHtml:
AEC — Agent Environment Cycle

AEC selects one agent at a time. The environment decides when committed actions affect dynamics and what each agent may observe; later selection does not imply visibility of another agent’s pending action. This is the natural formalization for turn-based games — card games, board games — where seeing what the previous player just did is exactly the information the next player is supposed to have.

A tiny worked example: a sequential (turn-based) variant of rock-paper-scissors, where player A moves first and player B can see A's move before choosing:

env.reset() env.agent_selection → "player_A" action_A = "rock" env.step(action_A) # player A's move is now recorded env.agent_selection → "player_B" obs_B = env.last() # obs_B sees that A played "rock" action_B = "paper" # B, seeing A's move, always wins by playing paper env.step(action_B) # In sequential play, going second with full information of the other's move # is a structural advantage — a fact that wouldn't even make sense to ask # about in the simultaneous version below.

The agent_selection attribute names whose turn it is; .last() returns that agent's own most recent observation/reward/done state. Selection order defines the API, not an information advantage. This particular sequential example reveals A’s action; a simultaneous AEC game can hide it until both commitments are collected.

sections.heading: Parallel
sections.sourceHtml:
Parallel

All agents submit actions simultaneously each timestep; the environment resolves every action together and returns a single batch of observations, rewards, terminations, and truncations, each as a dict keyed by agent id. Neither agent sees the other's action before committing to their own.

observations, infos = env.reset() actions = {"player_A": "rock", "player_B": "paper"} # chosen independently, same instant observations, rewards, terminations, truncations, infos = env.step(actions) # Both actions are submitted together — player_B's "paper" was not chosen # in response to seeing player_A's "rock"; it's the real, simultaneous # rock-paper-scissors, not the sequential-advantage version above.

The direct contrast with the AEC example above: nobody has an information advantage from acting second, because nobody acts second — every agent commits blind to what everyone else is doing this timestep.

sections.heading: Why Parallel is convenient for joint decisions
sections.sourceHtml:
Why Parallel is convenient for joint decisions

Every car on track makes its per-lap pit/stay decision independently, at the same point in the lap, without having observed what any other car decided this lap. Nothing about one car's decision this lap causally depends on having already seen another car's decision this lap — any interaction between cars (gaps closing, dirty air, an overtake attempt) is a consequence, computed after all of this lap's actions have been submitted and resolved together, via Phase 6's dynamics (assumed background). Parallel directly expresses that joint decision. AEC can also encode it by keeping pending choices hidden and resolving only after the complete action cycle; using AEC does not itself change the game’s information structure.

sections.heading: Selected-agent cleanup
sections.sourceHtml:
Selected-agent cleanup

In AEC, last() reports the selected agent’s own termination/truncation flags. Pass None for that dead agent, even if another agent remains live. Do not decide with all(env.terminations.values()). Parallel supplies an action for every current live agent; a finished one-round game leaves agents=[].

sections.heading: What the real plan does
sections.sourceHtml:
What the real plan does

The real plan's train_self_play seeds the checkpoint pool before any training happens: pool.add(learner, episode=0) stores a freshly initialized, entirely untrained network. Then pool.sample() sets epsilon = 0.0 — fully greedy — on whatever checkpoint it returns, including this very first one.

sections.heading: The general lesson, before the specific bug
sections.sourceHtml:
The general lesson, before the specific bug

A greedy policy over a randomly initialized network is not noisy, varied, or weak-but-fair. It is a deterministic function of that network's fixed random weights: given the same observation, it picks the same action, every single time, for as long as that checkpoint stays in the pool's rotation. "Untrained" describes how good the policy is. It says nothing about how varied the policy is — and those are independent properties that are easy to conflate.

Concretely, what goes wrong

If the untrained network's fixed initial weights happen to favor the "pit" action for whatever observation values it's fed, the very first opponent in the pool pits on lap 1 — and every lap after that, forever, because greedy selection over a network that never updates always returns the same answer. That's not merely a bad opponent; it's a bad opponent in a fixed, entirely predictable, non-representative way. The learner's very first training signal comes from a degenerate, repeatable game, not from anything resembling the range of strategies it will eventually have to handle.

sections.heading: Why this is easy to miss
sections.sourceHtml:
Why this is easy to miss

It looks superficially reasonable: "of course an untrained network makes a weak opponent to start with — that's fine, the learner will quickly outgrow it." That framing is about to be wrong in a way that isn't about weakness at all. The danger isn't that the first opponent is weak — a weak-but-varied opponent would be a perfectly fine, even useful, starting point. The danger is that it has zero variance: every one of the (up to) 1000 episodes before the next checkpoint is added is spent playing against the exact same fixed response, which teaches the learner to exploit one specific quirk of one specific random initialization rather than anything general.

sections.heading: The fix
sections.sourceHtml:
The fix

Either of two changes genuinely fixes this, for different reasons:

  • Seed with a stochastic policy — epsilon = 1.0, literally uniform-random action selection, for the pool's earliest entries. This restores genuine variance immediately, at the cost of the opponent being uniformly unskilled rather than merely simple.
  • Seed with Phase 3's rule-based agents (assumed background) — the real plan's stronger suggestion. These are simultaneously competent and diverse (several different named strategies), giving the learner a meaningful curriculum from episode 0 rather than either noise or a degenerate greedy trap.
The reusable shape of this trap

"A greedy policy over an untrained or random function is not automatically a random baseline" generalizes well past self-play. Anywhere code substitutes "hasn't learned yet" for "behaves like noise" — an untrained classifier used as a control group, an unfitted model used as a null hypothesis — the same gap can hide: the thing that's supposed to represent variety may in fact be a single, silently repeatable answer.

sections.heading: The one-paragraph restatement
sections.sourceHtml:
The one-paragraph restatement

Phase 6's plan-as-written computes every car's race position purely by sorting cumulative total_time, ascending — there is no constraint anywhere in the dynamics that a car following closely behind another is ever actually held up by it. Under that model, pitting before a rival gains exactly as much track position as pitting whenever you simply happen to be faster: there is nothing for "the timing of a pit stop relative to a rival's" to add on top of "being faster," because being ahead or behind on track never costs or saves any time purely by virtue of position. An undercut and "being faster" collapse into the same event.

sections.heading: The mechanical consequence for self-play, spelled out
sections.sourceHtml:
The mechanical consequence for self-play, spelled out

Train 20,000 self-play episodes against a position model with no blocking constraint, and there is structurally no reward signal that could ever teach either learning agent that pitting before a rival — rather than merely pitting whenever faster — has any distinct value of its own. The real plan's headline Definition of Done — a bimodal pit-timing histogram, with peaks at small negative (undercut) and small positive (overcut) deltas relative to a rival's pit lap — cannot appear, no matter how well the self-play mechanics (pages 01–05) otherwise converge, because the simulated world contains no mechanism whose presence such a histogram could even be evidence of.

sections.heading: A misdiagnosis worth naming directly
sections.sourceHtml:
A misdiagnosis worth naming directly

The real plan's own Risks table, written before this gap was found, lists "Undercut doesn't emerge" as a risk and suggests two fixes: increasing checkpoint frequency, and checking the out-lap warmup penalty. Both are worth naming as misdiagnoses. More frequent checkpoints and better recency tuning (page 03) address non-stationarity — they change how good an opponent's learned policy is, not what the environment's dynamics make possible for either agent to learn in the first place. The out-lap warmup penalty is implemented correctly elsewhere in the codebase and was never the cause. Neither fix touches the actual gap: a reward signal for "timing your pit relative to a rival" that does not structurally exist until Phase 6's dynamics gain a blocking constraint.

sections.heading: The fix, restated
sections.sourceHtml:
The fix, restated

if gap_to_car_ahead < OVERTAKE_ATTEMPT_GAP and not overtake_succeeded: lap_time = max(own_lap_time, car_ahead_lap_time + dirty_air_penalty(gap))

One line, added to Phase 6's multi-car lap-time model — not anything in Phase 8's own files. Once a trailing car within range of the car ahead is capped at that car's pace (plus the dirty-air cost) unless it has actually overtaken, being behind carries a real, ongoing cost that only an overtake ends — and pitting before a rival to force them into exactly that situation becomes a strategy with something to gain, not merely a synonym for having a faster car.

Reading the real plan's own Prerequisites section correctly

The real plan lists "Phase 6 complete" as a prerequisite. Per this page's argument, that line should be read as "Phase 6 complete and this blocking constraint added," not merely "Phase 6's files exist and its own listed tests pass" — Phase 6's originally-listed tests, worked through on Phase 6 page 10 (assumed background), don't check for this constraint at all, so passing them is no evidence it's present. Confirm the blocking-model test from Phase 6's Definition of Done actually passes before starting any of this phase's training runs.

sections.heading: The real plan's analysis, restated
sections.sourceHtml:
The real plan's analysis, restated

For every pit stop the trained agent makes, record the signed lap-gap to the nearest rival pit stop (agent's pit lap minus rival's pit lap), across many evaluation episodes. Plot a histogram of these deltas. Look for peaks at small negative deltas (the agent pits shortly before the rival — an undercut) and small positive deltas (shortly after — an overcut), with a dip near zero (pitting at the same time as the rival, which neither strategy actually is).

sections.heading: Why "looks bimodal" is a weaker claim than it sounds
sections.sourceHtml:
Why "looks bimodal" is a weaker claim than it sounds

Pit laps for both cars are already clustered near a handful of preferred stint lengths, independent of any interaction between them — Phase 0's calibration (assumed background) produces a preferred tyre window regardless of what any other car on track is doing. If both cars independently prefer pitting in, say, laps 18–22, then a good fraction of their pit-lap deltas will land near zero-ish values purely from two cars separately following similar schedules — with no dip at zero and no genuine bimodality required for that clustering to appear. A histogram that shows structure near small deltas is therefore consistent with reactive undercut/overcut behavior, but it does not, on its own, rule out "both cars just like similar lap windows."

sections.heading: A concrete null baseline: shuffle the pairing
sections.sourceHtml:
A concrete null baseline: shuffle the pairing

Take the exact same recorded lists — this agent's pit laps across all evaluation episodes, and the rival's pit laps across those same episodes — but break the real pairing between them: shuffle which episode's rival-pit-lap list each agent-pit-lap is compared against, so the agent's pit choice in episode 12 gets compared to the rival's pit lap from, say, episode 47 instead of its own actual race. Recompute the identical delta histogram on this shuffled, non-corresponding data.

real_deltas = [agent_pit_lap[i] − rival_pit_lap[i] for i in all recorded pit-stop pairs] shuffled_rival = random.permutation(rival_pit_lap) # same values, episodes reassigned at random null_deltas = [agent_pit_lap[i] − shuffled_rival[i] for i in all recorded pit-stop pairs] # real_deltas came from cars that actually raced each other and could react # null_deltas came from cars that never shared a race — any structure here # can only be an artifact of each side's own independent stint-length habits

Similar real and shuffled histograms weaken an interaction claim for that statistic and dataset; they do not prove independent behavior or no learning. A difference also need not establish causal reaction: scenario difficulty, weather or other shared conditions can affect both agents. Define a numerical statistic, preserve appropriate scenario strata, check exchangeability assumptions and use repeated valid permutations if conducting inference. The two-row lab illustrates pairing errors without claiming a significance test.

Naming the general technique

This is a permutation test by name: comparing an observed statistic (here, the shape of the delta histogram) against the same statistic recomputed under a randomized version of the data that destroys the specific relationship being tested for (here, the real pairing between an agent's race and its rival's race) is a standard, simple way to ask "could this pattern have happened by chance alone," without needing to assume any particular parametric distribution for pit-timing deltas. One technique, one paragraph — not a general course in hypothesis testing.

sections.heading: An addition to the Definition of Done, not a replacement
sections.sourceHtml:
An addition to the Definition of Done, not a replacement

The histogram itself stays — it's the intuitive, presentable result, and the real plan's Definition of Done is right to ask for it.
